66.exam_focus: Expect to name the four intensity domains, the boundary separating each pair, and the lactate and VO2 behaviour that defines them at a constant work rate. Applied items typically ask you to identify a domain from a described time course, to explain the two ventilatory inflection points and the region between them, or to justify why heart rate alone cannot prescribe or police HYROX intensity.

67.title: Hormonal responses to exercise
67.key_concept: Hormones are chemical messengers secreted by glands into the circulation; they reach every tissue but act only where a receptor for them exists. That clause carries most of the physiology. The receptor — its number, affinity and downstream signalling — governs the response, and receptor expression is itself altered by training, so a given blood concentration has no fixed effect. Two signalling speeds are examinable: steroid hormones (testosterone, cortisol, oestrogen) are lipophilic, travel protein-bound and act on intracellular receptors to change gene transcription over hours to days; peptide hormones and catecholamines bind membrane receptors and act through intracellular signalling cascades in seconds to minutes. The trap sits one step further on. Transient post-session rises in testosterone and growth hormone are real and easy to measure, but they predict subsequent hypertrophy and strength gain poorly or not at all — mechanical tension, effort close to failure and accumulated volume-load are the established drivers. Endocrinology earns its place in HYROX coaching through sleep, total stress load, fuelling and acute readiness, not through chasing spikes.
key_facts: The endocrine signal is only one input, and not the decisive one for the muscle. A loaded fibre responds mainly to LOCAL messages — mechanotransduction at the sarcolemma and costameres, autocrine/paracrine growth factors, satellite-cell and immune signalling — which act only on the fibres that did the work. Circulating hormones bathe every tissue equally, which is precisely why they cannot explain why only the trained limb grows.

The receptor, not the ligand alone, sets the response: number, affinity and post-receptor signalling all matter, and all are modifiable. Androgen-receptor content in loaded skeletal muscle responds to resistance training, though the time course is untidy — several studies report a fall in the hours immediately after a session followed by a rise over the following days, so a single time-point measurement is easy to over-read.

Read the acute profile as information about the session, not as the adaptation to it. Central drive and the contracting muscle both signal the endocrine glands, and what is released encodes two things at once: the degree of physiological disturbance (the catecholamine and cortisol arm) and the metabolic state of the work (the insulin/glucagon arm — insulin falling and glucagon rising as exercise draws on blood glucose). That is precisely why an acute hormone measurement is a decent index of what a session cost and a poor predictor of what it will build.

Speed distinction (a favourite exam item): steroid → lipophilic → crosses the membrane → intracellular/nuclear receptor → altered gene transcription → new protein, hours to days. Peptide (GH, IGF-1, insulin) and catecholamine → membrane receptor → intracellular signalling cascade — cAMP for catecholamines via G-protein-coupled receptors, JAK/STAT for GH, receptor tyrosine kinase and PI3K-Akt for insulin and IGF-1 — → existing proteins switched on or off, seconds to minutes. Catecholamines are fast because they modify proteins that already exist; steroids are slow because they build new ones.

Testosterone comes predominantly from the Leydig cells of the testes in men, with a small adrenal-cortical contribution (about 5%); in women the ovaries and the adrenal cortex both contribute, much of it via peripheral conversion of androgen precursors, with circulating concentrations typically about an order of magnitude lower. Its actions extend well beyond the training response: androgen signalling drives development of reproductive tissue and secondary sexual characteristics, and across adult life it is a maintenance signal for skeletal muscle and for bone — androgen deficiency is associated with reduced bone mineral density in both sexes, which is why a low reading alongside a bone stress injury is a referral trigger rather than a curiosity. It is lipophilic, so roughly 96–99% travels bound — loosely to albumin, tightly to sex hormone-binding globulin (SHBG) — leaving only a few per cent free (commonly quoted as 1–4%, typically about 2% in men, with real assay and population variation). Carrier binding slows hepatic and renal clearance and damps swings in the free concentration; because albumin binding is weak, albumin-bound hormone is conventionally counted as bioavailable, so 'bioavailable' is a wider category than 'free'. Total testosterone counts free plus bound; free testosterone (the unbound fraction) and bioavailable testosterone (free plus the loosely albumin-bound fraction, which dissociates readily and is accessible to tissue) are separate measurements again, and the three can move differently when SHBG shifts. Circulating testosterone also follows a diurnal rhythm that is HIGHEST in the early morning and drifts down across the day.

Heavy, large-muscle-mass, moderate-to-high-volume resistance work produces a transient rise in circulating testosterone, generally peaking around the end of the session and settling back toward baseline within roughly an hour. The size of the excursion scales with muscle mass recruited, load — the protocols that reliably produce it use heavy work, commonly cited above roughly 85% 1RM, though the response is graded rather than a threshold — and total work completed; training status matters too, with experienced lifters (often quoted as beyond about two years of consistent resistance training) showing larger responses than novices, largely because they can actually complete that kind of session. Note precisely what this describes: the conditions that move the hormone, not the conditions that build the muscle. The acute rise is far smaller in women — yet women hypertrophy at broadly similar RELATIVE rates to men, which was an early clue that the spike is not the mechanism.

The acute anabolic hormone hypothesis is not supported. Post-exercise elevations in testosterone, GH and IGF-1 have repeatedly failed to predict subsequent hypertrophy or strength gain (West, Phillips and colleagues, and the replications and reviews that followed); one analysis even reported the acute CORTISOL response as a weak positive correlate of lean-mass change, the opposite of a simple anabolic/catabolic model. The honest boundary: this refutes acute ripples inside the normal range, not testosterone itself — sustained supraphysiological concentrations from exogenous administration clearly increase muscle size and strength, even without training. Weeks of markedly elevated concentration and an excursion lasting tens of minutes to about an hour are different phenomena. Rest intervals are the clearest test case: short inter-set rest (roughly 30–60 s) reliably produces a LARGER acute GH response than long rest, and often though less consistently a larger testosterone response, yet controlled trials comparing about 1 min with about 3 min report equal or GREATER hypertrophy and strength with the longer rest, because short rest cuts the reps completed and therefore the volume-load. Choose rest from the volume-load and movement quality you intend to achieve, or from a competition demand, never from the hormonal response.

Endurance training and testosterone: intense endurance exercise can raise it acutely, while some long-term endurance-trained men show lower resting concentrations than untrained comparisons. Much of that work is cross-sectional, and low energy availability plus chronic training and life stress are plausible mediators (day 23 covers the energy-availability arm and the bone consequences). It should not be read as endurance training being inherently harmful.

Growth hormone (somatotropin) is released from the ANTERIOR pituitary under hypothalamic control — GHRH stimulating, somatostatin inhibiting — in pulses, with the largest pulses in the early, slow-wave-dominant part of the night; laboratory sleep restriction blunts that nocturnal profile (day 4). High-lactate, short-rest work produces the largest acute exercise-induced GH release. Distinguish GH's OWN actions — lipolysis and a glucose-sparing, anti-insulin effect — from its growth actions, which are largely mediated by IGF-1.

IGF-1 is produced by the liver in response to GH and is also expressed locally within muscle. It promotes amino-acid uptake and protein synthesis, drives satellite-cell proliferation and inhibits apoptosis (programmed cell death). Circulating and locally expressed IGF-1 are not the same story: hepatic output changes slowly, over many hours to more than a day, and falls with sustained low energy availability, whereas local expression tracks the tissue that was actually loaded. The axis is also not muscle-only — GH and IGF-1 act on bone and on tendon and cartilage matrix, supporting the remodelling that follows mechanical loading, which is the relevant arm in a HYROX build where running volume and the eccentric exposure of sandbag lunges and burpee-broad-jump landings (day 39) both draw on connective-tissue turnover. Note that this is a permissive maintenance role, not a case for chasing an acute GH excursion.

Catecholamines: adrenaline and noradrenaline are secreted by the adrenal MEDULLA, and noradrenaline is additionally released from sympathetic nerve terminals as a neurotransmitter. Cortisol draining from the cortex into the medulla induces PNMT, the enzyme that methylates noradrenaline to adrenaline — which is why medullary output is predominantly adrenaline (commonly cited around 80%). Effects: ↑ heart rate and contractility, vasoconstriction in non-essential beds with vasodilation in working muscle, bronchodilation, glycogenolysis and lipolysis, and enhanced skeletal-muscle contractile function via Na+/K+ pump activation — with arousal and central drive rising in parallel from central noradrenergic activity rather than from circulating adrenaline, which does not readily cross the blood-brain barrier. Release is ANTICIPATORY — it begins before the gun, alongside the feedforward phase-1 ventilatory jump of day 66 — and plasma half-life is short (on the order of 1–3 min), so concentrations fall quickly once work stops.

Cortisol is the principal glucocorticoid, released from the adrenal CORTEX under HPA-axis control (CRH → ACTH → cortisol), with a diurnal rhythm peaking about 30–45 min after waking and troughing late in the evening. It drives gluconeogenesis from amino acids, glycerol and lactate; raises proteolytic enzyme activity and restrains protein synthesis; and is anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory. It is necessary rather than villainous — it supplies glucose across a 60–110 min race and maintains the tissue responsiveness that catecholamines act through. The acute response scales with intensity, total work and how strongly glycolytic the session is: high-volume, short-rest, large-muscle-mass work produces the biggest excursions, and prolonged efforts raise it through the demand for hepatic glucose output. The catabolic effect is not uniform across the muscle either — type II fibres appear more susceptible than type I (day 63), so the force-producing qualities the sleds and wall balls draw on are the ones chronic elevation erodes first. The problem is chronic elevation with insufficient recovery, not its presence.

The testosterone:cortisol ratio is an intuitively attractive index of anabolic-to-catabolic status and a poor monitoring tool in practice. Both hormones are pulsatile and strongly diurnal, so sampling time and the previous day's training dominate the number; inter- and intra-individual variation is large; assays differ; and the ratio has repeatedly failed to predict performance or to separate functional from non-functional overreaching. The alternative is not a better blood marker but the load-and-readiness monitoring set already established in day 6; nothing in the endocrine literature displaces it.
67.training_link: Take four things from this material into a HYROX build and leave the fifth behind. Protect sleep first: the largest nocturnal GH pulses sit in the early slow-wave hours (day 4). Second, audit TOTAL stress, not training stress alone — work, travel and family load drive the same HPA axis, and chronic activation degrades recovery, immune function and availability to train (day 6). Third, fuel to the work done; sustained low energy availability has documented endocrine consequences (days 23–24). Fourth, treat start-line arousal as a coaching variable in its own right — the anticipatory sympathetic rise arrives before the gun whether you plan for it or not, so the job is reaching the line activated but not over-aroused (day 45). Build the warm-up backwards from the first three minutes of the race, and judge it by how the opening kilometre and the SkiErg feel, not by a hormonal rationale. What you leave behind is choosing rest intervals or session times to chase a spike: set rests from the race demand — work under incomplete recovery across 15 roxzone traverses, concentric-dominant sleds and 100 wall balls — and from the volume-load you intend to complete.

67.exam_focus: Expect to separate steroid from peptide/catecholamine signalling by receptor location, mechanism and time course; to state where each hormone is produced and what it does — including PNMT's role in making medullary output predominantly adrenaline, the anterior-pituitary GH → hepatic IGF-1 axis, testosterone's maintenance role in muscle and bone, and the total/free/bioavailable testosterone distinctions. The discriminating item is applied: given a training recommendation justified by an acute testosterone or growth-hormone 'spike' (short rests, exercise order, evening sessions), evaluate it correctly — name mechanical tension, effort and accumulated volume-load as the actual drivers, note that short rest raises the acute GH response while reducing volume-load, and identify the testosterone:cortisol ratio as an unreliable monitoring tool relative to the day 6 approach.

68.title: Thermoregulation & heat strain
68.key_concept: Heat strain is an accounting problem before it is a physiological one. Metabolic rate sets heat production, the four exchange avenues set heat loss, and the difference is stored — stored heat is what raises tissue temperature. Because only roughly a fifth to a quarter of energy turnover leaves the body as external work, most of what a hard-working athlete produces is heat, and production scales with metabolic rate. Relative intensity therefore sets the core temperature an athlete plateaus at whenever the environment can still carry the heat away; when it cannot — warm, humid, still air — nothing plateaus and every extra minute adds stored heat directly. Once skin temperature approaches or falls below ambient, conduction, convection and radiation stop helping and evaporation carries the entire load; evaporation is driven by the water vapour-pressure gradient between skin and air, so the moisture already in the air — not dry-bulb temperature alone — decides whether sweat cools or merely drips. Meanwhile skin blood flow and muscle blood flow bid for the same cardiac output. In a self-paced race the athlete resolves all of this behaviourally: rising skin temperature and thermal discomfort inflate perceived exertion and pull work rate down long before core temperature reaches anything dramatic.
key_facts: Heat storage = heat production − heat loss. Body temperature rises only while storage is positive, so the sign of that term, not any single measurement, is what a coach is managing.

Human mechanical efficiency is low — only about 20–25% of energy turnover emerges as external work, so heat production tracks metabolic rate almost directly. In a compensable environment relative intensity sets the core temperature the athlete settles at; in an uncompensable one — a warm, humid, still hall — storage keeps accumulating and duration matters as much as intensity. Both apply in HYROX: the sled push, sled pull and burpee broad jump are the peak heat-production segments, and wall balls (100 reps in every individual division) arrive when accumulated storage is already highest.

Four avenues of exchange: conduction (direct contact with a cooler surface), convection (heat carried away by moving air or water), radiation (electromagnetic exchange with surrounding surfaces and bodies) and evaporation (phase change of sweat). The first three follow the skin-to-environment temperature gradient and reverse direction — becoming heat GAIN — once the surroundings are warmer than skin.

Evaporation is effective because of the latent heat of vaporisation: converting water to vapour at skin temperature absorbs roughly 2.4 kJ per gram (on the order of 580 kcal per litre). Only sweat that actually evaporates removes heat — sweat that drips off or is wiped away costs fluid and returns nothing.

Evaporation is driven by the water vapour-pressure gradient between wet skin and the air, so it is the ambient water vapour pressure that sets evaporative capacity. Humidity is the usual proxy, but always read it together with air temperature: the same relative humidity is a far bigger problem in hotter air, because saturated air at 35 °C holds around two-thirds more water vapour than saturated air at 26 °C and the skin-to-air gradient collapses accordingly. Air movement matters because it strips away the near-saturated boundary layer sitting against the skin; in still air that layer approaches saturation and evaporation stalls. Wet-bulb globe temperature indices weight the wet-bulb term most heavily for exactly this reason.

Competing demand: cutaneous vasodilation for heat loss and locomotor muscle perfusion for oxygen delivery draw on one finite cardiac output, so heat imposes a genuine cardiovascular cost on top of its perceptual one (see day 65 on delivery, and day 21 on cardiovascular drift).

Behavioural thermoregulation is the first line of defence. In the framing developed by Schlader and colleagues, ambient heat raises skin temperature, which feeds thermal perception and cardiovascular strain, which raise perceived exertion, which lowers self-selected work rate — a chain that operates well before core temperature approaches any putative limit. In a self-paced race it shows up as pacing, not collapse. Core and skin temperature are separate variables, and skin is the underrated one: a measure that lowers thermal discomfort can buy back work rate even when deep-body temperature is barely touched, which is why cold ingested fluid and external skin cooling earn their place in a hot hall.

Field data undercut the idea of a fixed 'critical core temperature'. Measurements around 41 °C have been published in elite road cycling competition (Racinais and colleagues) in athletes who finished and were fine. Treat critical core temperature as a contested laboratory construct; do not teach any number as a safe threshold, and never clear or condemn an athlete on a thermometer reading rather than on signs.

Individual determinants of heat tolerance: higher body fat and higher BMI are associated with poorer performance on heat tolerance testing, higher VO2max and a higher surface-area-to-mass ratio with better (Lisman and colleagues). Note the confound: when body mass AND metabolic heat production are matched, large differences in body fat produce little or no difference in core-temperature rise or sweat loss in compensable conditions (Dervis and colleagues). The field association is driven mainly by greater total mass and absolute heat production, lower aerobic capacity and poorer economy — not by adiposity acting on its own.

Movement economy is a determinant of heat strain in its own right, separate from aerobic fitness: a less economical athlete spends more energy — and so liberates more heat — to hold the same external speed, so economy shifts the thermal load even between athletes with matched aerobic capacity. Technical work on running, ski, row, burpee and sled mechanics is therefore also heat management.

Heat acclimation/acclimatisation adaptation set: plasma-volume expansion (early, and among the first to decay), earlier sweat onset, higher sweat rate, more dilute sweat, lower core temperature and heart rate at a fixed workload, and improved thermal comfort. Induction typically runs 5–14 daily exposures of roughly 60–90 min at modest intensity, with adaptations decaying over the following weeks unless topped up. Day 25 carries this as a one-line definition only.

Heat-illness spectrum: heat exhaustion presents as an inability to continue with dizziness, nausea, weakness and often collapse, but with an intact sensorium; exertional heat stroke is distinguished by central nervous system dysfunction — confusion, disorientation, irrational or aggressive behaviour, ataxia, seizure, loss of consciousness. Exertional heat stroke is a medical emergency: call emergency medical services immediately AND begin aggressive whole-body cooling on the spot — cold-water immersion where available, otherwise continuous cold water, ice packs to neck, axillae and groin, and fanning. Cool first, transport second, because outcome tracks how fast core temperature comes down. Rapid cooling is recognised first aid, not treatment; what sits outside coaching scope of practice (day 1) is diagnosis, medication, and the decision to stop cooling or clear the athlete — as injury management generally does (day 7).

Cooling has reasonable support at both ends. Pre-cooling (cold-water immersion, cooling vests, ice-slurry ingestion of roughly 5–10 g/kg before the start) improves endurance performance in the heat; per-cooling during exercise performs at least as well in meta-analysis (Bongers and colleagues) — its limitation is delivery in competition, not size of effect. In a HYROX hall the realistic levers are pre-race cooling, a shortened warm-up in minimal kit, cold fluid at the 15 roxzone traverses (day 25 covers the drinking plan) and anything that lowers thermal perception.
68.training_link: Treat the hall as a measurement, not a hope. Get your athlete in early enough to feel it: note whether any air is genuinely moving over the run loop, and read humidity alongside temperature — a still 26 °C hall at 70% humidity is a harder thermal problem than a dry, breezy 30 °C course, and cool-gym splits will lie to them. Reset the race model before the gun rather than discovering it on run five (day 16): a few seconds per kilometre off the opening two runs and a slightly softer sled push cost less than the back-half collapse they prevent. Build heat exposure into the final weeks — roughly five to ten easy 60–90 min sessions in genuinely warm conditions, kept away from key quality days — then rehearse the controllables: minimal warm-up kit, cold fluid or an ice towel in the holding pen, and one cold mouthful at a named roxzone (day 25). Finally, agree the emergency plan out loud before you need it: who calls, where the ice and water are, and that cooling starts immediately rather than after the ambulance arrives.

glossary.def: The accounting relationship in which stored heat equals heat produced minus heat lost. Body temperature rises only when storage is positive, so the coaching levers are either lowering production (pacing, economy) or raising loss (evaporation, airflow, cooling).

glossary.def: The heat liberated by energy turnover that does not appear as external work — the large majority of it, given human mechanical efficiency of roughly 20–25%. It scales with metabolic rate, which is why relative intensity sets the temperature an athlete plateaus at whenever the environment can still dissipate the load, and why duration bites hardest when it cannot.

glossary.def: Collective term for conduction, convection and radiation. All three follow the temperature gradient between skin and the surroundings, and all three reverse into heat gain once the environment is warmer than the skin.

glossary.def: Heat removed when sweat changes phase from liquid to vapour at the skin surface. The only avenue that still works when ambient temperature meets or exceeds skin temperature, and the only one that credits sweat which actually evaporates rather than drips.

glossary.def: The energy required to convert liquid water to vapour without changing its temperature — roughly 2.4 kJ per gram at skin temperature. This is the physical reason sweating is such a powerful cooling mechanism relative to the small mass of fluid involved.

glossary.def: The difference in water vapour pressure between wet skin and the surrounding air; the actual driving force for evaporation. Moist air flattens the gradient, which is why a humid warm hall can defeat cooling more thoroughly than a hotter dry environment — and why the same relative humidity is far more punishing in hotter air.

glossary.def: Down-regulation of work rate, and other voluntary heat-avoiding behaviour, driven by skin temperature and thermal discomfort acting through perceived exertion. The first and most powerful line of defence, and in a self-paced race the reason heat shows up as slower splits rather than as physiological failure.

glossary.def: The laboratory idea that voluntary exhaustion occurs at a reproducible core temperature. Contested: field measurements in competition have recorded values around 41 °C — roughly a degree above the laboratory figure — in athletes who finished uneventfully, so it should be taught as a construct under debate rather than a threshold to plan around, and never as a safe/unsafe cut-off.

glossary.def: Two labels for repeated heat exposure that differ only in setting — 'acclimation' for artificially induced exposure (heat chamber, hot room, deliberately overdressed sessions), 'acclimatisation' for living and training in a genuinely hot climate. The adaptation set is the same either way and is defined on day 25; what the distinction buys a coach is that an induction block can be manufactured at home rather than requiring travel, and that both routes decay within weeks unless topped up.

glossary.def: The severe end of the heat-illness spectrum, marked by central nervous system dysfunction — confusion, ataxia, irrational behaviour, seizure or unconsciousness — during or shortly after exertion. A medical emergency: call emergency services and start aggressive whole-body cooling immediately. Cool first, transport second, because outcome tracks how fast core temperature falls. Cooling is first aid; diagnosis, medication and clearing the athlete belong to medical staff.

68.exam_focus: Reasoning from the heat-balance equation — why low mechanical efficiency makes intensity the driver of heat production, why evaporation becomes the only useful avenue in a warm hall, and why the skin-to-air vapour-pressure gradient rather than dry-bulb temperature governs it — and then applying behavioural thermoregulation, the individual determinants of heat strain, and the heat-exhaustion versus exertional-heat-stroke distinction (cool first, transport second) to a HYROX race plan and to a coach's scope of practice.

69.title: Body fluids, sodium & the dehydration evidence
69.key_concept: Water is roughly 45-75% of body mass -- conventionally about 60% in lean young men and about 50-55% in women, with lower values in older and higher-fat athletes. It is a range rather than a constant because adipose tissue holds far less water per kilogram than lean tissue, so body-water percentage tracks leanness. Distribution matters more than the total. About two-thirds of body water is inside cells; of the extracellular third, most is interstitial and only a minority is plasma. Plasma is the smallest of the three major compartments and the one that acutely decides stroke volume, skin blood flow and therefore pace. Sweat is a hypotonic secretion -- the gland puts out a near-isotonic fluid and then reclaims sodium and chloride in the duct -- so sweating concentrates what remains: extracellular sodium rises, water is drawn out of the cells down the osmotic gradient, and plasma volume is partly defended. That is why sodium's contribution to performance is mostly indirect. Underneath day 25's practical plan sits a genuinely contested evidence base -- laboratory trials show decrements from around 2% body-mass loss, field data often do not, and a coach should be able to name why the two disagree.
key_facts: Total body water is roughly 45-75% of body mass -- conventionally about 60% in lean young men and about 50-55% in women, with lower values in older and higher-fat athletes. It varies with age (it declines), sex (lower on average in women, largely via body composition) and adiposity -- adipose tissue is markedly lower in water content per kilogram than lean tissue, so body-water percentage tracks leanness.

Two athletes of identical mass therefore do not have identical reserves: the same absolute sweat loss represents a larger fraction of total body water in the higher-body-fat athlete, so a 2%-of-body-mass rule is not an equally severe stress for both.

Teach the compartments as FRACTIONS, not as one person's litres: about two-thirds of total body water is intracellular; the extracellular third is mostly interstitial and plasma, splitting roughly three-quarters to one-quarter once the small transcellular fraction (synovial, cerebrospinal, gastrointestinal and ocular secretions) is set aside. Textbook litre figures describe a reference individual only.

Plasma is the smallest of the three MAJOR compartments (transcellular fluid aside, which is smaller still but is not a circulating reserve) and the acutely decisive one -- it is the fluid that sets circulating volume, so small absolute shifts out of plasma have disproportionate cardiovascular consequences.

Plasma osmolality is defended within a narrow band, conventionally about 285-295 mOsm/kg. Sodium with its accompanying anions is the principal determinant of extracellular osmolality; water crosses cell membranes passively down osmotic gradients, so wherever the solute goes, water follows.

As sweating concentrates the extracellular space, rising extracellular sodium pulls water from the intracellular compartment, partially defending plasma volume and hence stroke volume, cardiac output and skin blood flow (day 68). The same osmotic rise is sensed by hypothalamic osmoreceptors, generating thirst and vasopressin release, which reduces renal water loss.

The sodium-potassium ATPase exports three sodium ions and imports two potassium ions per ATP hydrolysed, maintaining the resting membrane potential that makes action potentials -- and therefore motor-unit recruitment and muscle contraction (day 63) -- possible. Its running cost is substantial, commonly estimated at roughly a fifth to a third of resting energy turnover depending on tissue and method.

Sweat is HYPOTONIC to plasma: the gland secretes a near-isotonic fluid and reabsorbs sodium and chloride as it travels up the duct, so whatever an individual's sweat sodium concentration (day 25), it sits far below plasma's ~135-145 mmol/L. Sweating alone therefore tends to RAISE plasma sodium concentration, and sodium loss is not the usual route to exercise-associated hyponatraemia -- excess intake of dilute fluid is (day 25). Duct transit time is also why sweat runs saltier at high sweat rates and more dilute with heat acclimation, so a single test value is not a fixed personal constant.

Sodium supplementation evidence is MIXED. The systematic review by Heffernan and colleagues (2019, ~15 trials, ~385 participants) found roughly a third of trials supporting improved sodium balance, more so in the heat, and roughly a third showing no benefit; there is no consistent ergogenic effect in healthy athletes in temperate conditions. A high-dose pre-exercise sodium beverage (around 160 mmol/L) has some support for improving exercise tolerance in hot conditions. Established roles are indirect: plasma-volume maintenance (Sawka and colleagues), better post-exercise retention at roughly 40 mmol/L and above, possibly reduced perceived exertion in the heat (Sims and colleagues), and assistance with intracellular-to-extracellular fluid shifts (James and colleagues).

The kidney matches sodium excretion to intake across a wide range -- shown decades ago in heat-acclimatised outdoor workers (Malhotra, 1960), where sweat and urinary losses tracked intake. Chronic salt loading in a temperate climate therefore mostly produces expensive urine. It also means a single sweat-sodium value partly reflects habitual diet and acclimation state.

Not all body-mass loss during exercise is fluid loss: oxidising stored substrate consumes mass and releases metabolic water, and water bound to glycogen is freed as glycogen is used. Day 25's field simplification of 1 kg to about 1 litre remains the correct practical tool; the caveat is that a small part of the measured change is not a fluid deficit of the same size.

The proportion of laboratory studies reporting a performance decrement climbs steeply with the size of the deficit -- around 2-3% the results are close to a coin flip, and beyond 4% a decrement becomes the common finding, particularly in hot or still conditions. Even at those larger deficits, cool, well-ventilated, self-paced protocols still return null results, which is itself part of the disagreement.

Field data cut the other way: across 643 marathon finishers, percentage body-mass change was INVERSELY related to finishing time -- the fastest lost the most (Zouhal and colleagues, 2011) -- and long-course triathlon fields show the same pattern, with some finishers well beyond 5% (Wharam and colleagues, 2006). That is heavily confounded -- fast finishers are on course for less time, stop less often, drink less, and are typically leaner and fitter -- so it is evidence that laboratory protocols overstate the field effect, NOT evidence that dehydration improves performance. A real cost nonetheless exists at the muscle: dehydration accelerates muscle glycogen use and raises heart rate, core temperature and perceived exertion at a fixed workload (Logan-Sprenger and colleagues), so the disagreement is about magnitude and threshold in the field, not about whether fluid loss does anything at all.
69.training_link: Measure three things and stop guessing at the fourth. First, starting state: a week of first-morning nude body mass gives a stable baseline, so on race morning you know whether the athlete is already down a kilogram before the gun -- that is the deficit day 25's pre-race protocol exists to prevent, and the one you genuinely control. Second, classify the sweat: white crusting on kit and skin, plus a bad history in hot halls, justify a sweat-sodium test to place the athlete in a band, not to prescribe milligrams. Treat repeated cramping as a prompt to look, not as a diagnosis -- the electrolyte explanation for exercise-associated cramp is contested and the neuromuscular-fatigue explanation (load, pace, novelty) is at least as likely, so review the training and pacing before the salt. Third, plan roxzone intake capped at measured sweat rate (day 25). What you should not do is chase individualised replacement to the milligram, or load salt for weeks in a temperate climate -- the kidney simply excretes it. And tell the athlete plainly that 2% is a planning line, not a trapdoor, so they neither panic mid-race nor ignore it entirely.

glossary.def: All water in the body, roughly 45-75% of body mass -- conventionally about 60% in lean young men and about 50-55% in women, with lower values in older and higher-fat athletes. Higher in leaner and younger athletes because lean tissue is far more water-rich than adipose tissue, which is why the same litre deficit is a different physiological insult in two athletes of equal weight.

glossary.def: A small, separately listed category of extracellular water held behind epithelial layers -- synovial, cerebrospinal, ocular, pleural and gastrointestinal secretions. glossary.def: Solute concentration expressed per kilogram of solvent (mOsm/kg), defended in plasma within roughly 285-295 mOsm/kg. Osmolarity is the near-equivalent term expressed per litre of solution; the two are used loosely but osmolality is the physiologically preferred measure.

glossary.def: The membrane pump that exports three sodium ions and imports two potassium ions per ATP, sustaining the resting membrane potential behind every action potential and muscle contraction. Its continuous operation accounts for a substantial share of resting energy expenditure.

glossary.def: Sweat leaves the secretory coil near-isotonic and has sodium and chloride reclaimed as it passes up the duct, so what reaches the skin is more dilute than plasma and removes proportionally more water than sodium. Pure sweating therefore raises plasma sodium concentration -- dehydration by sweating is a concentrating process, not a diluting one. Less duct time at high sweat rates means saltier sweat; heat acclimation moves it the other way.

69.exam_focus: Explaining where body water sits, why plasma volume is the compartment that matters acutely and how sodium osmotically defends it, then reconciling the laboratory and field dehydration literatures -- naming the confounds on both sides -- without overstating either.

70.title: Movement screening & physical testing
70.key_concept: Movement competency is the ability to perform fundamental patterns optimally, and optimally must mean something specific: pain-free, with joint alignment, muscular coordination and postural control a coach will accept. Kritz and Cronin's model proposes the chain that follows — a muscle disproportionately strong, weak, mistimed or short unbalances the support around a joint, the pattern distorts, and joint function and output fall with it. Hold that as a coaching model for organising observation, not a validated mechanism. In a HYROX athlete the patterns worth watching are a loaded lunge with a rotational component, an upper-body push, an upper-body pull, a hip-dominant bend and gait, seen from front and side inside a fixed 10-20 minute window two or three times a year. The Functional Movement Screen standardises that description usefully; its composite out of 21 does not forecast injury. And because the race demands explosive station work, 8 km of running, sustained high-force output and technique that survives fatigue, mechanical output is sampled separately, in an order that decides whether the numbers mean anything.
key_facts: Movement competency = the capacity to perform fundamental patterns optimally, where optimal is operationalised as pain-free, with joint alignment inside acceptable bounds, coordinated and correctly timed muscular contribution, and postural control held through the range. Kritz and Cronin's movement-competency work proposes the causal chain: muscles that are disproportionately strong, weak, poorly timed or short disrupt the balance of support around a joint, which produces a faulty pattern, which degrades joint function and output. Treat it as a model that structures what you look for — the same faulty-looking pattern can equally arise from unfamiliarity, skill, pain avoidance or limb proportions.

The high-yield patterns for a HYROX athlete: a loaded lunge with a rotational component (sandbag lunges, 100 m of them, arrived at already fatigued), an upper-body push, an upper-body pull, a hip-dominant bend (sled pull, row finish, farmers pick-up) and gait. Observe each from both the front and the side — one plane alone hides either frontal-plane collapse or sagittal compensation; this is the multi-plane discipline of day 10, which also sets out the screen-versus-analysis distinction and the compensation vocabulary the 0-3 scale depends on. Keep the whole screen to a fixed window of roughly 10-20 minutes per athlete and repeat it only two or three times a year: competency is a slow-moving quality, and screening it monthly buys noise. That is deliberately the opposite cadence to the weekly monitoring of day 49.

A static posture screen is the cheapest observation available: unshod, with the ankle, knee, hip and shoulder landmarks visible, and with a fixed vertical or horizontal reference in the field of view so alignment is judged against something rather than an eyeballed plumb line. From the front you are reading side-to-side level at head, shoulders and hips, knee and ankle alignment and foot position; from the side, head carriage, thoracic curve, anterior versus posterior pelvic tilt, and whether the knees sit habitually flexed or hyperextended. Note limb dominance alongside the findings, because small and consistent side-to-side differences are the norm in trained adults and carry no diagnostic weight on their own. The honest caveat, which the movement-competency literature states plainly: static posture is easy to assess, but its relationship to dynamic movement quality is unclear (Kritz and Cronin, 2008), and no better case exists for reading it as an injury indicator. So it is a hypothesis generator, never a diagnosis — anything noticed standing still must be confirmed or discarded in a loaded, dynamic pattern before it earns programme time.

The Functional Movement Screen (Cook and colleagues) is seven tests: deep squat, hurdle step, in-line lunge, shoulder mobility, active straight leg raise, trunk stability push-up and rotary stability — two of which are essentially mobility items rather than movement tasks. Each is scored on a 0-3 ordinal scale (3 = performed without compensation, 2 = performed with compensation, 1 = unable to perform, 0 = pain provoked), giving a composite out of 21; most reasonably trained adults land in the mid-teens and a clean 21 is rare. Five of the seven items are scored on each side separately and only the lower of the two sides enters the composite, so the asymmetry must be recorded alongside the item score — it is invisible in the total by construction. Three clearing tests (shoulder impingement, spinal extension press-up, spinal flexion posterior rocking) are run pass/fail, and pain on a clearing test drops the associated item to 0.

The composite cut-off of 14 or less (<=14) — at or below it, supposedly elevated injury risk — is the single most contested claim attached to this screen. It originates in small, specific cohorts (Kiesel and colleagues' work in professional American football and later in firefighters). Subsequent systematic reviews and meta-analyses (Dorrel and colleagues, 2015; Moran and colleagues, 2017; Bunn and colleagues, 2019) report pooled sensitivity of roughly 0.2-0.3 against a specificity of roughly 0.85 — the composite labels most uninjured athletes correctly but misses around three-quarters of those who go on to be injured, which is fatal for a screen whose job is to rule risk out. Note what is and is not being criticised: scored by trained raters, the composite's inter-rater reliability is generally acceptable; it is the predictive validity that fails. Do not repeat the cut-off to an athlete as a risk statement.

Why a composite fails as a matter of measurement, not just evidence: summing seven ordinal ratings discards exactly the information that carries meaning. A 14 built from seven 2s (mild global compensation) and a 14 built from three 3s, two 2s, a 1 on the in-line lunge and a 0 on the hurdle step (9 + 4 + 1 + 0 — one failed pattern, asymmetrical, plus a painful one) demand completely different responses. The sum also treats ordinal ranks as if they were interval units and gives every test equal weight, when a painful hurdle step and a stiff shoulder are not interchangeable.

The examinable measurement point: a screen meant to rule problems out needs high sensitivity, and its usefulness collapses further when the base rate of the outcome is low. Take a squad injury rate around 10% with the pooled figures above — the large majority of flagged athletes will never be injured, and most of the injuries that do occur will arise in athletes the screen passed, so the flag barely moves your estimate off the base rate. That is how a test can be reliable, respectably specific, and still useless for the decision it is being used to make.

Used properly, the screen is genuinely valuable: it is a standardised, reasonably reliable way to DESCRIBE movement competency in shared language, to structure a coach-athlete conversation about a specific pattern, and to track change in that pattern over months against the athlete's own earlier footage. Record the item scores and the asymmetries, not just the total. A score of 0 — pain reproduced — is a referral trigger under scope of practice (day 1), not a corrective-exercise cue.

Pattern-to-race mapping: overhead position and squat depth underpin 100 wall balls in every individual division and the loaded take-off of burpee broad jumps; split-stance stability underpins sandbag lunges and the sled push, where the sled is concentric-dominant and foot placement narrows toward instability as fatigue builds; shoulder mobility plus trunk stability underpin SkiErg arm drive and posture under the farmers carry; hip mobility and anti-rotation control underpin stride mechanics (days 30 and 33) and limit energy leaks across the carries and the 15 roxzone traverses.

Because the race asks for explosive station work, 8 km of running, sustained high-force output and technique that survives fatigue, one battery has to sample several qualities in a single session (the pillar vocabulary of day 62) — which is what makes the order decisive: reactive and explosive power first, then maximal strength, then strength endurance, and complex multi-joint tests before simple single-joint ones. The reason is contamination, not tradition — residual fatigue degrades a power measure far more than an endurance measure, so an out-of-order battery produces a jump height that is largely a measurement of the previous test. A power number collected after heavy lifting or an erg piece is not comparable with the same athlete's rested number and should not be entered in the log as if it were.

Standardise and ramp: identical warm-up (duration and modalities), identical equipment, cueing and environment, a controlled interval from warm-up to first effort, and submaximal attempts building to maximal ones for both safety and accuracy. Allow inter-test recovery long enough to restore phosphagen availability — phosphocreatine resynthesis is roughly half complete within about 30 seconds but takes on the order of 3-5 minutes to approach completion, so allow at least 2-3 minutes between maximal power efforts and 3-5 minutes before and between maximal strength attempts, with much shorter rests acceptable for submaximal endurance items. Retest on a periodic cycle of roughly a couple of months, aligned to block boundaries, and judge change against the test's own error (day 49).

The mechanical menu, chosen so each entry answers a question the race asks: a bilateral squat or hinge to establish whether force capacity is even in the conversation (back squat, deadlift, front squat); a unilateral lower-body test, because much of the race's high-force work happens on one leg at a time (single-leg squat and split-stance variants); an overhead push, to check force can still be expressed in the position wall balls demand (overhead press, with a bench press if the horizontal push is also wanted); and a pull, to check the same for a hinged, hands-loaded position (pull-up or chin-up, row variants). Power is sampled separately — a paused concentric-only squat jump and a countermovement jump for the lower body; for the upper, a seated medicine-ball throw from a fixed bench position and a short maximal SkiErg effort held to roughly 6-10 seconds (fix and record the stroke count) so that the phosphagen system supplies most of the ATP, since glycolytic contribution rises steeply beyond about 10 seconds and is the dominant supplier well before 30 (day 18). Take the smallest set that covers force, unilateral force and power in both halves of the body, and note that prescribing the lifts themselves belongs to day 37.

Eccentric utilisation ratio (EUR) = countermovement jump divided by concentric-only squat jump, used as an index of how much an athlete gains from the stretch-shortening cycle; values around and slightly above 1.0 are typical across sports (McGuigan and colleagues), and the familiar low/normal/high bands are rules of thumb rather than validated norms. Four cautions: it is a ratio, so a low value can mean a poor countermovement jump OR an unusually strong squat jump, and it does not isolate elastic function; the squat jump is hard to standardise because athletes smuggle in a small countermovement, inflating the denominator; the value differs depending on whether it is computed from jump height or peak power, so the version must always be stated; and it depends on measurement method (force plate versus jump mat). Track it within-athlete against their own baseline, alongside the raw jump heights, never as a cross-sectional classification.
70.training_link: Run the movement screen once at the start of a build and once mid-season, in the same short slot, filmed from front and side so you compare footage rather than memory. Write down three things per pattern: what failed, whether it failed on one side only, and whether anything hurt. Those notes outrank any total, and pain converts the finding from a training problem into a referral (day 1). On a separate day, run the mechanical battery in order — jumps, then heavy low-rep lifting, then the strength-endurance items — with 2-3 minutes between power efforts and 3-5 minutes before maximal attempts, and an identical warm-up every time. Repeat roughly every couple of months at a block boundary, next to the race-specific benchmarks of day 49. Screening tells you how the athlete moves; the benchmarks tell you what that movement costs them across 8 km, eight stations and 15 roxzone traverses.

glossary.def: The ability to perform fundamental movement patterns optimally — pain-free, with acceptable joint alignment, coordinated and well-timed muscular contribution, and postural control retained through the range. A construct about movement QUALITY, distinct from the tissue-capacity screens of day 38 and the performance benchmarks of day 49.

Cheap and easy to standardise, but its link to dynamic movement quality is unclear, so it functions as a source of hypotheses to test under load rather than as a finding to treat.

Five items are scored bilaterally with the lower side entering the composite, and three pass/fail clearing tests can force an item to 0 on pain. Best understood as a common descriptive language for movement competency and a way to track a single pattern over time.

glossary.def: One number formed by adding several ordinal ratings, as in the FMS total out of 21. The sum treats ranks as interval units, weights every item equally, and discards which pattern failed, whether the failure was asymmetrical and whether it was painful — so two identical composites can describe athletes needing opposite interventions.

glossary.def: Of the athletes who go on to sustain the outcome, the proportion the screen flagged in advance — true positives divided by all eventual cases. A test used to rule a problem out needs it high; when it is low, most of the events arise in athletes the screen passed, whatever cut-off is chosen. Distinct from positive predictive value, the proportion of FLAGGED athletes who actually go on to be injured, which additionally depends on the base rate. Its partner term, diagnostic specificity, is the proportion of those who stay healthy that the screen correctly passes — not the training-specificity sense of 'specificity' defined on day 49.

glossary.def: How common the outcome is in the population being screened. When the base rate is low, even a respectably specific test yields mostly false positives, so a flag adds little to what you already knew — the reason plausible-looking screening cut-offs routinely fail in practice.

glossary.def: A vertical jump from standing with hands fixed, using a self-selected downward dip immediately reversed into the jump. Because the dip pre-loads muscle and tendon, it reflects the athlete's combined muscular and stretch-shortening-cycle output.

70.exam_focus: Defining movement competency and stating the causal chain the literature proposes without overselling it; running a defensible screen (which patterns, both viewing planes, a fixed short window, two or three times a year) and reading a static posture finding as a hypothesis rather than a diagnosis; above all, dismantling the FMS composite as an injury predictor on measurement grounds — ordinal summation destroying pattern, asymmetry and pain information, plus pooled sensitivity of roughly 0.2-0.3 set against a low base rate, while conceding that its inter-rater reliability among trained raters is acceptable and its specificity respectable, so the failure is specifically predictive validity — and still using the screen for description, conversation and pattern tracking, with a score of 0 treated as a referral. Then sequencing a within-session battery correctly, justifying the sequence by fatigue contamination and phosphocreatine resynthesis, and interpreting a ratio measure such as EUR against the athlete's own baseline.

71.title: Training adaptation — dose, response & load models
71.key_concept: Training does not build fitness by doing work; it builds fitness by being detected. A session displaces the internal steady state, that displacement is sensed, and the sensing is what switches on the signalling that eventually remodels tissue. The coaching corollary is the whole lesson: the adaptive signal scales with the disturbance relative to the athlete's present capacity, not with the absolute work on the whiteboard, so two athletes completing the identical sled-and-run block are running two different experiments. Load models compress the dose into intensity multiplied by duration — genuinely useful bookkeeping and irretrievably lossy, since a short brutal effort and a long easy one can land on the same number. Recovery is then not one clock but several, spanning minutes to days, which makes "recovered" always a question of for what. The impulse-response account explains why performance dips before it rises without invoking any mystical rebound, and the acute/chronic load charts built on that logic are a ledger to read, never a verdict to obey.
key_facts: Adaptation is a response to a DETECTED disturbance rather than to work performed: the session displaces homeostasis, candidate sensors register the displacement (cellular energy charge, calcium flux, mechanical strain, redox state, local oxygen tension), and downstream signalling drives remodelling over hours to weeks. Because detection is relative, the signal scales with the disturbance measured against the athlete's current capacity — which is why an identical session is a different stimulus in two athletes. Treat the named sensors as candidates rather than a settled pathway; day 42 carries the AMPK/mTOR account and day 72 the intensity-signalling argument.

Training load is conventionally estimated as a product of intensity and duration — day 40 notes there is no single agreed formula, and day 5's session-RPE (rating × minutes) is the field implementation used in the numbers below. It is useful because it yields one comparable number per session and lets you sum a week; it is lossy because two sessions with entirely different physiological signatures collapse onto the same value — 25 min rated 10 gives 250 units and 62 min rated 4 gives 248, under 1% apart on paper and almost wholly different in what they disturb. Every load model built on that product inherits the same blindness.

Training status changes both quantities a coach cares about: how large a disturbance a given workload produces, and how quickly baseline is regained. A fitter athlete tolerates more work before homeostasis is meaningfully displaced AND returns faster; a less-trained athlete reaches the same displacement on much less work and stays displaced longer. Hence prescription must be relative — a fraction of critical speed or threshold pace, a percentage of a recent tested best, a share of today's unbroken set — rather than absolute paces and loads copied between athletes.

Recovery is a family of clocks, not one. Day 4 already frames restoration in four compartments — substrate, fluid and electrolytes, tissue repair, central and autonomic function — so what matters here is the finer resolution inside them and the order it puts things in. Typical orders of magnitude: phosphocreatine resynthesis and catecholamine normalisation within minutes; intramuscular and blood pH within minutes to tens of minutes; muscle glycogen over many hours to a day or more, strongly dependent on carbohydrate intake; autonomic and endocrine markers such as HRV and cortisol over roughly a day or more; structural repair, force restoration and soreness across several days. These are typical rather than fixed, and vary with the session, the athlete, fuelling and training age.

Because the clocks dissociate, "recovered" is meaningless without "for what". An athlete can be glycogen-replete and neurally flat, or feel perfectly well and be structurally unready after eccentric-heavy work. Decide which quality the next session actually requires, then judge readiness against that clock alone. Day 4 owns the four-compartment framing and the modalities used to shorten each window; the contribution here is the ordering above and the prescription rule it forces.

Supercompensation is a teaching diagram — dose, dip, rebound above baseline. The impulse-response family developed by Banister is the quantitative account and needs no rebound mechanism at all: one dose raises two traces, a fitness trace and a fatigue trace, and modelled performance is their difference. Fatigue is the larger in magnitude but decays with the shorter time constant, so the difference is negative early and positive later. Two scheduling consequences fall straight out: train again while the fatigue trace is still high and you stack fatigue rather than net gain; wait far too long and the fitness trace has already decayed. Repeat an UNCHANGED dose indefinitely and note what the model can and cannot say. Because its input is a fixed number that takes no account of rising capacity, a constant dose drives BOTH traces to plateaus and modelled performance to a positive plateau — the model does not itself generate accommodation. Accommodation comes from the relative-disturbance logic instead: as capacity rises, the same absolute workload is a progressively smaller displacement relative to that capacity, so the detected signal shrinks toward maintenance level (day 40) and the athlete stops adapting while the session stops feeling hard. The fix is therefore to restore the disturbance relative to current capacity rather than simply to add sessions.

Be honest about the model's status. Its gain terms and decay constants are fitted retrospectively to one athlete's own performance data, generalise poorly between athletes and between blocks, and become unstable when training changes character. It describes the shape of a performance curve rather than identifying a mechanism, and its "fitness" and "fatigue" are fitted quantities, not measured physiological entities.

Same cycle, two trajectories: when recovery is sufficient the repeated bouts produce a rising staircase, and when it is not the dips deepen and the trajectory declines into maladaptation. What decides it is the stress-recovery balance and the DISTRIBUTION of load, not total work alone. Day 6 owns the overreaching continuum and the fact that its stages can only be named retrospectively — do not attempt to label a stage prospectively.

The performance-management-chart family quantifies the dose. Acute training load is a short-window exponentially weighted average of daily training stress, conventionally a time constant of about seven days, standing in for accumulated fatigue. Chronic training load is a long-window exponentially weighted average, conventionally about forty-two days, standing in for accumulated fitness. Training stress balance is chronic minus acute, read as a freshness proxy: negative while fatigue is being carried, positive once acute work has fallen away. The planning intent that follows is asymmetric: carry a high chronic figure with acute work stacked on top of it through the build, then remove the acute load without letting the chronic figure decay in the final fortnight (day 43).

The exponential update makes the asymmetry explicit. With time constants of 42 and 7 days, a session pulls chronic load toward its own stress value by (session stress − current chronic)/42 and acute load by (session stress − current acute)/7 — the same gap is weighted six times more heavily in the acute figure, so the chronic number creeps where the acute number lurches. Three cautions. That /42 and /7 form is the standard linear approximation to the exact smoothing factor 1 − e^(−1/τ); with the exact factors the sensitivity ratio is closer to 5.7. The weighting is arithmetic from the chosen window lengths and not a measured physiological property. And the daily increments themselves stand in a 6:1 ratio only while acute and chronic load happen to be equal — once they diverge, each figure is closing a different gap.

Read the chart sceptically. It inherits the intensity × duration collapse wholesale; the seven- and forty-two-day windows are conventions rather than measured constants; training stress balance is a modelled bookkeeping figure and not a validated measurement of readiness; and the closely related acute:chronic workload ratio has been substantially criticised on methodological grounds. Days 5 and 39 carry that critique and the thresholds it undermines; nothing here softens it. Use the chart to notice load spikes and drift, then confirm with a repeatable benchmark.

The central adaptation is structural. Sustained endurance training produces ECCENTRIC left-ventricular hypertrophy — cavity enlargement with roughly proportionate wall thickening, the volume-loading pattern — as distinct from the concentric pattern of wall thickening without cavity enlargement associated with pressure loading. The mechanical chain: expanded blood and plasma volume raise venous return and filling pressure, so end-diastolic volume rises and the stretched myocardium generates more force via the Frank-Starling mechanism; a lower submaximal heart rate lengthens diastole, improving filling further; added left-ventricular mass increases contractile force; and reduced total peripheral resistance lowers afterload so the ventricle empties more completely. Treat the volume-versus-pressure dichotomy as a first approximation — real athletes show mixed patterns and effect sizes in recreational athletes are modest. Day 65 carries stroke volume, Q = HR × SV and plasma volume themselves.

What that remodelling looks like in the field: heart rate falls at every submaximal running speed while maximal heart rate is essentially unchanged (it does not rise with training and often drifts slightly down), maximal cardiac output rises, and post-exercise heart-rate recovery quickens. HRR over roughly 60 s is a cheap marker of autonomic control and cardiorespiratory fitness — but a marker only, confounded by heat and humidity, hydration status, the intensity of the preceding effort, caffeine and residual load, so read its trend under standardised conditions rather than a single value.
71.training_link: Three habits follow. Write intensities relative to something current and individual — the 1 km repeats as a fraction of each athlete's own critical speed, the sled as a percentage of a recently tested load or a target time band, wall balls against today's unbroken set — because the same 4:10/km is comfortable aerobic work for one athlete and a severe-domain effort for another. Match the recovery window to the quality you need back: the eight 1 km legs and 15 roxzone traverses need autonomic and metabolic readiness, so a day is often sufficient, whereas sandbag lunges and burpee broad jump landings leave structural debt that outlives the glycogen, and the concentric-dominant sleds cost far less repair than their difficulty suggests (days 6 and 39). Treat ATL, CTL and TSB as a ledger read alongside a benchmark, never as the verdict. The adaptation you are chasing announces itself as a falling heart rate at a fixed run pace.

71.exam_focus: Expect to be tested on what actually triggers adaptation: a disturbance that is detected, sized relative to the athlete's current capacity, not the work performed. Know that training load is conventionally estimated as intensity × duration, and be able to state its central weakness in one line. Be able to define ATL, CTL and TSB with their conventional windows — both windows exponentially weighted in the performance-management chart — and get the sign convention right: TSB = chronic − acute, so negative means fatigue is being carried. Order the recovery timescales from phosphagens and catecholamines through pH, glycogen and autonomic markers to structural repair, and be ready to argue that "recovered" needs a "for what". The likely trap is the two-component model: fatigue is larger in magnitude but decays faster, so the dip-then-rise needs no rebound above baseline — and because its parameters are fitted retrospectively it describes a curve rather than a mechanism, which is also why it cannot on its own explain accommodation. On the cardiovascular side, the answer is ECCENTRIC left-ventricular hypertrophy, with submaximal heart rate falling, maximal heart rate essentially unchanged and maximal cardiac output rising; HRR is a marker, not a measurement. Cross-reference days 4, 5, 6, 19, 39, 40, 42, 43, 65, 66 and 72 rather than re-deriving them.

72.title: HIIT — targets, formats & manipulation
72.key_concept: HIIT is defined by where the work sits, not by the fact that the session is chopped into pieces. The work bouts must exceed the second threshold — LT2 / maximal metabolic steady state, or its critical-speed and critical-power estimates, which describe the same boundary region from different tests and sit slightly above MMSS rather than on it (day 66) — and are separated by low-intensity exercise or complete rest. Bouts below that boundary are interval training but not high-intensity interval training, however unpleasant they feel. The recovery periods are the mechanism, not an afterthought: they make an intensity that could never be held continuously accumulable in a usable dose. Intensity earns its place mechanistically, on two grounds. The magnitude of the homeostatic disturbance appears to scale the signalling response that drives adaptation (Fiorenza and colleagues, 2018); and intensity is specifically implicated in mitochondrial protein FUNCTION, whereas accumulated volume drives mitochondrial CONTENT (Granata and colleagues, 2018). Programming therefore starts from the physiological target — aerobic, anaerobic, neuromuscular — and picks a format afterwards, never the reverse.
key_facts: Definition and boundary test: repeated bouts of work above the second threshold (LT2 / MMSS, or its critical-speed / critical-power estimate — day 66), interspersed with low-intensity exercise or complete rest. These markers estimate the same boundary but are not numerically identical — critical speed / critical power typically sits slightly above an LT2 or MLSS estimate, so state which anchor a prescription is a percentage OF (day 66). A work-and-rest structure alone does not qualify a session as HIIT; if the bouts sit at or below that boundary the disturbance stops escalating — glycolytic flux is elevated but appearance and clearance still balance, so lactate plateaus instead of climbing (days 20, 66) — and you are prescribing broken tempo rather than HIIT.

The boundary moves as the athlete improves, so any prescription written in absolute terms decays. If a block lifts threshold pace from roughly 4:05 to 3:58 per km, reps still run at 3:52 have slid from about 106% of threshold speed to under 103% — the same session on paper, now sitting barely above the boundary and delivering a weaker signal. Re-anchor interval targets to a fresh LT2 / critical-speed estimate every few weeks (day 19).

Mitochondrial CONTENT versus FUNCTION is the most useful single idea here, and the two adaptations answer to different training. Content — mitochondrial volume per unit of muscle — responds primarily to accumulated high-volume, longer-duration work (day 19 treats density as a base-training outcome; day 42 covers biogenesis in the concurrent-training context). Respiratory FUNCTION — output per unit of mitochondria — is more closely tied to high-intensity work (Granata and colleagues, 2018). They are complementary, not interchangeable, which is the physiological argument for a distribution holding both large easy volume and genuinely hard sessions: moderate work under-delivers on both axes, buying neither the accumulated hours that build content nor the disturbance that appears to drive function.

Why intensity at all: the bigger the disturbance of homeostasis, the larger the signalling response that initiates adaptation (Fiorenza and colleagues, 2018). Read directionally rather than as a dose-response curve with a known slope — 'harder is always better' does not follow, because the recovery cost rises with the disturbance and unrecovered sessions cannot be repeated (day 71).

The polarised corollary — stated as a consequence, not as a periodisation model (intensity distribution itself is day 40): if hard sessions must be genuinely hard to produce the signal, easy sessions must be PHYSIOLOGICALLY easy, not merely comfortable, because their job is to accumulate volume without mortgaging the next hard session. The common failure mode is a week of moderate work that is too fatiguing to recover from and too tame to signal strongly.

Know the target before the format — the organising logic of Buchheit and Laursen's HIIT framework, which sorts sessions by the response system they bias rather than by their shape. A HIIT session biases toward three response systems, and 'hard' is not one dimension: AEROBIC — central (cardiac output, oxidative function, high respiratory work) and peripheral (oxidative enzyme activity, muscle deoxygenation); ANAEROBIC (glycolytic contribution, glycogen use, lactate kinetics and transport — day 20); NEUROMUSCULAR (mechanical and neural strain, peak power, soreness, altered contractile function, which is the column counter-movement jump height tracks as a field marker — day 5 covers the monitoring toolkit itself).

LONG INTERVALS — the cornerstone format for HYROX. Typically bouts longer than about a minute at roughly 105–115% of threshold, recoveries of a few minutes (passive or active), accumulating in the region of 20–45 min of work, though the top of that band is rarely warranted and most prescriptions in practice sit in its lower half. Signature: very high aerobic demand — the format that accumulates the most total time above threshold (short intervals can accumulate comparable time near VO2max, because oxygen uptake stays elevated through the brief recoveries; the difference is accumulation versus peak, not a settled hierarchy) — substantial glycolytic contribution because the work sits above threshold, and modest neuromuscular strain (Vuorimaa and colleagues, 2006). Note the anchor: day 19 describes the same session family as a percentage of vVO2max with a 12–25 min accumulation, whereas the format taxonomy anchors to threshold with a 20–45 min accumulation. The windows overlap heavily but do not coincide, so state which anchor a prescription uses — mixing them is how a session ends up either below the boundary or well past the intended dose.

SHORT INTERVALS — bouts under a minute at roughly 110–125% of threshold with recoveries also under a minute, total accumulation in a broadly similar region, in practice often a little lower — roughly 15–30 min of work. Signature: high aerobic demand with a larger glycolytic component and somewhat more neuromuscular strain than long intervals. Their real virtue is manipulability — work and recovery durations can be nudged in seconds to shift the balance — which makes them a good precursor block before long intervals.

REPEATED SPRINT TRAINING — very short maximal efforts, typically a few seconds (roughly 3–10 s), with incomplete recoveries that always exceed the work duration (commonly 15–60 s). Signature: lower aerobic demand, high glycolytic contribution, and the highest peak mechanical and neural strain per effort of the four formats, because every rep is a maximal acceleration.

SPRINT INTERVAL TRAINING — all-out efforts of roughly half a minute (typically 25–45 s) with long recoveries of several minutes. Signature: the highest glycolytic contribution of the four formats and high neuromuscular strain, with the lowest aerobic demand AT SESSION LEVEL (long recoveries mean little total time at intensity, even though a single all-out effort drives VO2 close to maximal). Peak mechanical and neural strain per effort is generally greatest in the short maximal sprints of RST, so treat RST and SIT as the two high-neuromuscular formats rather than ranking SIT strictly above RST. Treat all four sets of numbers as typical prescriptions rather than rules.

The ordering logic is the examinable part, and it tracks intensity and the completeness of recovery rather than bout length alone: as bouts move closer to maximal and recoveries stop restoring, aerobic contribution falls while glycolytic and neuromuscular strain climb. Note the length trap — SIT bouts (25–45 s) are LONGER than RST bouts (3–10 s), so the ranking is not a simple duration sequence. The two maximal formats therefore cost the most recovery for the least aerobic return, which is why for an event of HYROX's duration they are a supplement — useful for peak power, anaerobic capacity and doubles-specific output — rather than a staple.

Manipulation variables: interval intensity and duration; recovery intensity and duration; the number of intervals and their organisation into series; the intensity and recovery between series; plus exercise mode and surface, nutritional state and environment. Mode is not cosmetic — erg, sled and running intervals load the three target systems differently even at matched perceived intensity, because active muscle mass, the eccentric component and the mechanical ceiling on output all differ; the heart-rate and pace-or-power response to a nominally identical prescription is therefore modality-specific (day 65), and one athlete's ceiling on one machine predicts little about another. Heat and altitude both change what the recovery between reps actually restores.

Directional logic, and the catch: raising rep intensity or shortening rep duration pushes emphasis toward anaerobic and neuromuscular; lengthening reps, or shortening recoveries so the next rep starts less restored, pushes toward aerobic. The variables are interrelated — most of them act by changing the effective intensity — so altering one silently changes the dose of the others. Move one lever at a time and judge the session against the target you named before you wrote it.
72.training_link: HYROX is a heavy-domain effort with repeated severe excursions on the stations (day 66), so long and short intervals should carry most of the interval load, and the most specific version is the couplet: 1 km at target race pace into a station dose, repeated, so the interval boundary is a transition rather than a whistle — that trains the demand no erg session reproduces. Budget the neuromuscular column before you spend it: 100 wall balls in every individual division, sandbag lunges and burpee broad jump landings already deliver mechanical strain and soreness, while the concentric-dominant sleds deliver high force at low eccentric cost (day 39). Bolting sprint interval work onto that usually buys glycolytic and neuromuscular stress you have already bought, for little aerobic return. Choose mode deliberately — and anchor each mode to its own threshold rather than to one heart-rate number — then re-anchor interval paces to a fresh threshold estimate (day 19) rather than to last block's numbers.

glossary.def: Repeated work bouts performed above the second threshold (LT2 / MMSS, or its critical-speed / critical-power estimate — related boundary estimates, not identical values; day 66), separated by low-intensity exercise or complete rest; the recovery is what makes the intensity accumulable.
