72.exam_focus: Two traps carry most of the marks. First, the definition: HIIT is not 'any session with rest periods' — the work must sit above the second threshold (LT2 / MMSS, or its critical-speed / critical-power estimate, which are related boundary estimates rather than identical values), and because that boundary rises with fitness, an unchanged absolute prescription stops being HIIT. Second, the content-versus-function split: volume for mitochondrial content, intensity for mitochondrial function, complementary rather than interchangeable, which is what makes 'hard days genuinely hard, easy days physiologically easy' a physiological argument rather than a slogan. Be able to name the three target systems (aerobic, split central and peripheral; anaerobic; neuromuscular) and to rank the four formats on each — aerobic demand falling and glycolytic/neuromuscular strain rising as the work moves from above-threshold to all-out (long intervals, short intervals, then the two maximal formats), remembering that bout length is not monotonic across that order, since SIT bouts are longer than RST bouts. Two hedges worth carrying: long intervals accumulate the most time above threshold, but short intervals can accumulate comparable time near VO2max; and SIT's distinguishing feature is maximal glycolytic strain with the lowest aerobic demand at session level, while peak mechanical and neural strain per effort is generally greatest in RST. Know the manipulation variable set and the direction each lever pushes, plus the caveat that the levers are interrelated. Cite Granata and colleagues (2018) and Fiorenza and colleagues (2018) for the intensity case, and Buchheit and Laursen for the target triad, the four-format taxonomy and the manipulation-variable set — it is a framework for organising prescription, not a set of physiological laws. Present all durations, percentages and work totals as typical prescriptions, not laws. Cross-reference days 19, 20, 40, 42, 65, 66 and 71 rather than re-deriving them.

73.title: Altitude & hypobaric hypoxia
73.key_concept: Heat and hypoxia are the two environmental loads that rewrite an athlete's numbers; days 68 and 69 own heat, and this day owns thin air. The physics is narrow. Air holds roughly 20.9% oxygen at any elevation, so the composition of the mixture is untouched; what falls is barometric pressure, and with it the share of that pressure oxygen contributes. That is hypobaric hypoxia. Day 65 built the cascade from atmosphere to mitochondrion; altitude lowers its first term, and every downstream gradient shrinks in sympathy: alveolar PO2 falls, pulmonary diffusion slows, arterial saturation drops, and the capillary-to-fibre diffusion gradient narrows with it. Because saturation sits on the flat shoulder of the dissociation curve near sea level, small elevations cost almost nothing; once PO2 slides onto the steep limb, losses accelerate. That non-linearity is why altitude bands exist at all. Everything else here — the ventilatory response, the alkalosis it creates, the renal correction, the fall in maximal cardiac output — is the body negotiating with a smaller pressure head.
key_facts: The oxygen FRACTION of air is essentially invariant with elevation (~20.9%); barometric pressure is what falls, from roughly 760 mmHg (about 101 kPa) at sea level. The fall is non-linear with height and is further modulated by weather systems and latitude, so two venues at the same stated elevation need not present the same inspired oxygen pressure.

Hypobaric hypoxia (real altitude, low total pressure) is not interchangeable with normobaric hypoxia (a tent, mask or chamber that dilutes the oxygen fraction at normal pressure). They lower inspired PO2 by different routes and the reported responses — ventilation, fluid shifts, symptom load — are not identical, so treat simulated exposure as an approximation of the real thing rather than an equivalent.

The consequence runs down day 65's cascade in one direction: lower inspired PO2 gives lower alveolar PO2, a narrower alveolar-to-capillary gradient, slower pulmonary diffusion, reduced arterial saturation (hypoxaemia) and less oxygen delivered per litre of blood. The same gradient logic repeats at the muscle: the arterial-to-tissue PO2 difference narrows too, so oxygen crosses into the fibre more slowly at exactly the moment the fibre wants more of it. Note the distinction carefully — the diffusive push into the fibre weakens even though whole-body extraction (day 65's a-vO2 difference) tends to WIDEN as a compensation. Delivery is the term that is unambiguously taxed.

The dissociation curve's shape (day 65) explains why the effect is not proportional to metres climbed. At sea-level arterial PO2 the athlete sits on the flat upper shoulder, so modest elevation costs almost no saturation; once PO2 falls onto the steep limb, each further drop in pressure strips saturation quickly. Altitude bands are a practical shorthand for that acceleration, not a physiological discontinuity.

Conventional bands, and their meaning: near sea level (below roughly 500 m) no meaningful effect; low altitude (about 500-2000 m) small performance loss that largely recovers with acclimatisation; moderate altitude (about 2000-3000 m) measurable loss of aerobic capacity with partial recovery, and acute mountain sickness becomes possible from roughly 2500 m, particularly on a fast ascent; high altitude (about 3000-5500 m) acute mountain sickness common, with a decrement acclimatisation cannot fully restore; extreme altitude (above roughly 5500 m) progressive deterioration rather than adaptation. Boundaries are conventions and individuals straddle them.

The hypoxic ventilatory response is the first defence. Low arterial PO2 stimulates the peripheral chemoreceptors (day 66 owns chemoreceptor control as a topic), and ventilation rises immediately — at rest and at any submaximal work rate — largely through greater tidal volume. It does not plateau on arrival: the response continues to climb over the following hours and days, so an athlete typically breathes harder on night three than on night one.

Blowing off CO2 lowers arterial PCO2 and produces a respiratory alkalosis. Renal compensation follows over days by excreting bicarbonate, which drags pH back toward normal — at a real cost. Less circulating bicarbonate means reduced blood buffering capacity, which is precisely the reserve an athlete draws on for high-intensity work (day 20). Expect quality sessions to feel disproportionately punished during that window.

The left-shift trade-off is the examinable point and cuts both ways. Alkalosis raises haemoglobin's affinity for oxygen, which HELPS loading in the lung where PO2 is low, and simultaneously HINDERS unloading at the tissue where oxygen must come off. Over the following days 2,3-DPG rises and shifts the curve back rightward, partly offsetting the alkalotic left shift — so the working position of the curve is a moving target across an acclimatisation period, not a fixed adaptation.

Get the haematological timing right, because it hides the classic trap. Erythropoietin, released through the renal oxygen-sensing (HIF) pathway, rises within hours and typically peaks in the first day or two, but a measurable gain in red-cell mass takes weeks. Plasma volume meanwhile falls quickly through respiratory water loss and a bicarbonate-driven diuresis (reported magnitudes vary widely with altitude, duration and individual). So an early rise in haematocrit is mostly HAEMOCONCENTRATION, not new red cells — and day 65 already established that a higher haematocrit is not automatically more oxygen-carrying capacity.

Submaximal cardiovascular responses go one way, maximal responses the other. Acutely, sympathetic drive raises heart rate (and lowers HRV) to defend cardiac output despite a reduced stroke volume from the smaller plasma volume and filling pressure. That inefficient early pattern typically subsides across roughly the first week to ten days as peripheral extraction improves and heart rate settles toward more familiar values at a given effort.

At maximum there is no rescue. VO2max falls immediately, driven mainly by the reduced arterial oxygen content. Over the following days maximal stroke volume falls as plasma volume contracts and maximal heart rate falls with reduced beta-adrenergic responsiveness and raised parasympathetic tone (the fall in HRmax is small at moderate altitude and grows with elevation and duration), so maximal cardiac output falls too. This is why hard interval work degrades far more visibly at altitude than easy aerobic work, where a few extra beats can cover the shortfall.

Metabolism and performance shift together. Carbohydrate reliance rises at a matched work rate, driven partly by elevated catecholamines (Brooks and colleagues, 1991; Roberts and colleagues, 1996). Note the practical complication: acute hypoxia also suppresses oxidation of INGESTED carbohydrate — reported at roughly half at a matched absolute intensity, an effect that eases with acclimatisation (Margolis and colleagues, 2020) — so the extra reliance is met largely from endogenous glycogen and in-session feeding is less efficient than at sea level. Lactate threshold occurs at a lower absolute work rate, so lactate accumulates earlier (Clark and colleagues, 2007), and the maximal metabolic steady state (day 66) is likewise lowered in acute hypoxia at 2000 and 3000 m (separate MLSS work). RPE is elevated at a matched pace and aerobic performance falls broadly in step with the hypoxaemia. The reduced-air-resistance benefit to sprinting, jumping and cycling is genuine outdoors and essentially irrelevant to an indoor HYROX race.

What a coach needs that the standard account omits: live-high/train-low separates the two competing demands, since haematological adaptation wants chronic exposure while training quality wants sea-level oxygen — evidence for performance transfer is real but contested and effect sizes are modest. Responsiveness varies substantially and well-documented non-responders exist. Iron status gates any erythropoietic response, so screening and repleting iron before a block is a prerequisite, not an optional extra (see day 23). Sleep is commonly disrupted by periodic breathing, which degrades recovery.
73.training_link: HYROX is indoors and almost every race sits near sea level, so altitude reaches a coach in three cases: an athlete living high, an elevated venue, or one back from a camp. Prescribe by perceived effort first and heart rate second, not by sea-level paces and loads — and sea-level HR zones do not transfer cleanly either: maximal heart rate falls while submaximal heart rate rises, so the usable range compresses from both ends. Treat the top of a sea-level zone as too high until re-tested on site. Expect threshold work to slow and the 1 km splits to drift most; the order still ends on 100 wall balls in every individual division, so an early redline on the sled push is paid for there. Cut load through the early acclimatisation window, lift fluid and daily carbohydrate intake (in-session feeding is oxidised less efficiently at first), and track resting heart rate and morning subjective markers (day 5). The payoff is reading an athlete's numbers correctly when the environment changed — not chasing an altitude effect.

glossary.def: The total pressure exerted by the column of atmosphere above a point, around 760 mmHg (about 101 kPa) at sea level. It falls non-linearly with elevation and varies with weather and latitude; it is the term that changes at altitude, not the composition of the air.

At sea level that is 0.209 x (760 - 47) = about 149 mmHg; at a barometric pressure of 560 mmHg it is 0.209 x (560 - 47) = about 107 mmHg. It sits one step below atmospheric PO2 in day 65's cascade and is the term altitude attacks, setting the ceiling for every step below it.

glossary.def: An abnormally low partial pressure of oxygen in arterial blood, and with it a low arterial saturation. It is distinct from a low oxygen CONTENT, which can also arise from anaemia with normal saturation. 73.exam_focus: Two traps dominate. First, the left shift: an assessment will offer 'alkalosis raises haemoglobin's affinity, so oxygen transport improves' and expect you to see only half the picture — higher affinity aids loading at the lung and impedes unloading at the tissue, and the rise in 2,3-DPG over the following days pulls the curve back rightward, so the net position moves across an acclimatisation period. Second, timing: EPO rises within hours and peaks in a day or two, but red-cell mass changes over weeks, so an early haematocrit rise is haemoconcentration from plasma-volume loss, not erythropoiesis. Beyond those, be able to state that the oxygen fraction is unchanged and barometric pressure is what falls; that submaximal cardiac output rises acutely via heart rate, while VO2max falls immediately through reduced arterial oxygen content and maximal stroke volume, heart rate and cardiac output fall over days; that renal bicarbonate excretion normalises pH at the cost of buffering capacity; and that the reduced-drag sprint benefit is an outdoor phenomenon with no bearing on an indoor HYROX race.

74.title: Periodising skill development — the practice-context ladder
74.page_refs: Embedding Skills in Athletes for HYROX Performance
74.key_concept: Two ladders run in parallel and coaches routinely conflate them. Day 29 progresses the MOVEMENT — load, range, stability, velocity, complexity. This lesson progresses the PRACTICE CONTEXT: how much of the competition environment a rehearsal restores. Five rungs describe that axis — drilling the component pattern in isolation; the intact skill performed unopposed, no opponent and no tactical decisions, but made to survive fatigue; manipulation of the race-day strategic parameters; a race-shaped bout capped below race effort and progressively raised; and full simulation, terminating in the race itself. The organising principle is representativeness: practice should preserve the informational constraints the athlete must act on in competition, and each rung restores more of them. The axes are independent — an athlete can sit at race load and full range yet only ever practise fresh, alone and unhurried. Order matters because each rung reintroduces information the previous one withheld, and a pattern that does not yet exist cannot be stabilised in a noisy environment; hence the top rung is a poor place to teach anything new. Contextual interference — the ordering of variations within a session — is a separate lever, dialled at any rung.
key_facts: Movement ladder (day 29) and practice-context ladder are independent axes. Top rung on one says nothing about the other; state which one you are advancing before you change a session.

Rung 1 — isolated drilling. Build the component pattern away from the implement: for the sled pull, an arms-extended squat to own postural control and trunk/leg engagement, since that is the chain that transmits force to the rope. Run it fresh, with dense feedback and a NARROW BAND of variation (day 27) — narrow, not zero. Even a novice needs the pattern to tolerate small changes in stance width, rope height and grip, because a repetition reproduced identically is not one that generalises. The novice-low/expert-high variability contrast is a tendency, not a rule: expertise changes how MUCH variation is useful and how fast it can be added, not whether any belongs early.

Rung 1 continued — isolate the pull itself against a taut rope. From a loaded squat position with the chest up, the weight carried forward over the forefoot and the elbows long, the athlete stands into the rope, extending hips and knees and settling the trunk backwards without letting the spine round — which rehearses the first phase of the pull and puts the load through the posterior chain. A rhythm progression adds four hard backward strides once extension is reached, with the rope never allowed to go slack.

Rung 2 — the intact skill, unopposed. Unopposed means no opponent and no tactical decision-making; fatigue is deliberately present at this rung. Its whole contribution is that the pattern must survive a degraded internal state, so pre-fatigue the same system rather than adding load: one worked illustration is three rounds of 12.5 m burpee broad jump into 12.5 m sled pull. Treat the numbers as an illustration, not a prescription.

Rung 3 — strategy, not technique, is the variable. Note the terminology trap: this rung is conventionally called variable practice, but what varies is the strategic parameter set, not the movement kinematics that day 28's variable practice manipulates. In HYROX the parameters worth manipulating are set size, pause placement, breathing pattern and, in doubles, the switch schedule. A singles athlete might rehearse a brief controlled-breathing pause every few pulls to hold momentum; a pair might rehearse a three- or four-pull switch so the sled never comes to rest between partners and the changeover costs as little time as possible.

Rung 3 is where a doubles pair rehearses the handover as a skill in its own right — grip release, position of the incoming partner, rope tension across the exchange — not as an incidental byproduct of taking turns.

Rung 4 — reduced-intensity context rehearsal. The station is approached and left at running pace, with a working set completed to a nominated strategy in between, and the whole bout capped below race effort so the athlete retains spare attention for execution quality and for the transitions either side: the target is context, not conditioning. Context and intensity are then raised progressively within this rung — low toward high — but only once entry, stated strategy and exit are reliable. Adding an opponent restores the reactive, self-regulating demand a solo rehearsal removes.

Rung 5 — full simulation, solo or doubles, and ultimately the race itself. It rehearses the parts athletes rarely practise: entry to the station, the roxzone transitions either side, and in-race decision-making. It is defined by whole-race structure, not by pace — a single station bout run at race pace is not a simulation, just a rung-4 bout run at the wrong intensity. Day 49 treats simulations as a TESTING tool; the same session used for skill rehearsal serves a different purpose, which changes what you measure and how often you run it. Declare the intent beforehand.

Why the order holds: early learners need dense feedback and a stable environment to build a pattern at all (days 27, 28); competent learners need the unpredictability that makes a skill robust and transferable. The ladder is therefore a representativeness continuum, not a contextual-interference schedule — interference is a distinct manipulation of practice ORDER (blocked versus interleaved) that can be raised or lowered independently at any rung.

Contextual interference has a counter-intuitive signature: higher-interference, more variable practice makes PERFORMANCE look worse inside the session while making LEARNING — retention and transfer measured on a later day — better. Low-interference blocked practice does the reverse: it flatters the session and under-delivers on race day. So rungs 3 and 4 are judged on whether the pattern holds when revisited in a later session, never on how good it looked on the day. A coach who demotes an athlete because the first fatigued or opposed rehearsal looked scrappy has misread the design working as intended.

Periodisation shape — lower rungs dominate general preparation when time is plentiful and competition is distant; middle rungs dominate specific preparation; upper rungs cluster in the weeks before racing, but never so close that a full simulation compromises the taper (day 43).

Track a rung PER SKILL, not per athlete. Someone can sit at race-context rehearsal on the SkiErg and at isolated drilling on the sled pull in the same week, because the race alternates 8 × 1 km runs with eight stations in fixed order (SkiErg, sled push, sled pull, burpee broad jump, row, farmers carry, sandbag lunges, wall balls), one run before each station, and competence across them is rarely even. Skills also regress: a rung revisited after illness, travel or a lay-off is maintenance rather than failure, and re-entry usually costs far less time than the first ascent.

Sled pull rewards this treatment more than most stations: it is technical, high-force, unfamiliar to almost every novice, worked hand-over-hand from a marked box, and — like both sleds — concentric-dominant (day 11), so it produces little next-day soreness. The conclusion to draw from that is a training one, not a safety one: the pattern can be rehearsed often without the recovery cost of eccentric-heavy lifting. The real risk on this station is position under high horizontal force — a flexed, over-reaching spine and a broken tension chain cost time first and load the low back second. Wall balls (100 reps in every individual division) sit last and reward the same ladder for the opposite reason: sheer fatigue exposure.
74.training_link: For a novice's first weeks, spend most of the skill budget on the bottom two rungs and be explicit that you are doing so. Put the pattern work early in the session while the athlete is fresh, one external cue at a time, with a narrow band of variation, then let a short fatigue pairing test whether it holds. Do not run a full simulation to 'see where they are' — you will only watch a pattern that does not yet exist get grooved under load. Move up a rung on an observable technical criterion probed under the condition the next rung imposes — rope tension maintained and spine neutral across every pull of a 12.5 m length taken immediately after burpee broad jumps, on two consecutive sessions — never on a date. Write the criterion down before the block starts, track a separate rung for each station, and judge the upper rungs by whether the pattern survives into a later session rather than by how tidy it looked on the day.

74.exam_focus: Expect to be asked to separate the movement progression from the practice-context progression, and to justify the sequence: isolated drilling → the intact skill unopposed but fatigued → strategic variation → race-shaped rehearsal below race intensity → full simulation and the race. Be able to work a station example (sled pull is the canonical one) through all five rungs and to name each rung's distinctive contribution — in particular that 'unopposed' means without an opponent rather than without fatigue, that rung-4 intensity is deliberately submaximal and is raised only late within that rung, and that the top rung is defined by whole-race structure rather than by pace. Know that contextual interference is a separate lever (practice order, not representativeness) and that it depresses in-session performance while improving retention and transfer, so upper-rung sessions are judged on a later day. Know too that the ladder is distributed across a season, tracked per skill, gated by observable technical criteria rather than dates, and that a simulation must be declared as rehearsal or as testing (day 49).

75.title: Proximal power in running — pelvis, shoulder girdle & the diagonal
75.page_refs: Running Biomechanics and Technique for HYROX Performance
75.key_concept: Treat the pelvis and trunk as the segment that initiates running movement and the limbs as the segment that transmits it. State plainly what this is: a coaching model with a plausible mechanism, not settled biomechanics. Propulsion in running comes principally from the hip extensors and ankle plantarflexors, and transverse pelvic rotation is substantially a passive consequence of contralateral leg swing rather than a primary propulsive action — the physics of a golf swing does not transfer to running. The model earns its place because of what it changes in the athlete: one cued to hold the trunk rigid and 'just move the legs' is being cued out of range they need. Three coupled components are taught separately and then integrate: permitted transverse pelvic rotation; a swing-side hip that travels up and forward while the stance side is driven down and back; and a scapula that slides on the ribcage to load a diagonal stretch across the trunk. Amplitude scales with speed. The movement is small and quick, not large and slow. Relaxation is the precondition, because unnecessary co-activation resists the very movement being coached.
key_facts: The proximal-initiation idea is a COACHING MODEL, not a mechanical equivalence to throwing or kicking. Running propulsion is dominated by hip extensors and ankle plantarflexors; transverse pelvic rotation is substantially a passive consequence of contralateral leg swing. Teach it because it changes what the athlete does with the trunk, not because the transfer from rotational sports is proven.

Permitting transverse pelvic rotation lets the trailing hip follow the trailing foot, which may slightly increase effective leg length and therefore the distance covered per step at unchanged cadence. Treat the scale as a coaching estimate, not a measurement: no per-step gain has been quantified for this in running, and the classical determinants-of-gait account of pelvic rotation lengthening the stride has been shown to overstate the effect. This lesson's calc items use roughly a centimetre per step as a WORKING ASSUMPTION for order-of-magnitude purposes only, not as a measured value. Step length, cadence and their relation to running economy are day 31's material; this lesson claims only that permitting rotation changes one input to that relationship, and it is never a substitute for aerobic fitness or strength.

Two faults to police. (1) Driving the pelvis straight BACKWARDS rather than rotating it in the transverse plane — lumbar extension dressed up as technique, compressing the posterior lumbar structures instead of lengthening the stride. (2) Producing the rotation ACTIVELY: a driven rotation shows as a forced, exaggerated, hip-swinging gait, a permitted one is barely visible. Expect a brief transient of over-doing after the instruction — the coaching rule of thumb is on the order of 10–15 seconds, a heuristic rather than a measured time course — before it settles. That transient is normal, not a failure.

The doing-versus-allowing distinction is the most transferable idea here and extends day 2's attentional-focus material: an instruction that makes an athlete consciously drive a segment tends to produce a forced, costly version of the movement, whereas an instruction that removes a restriction lets the pattern emerge. Permissive cues ('stop holding it', 'let it go') differ in kind from directive ones.

Three-dimensional coupling: the swing-side hip travels UP and FORWARD, and that reciprocal action is what expresses as DOWN and BACK on the stance side — claimed consequences being greater vertical force, self-stabilisation of the pelvis, and a faster forward recovery of the trailing limb instead of the foot trailing behind. Weyand and colleagues attributed faster TOP speeds to greater mass-specific support force applied to the ground rather than to faster limb repositioning, which gives a vertical-force rationale a defensible starting point. Two limits: that work concerns maximal sprinting and does not establish a benefit at 1 km race pace, where surplus vertical oscillation is a cost (day 30); and the specific contribution of pelvic mechanics to ground force has never been isolated. Coach the coupling for the reciprocal action and the faster limb recovery, not as a licence to chase vertical force.

A self-stabilising pattern and hip-abductor strengthening are NOT alternatives for contralateral pelvic drop. Pelvic drop is a real, studied phenomenon and targeted strengthening is a standard intervention (day 10). One route is claimed to reduce the demand placed on the frontal-plane stabilisers, the other demonstrably raises the capacity available to meet it; program both.

Amplitude scales with running speed. Expect and permit visibly more pelvic and shoulder-girdle movement at 1 km race pace than on an easy run, and do not correct a fast-running athlete toward stillness. The tempo target is small and quick, never large and slow.

Relaxation is a performance variable. Antagonist co-activation is metabolically expensive and mechanically counterproductive — it resists knee and foot lift and blunts the pattern. The common field observation that athletes speed up when told to relax and slow down when they brace is uncontrolled and unquantified; report it as an observation, not an effect size.

The shoulder girdle adds a slide, not just rotation: the scapula protracts and retracts on the ribcage. The scapulothoracic articulation is not a true synovial joint — the scapula floats on muscle over the thorax — which is precisely why it can slide, and why a retraction cue can pin it.

Coupling scapular slide with the opposite hip loads a diagonal stretch across the trunk that recoils. Be cautious: evidence for trunk elastic recoil contributing meaningfully to running propulsion is far weaker than for the lower-limb tendons, which day 30 covers. Coach it as coordination, not as a stated energy return.

The posture-cue distinction: restoring a NEUTRAL trunk and pelvis from a flexed, collapsed position (day 33, day 21) is a correct intervention. Cueing pinned, retracted scapulae — 'shoulders back', 'chest up', held military posture — fixes the shoulder girdle and kills the slide. Correct trunk POSITION; leave the shoulder girdle FREE.

Do not coach the by-product. Elite marathoners including Kipchoge and Kiptum are commonly observed circling the hands in front of the body. The plausible reading is that this is downstream of the shoulder slide rather than a technique they are executing — but that causal direction is inferred from video, not established, which is exactly why it should not be cued. Copying a visible epiphenomenon produces the shape without the mechanism — a recurring error in technique coaching.

The pattern needs a baseline of hip and thoracic mobility that athletes who sit for work often lack; conversely, running in this pattern is itself dynamic mobility exposure, which partly explains why athletes who already move well need comparatively little separate mobility work. Screen for the restriction; do not build a mobility programme off this lesson.
75.training_link: Seven of the eight runs are entered pre-fatigued, and this pattern is the first thing fatigue takes: the trunk stiffens, the pelvis stops rotating, the shoulders lock, and the athlete reverts to a short-strided limb-driven gait (day 33). So rehearse it in the compromised state, not only on fresh legs. Add a shoulder-girdle re-set to the existing transition cue stack — one relaxed exhale, hands and jaw loose, let the shoulder slide — for the first 100 m out of each roxzone. Note the conflict built into the race: the sleds and the farmers carry actively train the opposite pattern, a braced trunk with fixed shoulders, and that is correct FOR the station. The athlete needs a deliberate switch on leaving it. Teach the components separately, warn in advance that it will feel like too much and will later integrate, and use contrast reps rather than description (day 2, day 74).

glossary.def: Rotation of the pelvis about a vertical axis during gait, the trailing side turning back as the swing leg travels forward. Small in amplitude and largely a passive consequence of contralateral leg swing; coaching aims to permit it rather than produce it.

glossary.def: The diagonal relationship between one shoulder and the opposite hip during running, which loads a stretch across the torso that recoils on reversal. Coordinative in intent; its contribution to propulsion is not well quantified.

glossary.def: An instruction that removes a restriction so a pattern can emerge, rather than commanding a segment to move. Distinguished from directive cueing by what it asks of attention; an extension of the attentional-focus material in day 2.

glossary.def: The principle that the size of a movement component grows with running speed, so the same athlete correctly shows more pelvic and shoulder-girdle motion at race pace than at easy pace. A coach should judge amplitude against speed, not against stillness.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="40" cy="20" r="7" fill="#ff8fb0"/><path d="M47 16l10-5M47 24l10 5M33 16l-10-5M33 24l-10 5" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8" stroke-linecap="round"/><circle cx="60" cy="9" r="3" fill="#ffb86b" opacity="0.8"/><circle cx="60" cy="31" r="3" fill="#ffb86b" opacity="0.8"/><circle cx="20" cy="9" r="3" fill="#ffb86b" opacity="0.8"/><circle cx="20" cy="31" r="3" fill="#ffb86b" opacity="0.8"/><circle cx="40" cy="20" r="12" fill="none" stroke="#ff8fb0" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="2 3" opacity="0.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Coaching a visible downstream consequence of a mechanism as if it were the mechanism — for example, instructing an athlete to circle the hands because elite marathoners are seen doing so. Produces a mimicked shape without the underlying coordination.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="26" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2.4"/><path d="M17 11l18 18" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M44 20h10M50 16l4 4-4 4" fill="none" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.5" stroke-linecap="round" stroke-linejoin="round"/><circle cx="64" cy="20" r="8" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2.2"/><circle cx="64" cy="20" r="2.6" fill="#67e8b0"/></svg>

75.exam_focus: Expect to be tested on the honest status of the proximal-initiation model (a coaching model with a plausible mechanism; propulsion is hip-extensor and plantarflexor driven, and pelvic rotation is largely passive) rather than on reciting it as fact. Know the two pelvic-rotation faults — added lumbar extension from driving the pelvis backwards, and actively producing rather than allowing the rotation — and the observable tell of each. Be able to reconcile the posture-cue warning with the tall-posture cue of day 33: correcting trunk POSITION out of a flexed, collapsed state is right; pinning the scapulae with 'shoulders back, chest up' is wrong. Know that the scapulothoracic articulation is not a true joint, that a self-stabilising pattern and hip-abductor strengthening are complementary rather than competing (day 10), and that amplitude scales with speed. Know the limit on the Weyand citation — it concerns maximal sprint speed, not 1 km race pace. Calc items work per-step gains across 8 km and must be labelled as modelled upper bounds built on an assumed per-step figure, not measured effects.

76.title: The junior athlete
76.key_concept: Juniors are not scaled-down adults. They are moving through maturation, and the coaching problem is sequencing training to biological rather than chronological age. Two children of the same birth year can be several years apart in maturity, which distorts talent judgement (the relative age effect) and changes what loading is appropriate. The organising model is long-term athletic development: build broad movement competence and general athleticism first, layer sport-specific work later, and treat resistance training as a skill to be coached rather than a risk to be avoided — supervised, technique-led strength training is safe and reduces injury risk. Around the growth spurt, coordination temporarily degrades (adolescent awkwardness) and growth-plate and apophyseal tissues become vulnerable, so volume, plyometric load and technical expectations all need dialling back. HYROX adds a specific caution: it is an adult competitive format with fixed loads, so the coach's job is to modify loads, distances and station demands rather than expose an immature athlete to the standard race.
key_facts: Biological age ≠ chronological age. Sequence training to maturity status, not birth year.
Relative age effect: athletes born early in a selection year are over-represented in squads because they are bigger and more mature, not more talented. Guard against it when judging juniors.
Peak height velocity (PHV) is the fastest phase of the growth spurt and the key reference point for programming; it typically arrives earlier in girls than boys, with wide individual variation.

Around PHV expect a transient dip in coordination and a rise in apophyseal complaints (Osgood-Schlatter at the tibial tuberosity, Sever's at the calcaneus). Reduce impact volume and hold technique standards rather than chasing loads.

Supervised, well-coached resistance training is safe for youth and lowers injury risk; the old 'lifting stunts growth' claim is not supported. Technique and supervision are the safety mechanism, not load avoidance.
Train fundamental movement skills and general athleticism early — running, jumping, landing, hinging, squatting, pushing, pulling, bracing — before HYROX-specific station work.
Early diversification (multiple sports) is generally preferable to early single-sport specialisation, which is associated with higher overuse-injury and burnout risk.
Children have relatively high aerobic recoverability but lower anaerobic and glycolytic capacity than adults; long, heavy lactate work is a poor fit and low-yield.
Thermoregulation is less efficient in younger children (higher surface-area-to-mass ratio, lower sweat rate). Manage heat exposure and drink access proactively.
For HYROX specifically, modify: shorter run legs, lighter sleds, lighter sandbags, reduced wall-ball weight and target height, fewer total stations. Do not default to open-division loads.
Motivation should be mastery- and fun-led; adult-style outcome pressure predicts dropout. Long-term retention in sport is itself a performance outcome.
Safeguarding and the coach-parent-athlete triangle sit above programming: consent, supervision, appropriate contact and clear communication with parents are non-negotiable.
Monitor growth (standing height every 4-8 weeks) as a practical, low-cost flag for entering the vulnerable window.
76.training_link: If you take a 14-year-old into a HYROX gym, start by measuring height every month or two rather than testing a sled max. A rapid jump in standing height tells you they are in or near the growth spurt — that is your cue to cut impact volume, keep plyometrics low and crisp, and stop expecting technical progress for a while. Coach strength as a skill: light loads, high supervision, hinge and squat patterns done well, because that is what actually protects them. Build the general engine and movement vocabulary now and leave race-specific station grinding for later. When they do a HYROX-style session, scale it honestly — shorter runs, lighter sled, lighter bag, lower wall-ball target — and judge the session on movement quality and whether they want to come back, not on the clock.

glossary.def: An athlete's maturity status relative to their own growth timeline, as distinct from years since birth. It is the correct reference for sequencing youth training load.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: The period of most rapid growth during the adolescent spurt. It marks a window of raised injury vulnerability and temporarily reduced coordination.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Over-selection of athletes born early in a cut-off year, whose greater maturity is mistaken for greater talent. A systematic bias in junior identification.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: A staged approach that builds broad movement competence and general athleticism before sport-specific specialisation, prioritising lifelong participation alongside performance.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Irritation at a growth-plate tendon attachment, common around the growth spurt — for example Osgood-Schlatter at the knee or Sever's at the heel. Managed by load reduction, not rest alone.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Restricting a young athlete to a single sport year-round before maturity. Associated with elevated overuse injury and dropout risk relative to sampling several sports.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

76.exam_focus: Given a junior athlete's maturity status and training history, justify appropriate load modification, station scaling and the decision to prioritise general athleticism over HYROX-specific work.

77.title: The female athlete
77.key_concept: Coaching female athletes well means separating three things that often get merged: physiological sex differences that genuinely change race strategy, the menstrual cycle and hormonal contraception, and low energy availability. The performance-relevant sex differences in HYROX are mostly about body composition and absolute strength — women carry proportionally less upper-body muscle mass, which makes the fixed absolute loads of the sled and wall ball relatively harder, even though the race prescribes lighter loads for the women's division. Aerobically, women tend to show greater fatigue resistance and often better pacing discipline. On the menstrual cycle, the honest position is that group-level performance effects across cycle phases are small and inconsistent in the research, while individual symptom burden can be large and very real; so the coaching action is individual tracking and symptom-led adjustment rather than a fixed phase-based template. Low energy availability and RED-S are the highest-stakes issue, because the consequences run through bone, endocrine and cardiovascular health as well as performance.
key_facts: Sex differences that matter in HYROX are mostly relative-strength ones: less upper-body lean mass means the sled, SkiErg and wall ball sit at a higher percentage of maximum for women even at divisional loads.
Women generally show greater fatigue resistance at a given relative intensity and a higher proportional reliance on fat oxidation, which favours the long aerobic middle of a HYROX race.

Wall balls are frequently the disproportionate limiter for women because the 6 kg / 9 ft (open) demand is a repeated overhead throw at a high fraction of upper-body capacity. It rewards targeted upper-body and trunk work.

Menstrual-cycle research on performance is heterogeneous and mostly low-quality; group mean effects across phases are small. Do not apply a rigid phase-based programming template as if it were settled science.
Individual symptom burden (dysmenorrhoea, heavy bleeding, migraine, GI symptoms, sleep disruption) can be substantial and is the actionable signal. Track symptoms and adjust the individual athlete.
Hormonal contraception changes the hormonal profile and often the bleed pattern; athletes on it cannot be programmed as if they were naturally cycling. Ask, do not assume.
Low energy availability (LEA) is the central risk: insufficient energy intake relative to exercise energy expenditure and fat-free mass, whether intentional or not.
RED-S is the syndrome arising from sustained LEA, affecting bone health, menstrual and endocrine function, immunity, mood, GI and cardiovascular health, and performance. It is not exclusive to women.
Amenorrhoea in a training athlete is a red flag, not a convenient side effect. It warrants referral, not reassurance.
Bone stress injuries cluster with LEA and with rapid load progression; a female athlete with menstrual disturbance plus new bone pain needs medical assessment.
Iron deficiency is more prevalent in menstruating athletes and degrades endurance performance before frank anaemia appears. Suspect it with unexplained fatigue and refer for testing.
Pregnancy and postpartum return require individualised, clinician-led progression — pelvic floor and abdominal wall load tolerance, not just cardiovascular fitness, govern the timeline.

Coaching conduct matters: avoid casual body-composition talk, weigh-ins without clinical purpose, and 'lighter is faster' framing. These are the proximate drivers of disordered eating in endurance settings.
77.training_link: Ask the questions most coaches skip: is her cycle regular, is she on hormonal contraception, has she ever lost her period, and is she fuelling the training she is actually doing. Track symptoms across a couple of months alongside session quality and let her pattern — not a textbook phase chart — drive any adjustment; for most athletes that means moving a hard session by a day or two in a bad week rather than rebuilding the block. Treat wall balls and the sled as likely limiters and give them dedicated upper-body strength-endurance work rather than hoping race practice fixes them. If you see amenorrhoea, unexplained fatigue, repeated bone pain or restrictive eating patterns, stop programming around it and refer — that is a scope-of-practice line, not a judgement call.

glossary.def: Dietary energy intake minus exercise energy expenditure, expressed relative to fat-free mass, falling below the level needed to support normal physiological function.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: Relative Energy Deficiency in Sport — the multi-system syndrome caused by sustained low energy availability, spanning bone, endocrine, immune, cardiovascular, psychological and performance outcomes.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Loss of menstruation driven by suppressed hypothalamic signalling under energy deficit and stress. A clinical red flag requiring referral, not a benign training adaptation.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: The two principal phases of the menstrual cycle, before and after ovulation, with differing oestrogen and progesterone profiles. Group performance differences between them are small and inconsistent.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: An external load expressed as a fraction of the individual's maximum capacity. Fixed absolute race loads impose different relative loads on different athletes.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A spectrum from stress reaction to stress fracture caused by repetitive loading outstripping bone remodelling capacity, strongly associated with low energy availability.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

77.exam_focus: Identify RED-S / low energy availability risk from an athlete presentation and state the correct referral and programming response; explain why fixed absolute station loads impose different relative demands.

78.title: The masters athlete
78.key_concept: Masters athletes are conventionally defined from about 35 years of age, though the practical category most coaches recognise begins nearer 40 and the qualifying age varies widely by sport. The central pattern is that explosive and maximal qualities decline faster than endurance qualities: sprint and power performances drop off earlier and more steeply than long-distance performance, which is why older athletes remain competitive in marathon and long-course racing. Strength declines roughly 5-10% per decade in athletes who keep training hard, against 10-15% per decade after 30 in sedentary adults, accelerating substantially after 60. On the endurance side, VO2max is the main driver of decline — roughly 10% per decade when sedentary, 5-7% when active, 3-5% in highly trained athletes and as little as 2-3% per decade in well-trained masters until around 50, after which decline accelerates. Crucially, exercise economy and threshold values are relatively well preserved, so the aerobic middle of a HYROX race ages better than the explosive elements. Training intensity must be maintained, not just volume, and recovery capacity plus tissue tolerance become the binding constraints.
key_facts: Masters status is commonly set at 35+, but the threshold varies by sport (swimming classifies masters from around 25) and the practical coaching category is usually 40+.
Decline is quality-specific: sprint and explosive performance fall earlier and faster than endurance performance. Expect burpee broad jumps and wall-ball power to age worse than the runs.
Strength declines ≈5-10% per decade in consistently training masters; ≈10-15% per decade after 30 when sedentary, and up to ≈30% per decade after 60. Inter-individual variation is large.

Determinants of strength that age: muscle cross-sectional area, fibre-type distribution and fast-twitch recruitment, motor unit number and firing rate, neuromuscular coordination, and tendon stiffness.
Motor unit loss becomes pronounced after roughly 70 and tracks with strength loss, but firing rate and coordination remain trainable — 'use it or lose it' is mechanistically accurate here.

Tendons lose stiffness and elasticity with age, reducing elastic energy return in running and raising injury risk under impact. Strength and plyometric training promote collagen remodelling and can maintain or improve tendon stiffness.
VO2max decline by activity level: ≈10% per decade sedentary, ≈5-7% active, ≈3-5% highly trained, and as little as ≈2-3% per decade in well-trained masters until ~50, accelerating thereafter.

The VO2max fall is driven mainly by central factors: reduced maximal cardiac output, itself driven mainly by reduced maximal stroke volume, plus a maximal heart rate decline of roughly 0.2 beats/min per year.
Mechanisms of maximal heart rate decline include slower cardiac conduction velocity and reduced sinoatrial node responsiveness to sympathetic drive.
Exercise economy and lactate/ventilatory thresholds are comparatively preserved with age. Endurance performance therefore declines less steeply than VO2max alone predicts.
Because economy and threshold hold up, HYROX's long aerobic demand suits masters athletes better than short maximal efforts — but compromised running still punishes lost leg stiffness.
Maintaining intensity matters more than maintaining volume: much of the apparent 'ageing' decline in the research is confounded by athletes reducing training intensity and volume as they age.
Injury risk rises with reduced tissue compliance and slower recovery, so masters programming buys its hard sessions with more recovery days rather than by removing intensity.
78.training_link: With a 48-year-old athlete, the instinct is to soften everything — that is exactly backwards. Keep the hard sessions hard, because intensity is what defends VO2max and motor unit firing rate; buy them with an extra easy or off day rather than by turning intervals into tempo. Put real strength training and low-volume, crisp plyometrics in the week specifically to defend tendon stiffness and power, since those are the qualities decaying fastest and the ones the burpee broad jump and wall balls will expose. Lean into what ages well: their economy and threshold are largely intact, so the eight runs and the aerobic middle of the race are where they stay competitive. Then watch tissue tolerance closely — niggles that a 25-year-old runs through will become the thing that ends the block.

glossary.def: An athlete competing in an age-graded category, conventionally from 35 or 40 years upward depending on sport, typically in competition designed for older participants.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Age-related loss of muscle mass and function, driven by fibre atrophy, motor unit loss and reduced anabolic signalling, and substantially attenuated by strenuous resistance training.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: The greatest volume of blood the heart can pump per minute — the product of maximal heart rate and maximal stroke volume. Its age-related fall is the main driver of declining VO2max.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: A tendon's resistance to lengthening under load, governing how efficiently force transfers from muscle to bone and how much elastic energy is returned in running. Declines with age but is trainable.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The oxygen or energy cost of moving at a given submaximal speed or power. Comparatively well preserved with age, which cushions endurance performance decline.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: A motor neuron and all the muscle fibres it innervates. Numbers fall and firing rates slow with age, degrading force production and fine control unless training defends them.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

78.exam_focus: Explain which performance qualities decline fastest with age and why, quote approximate decline rates by training status, and justify a masters programme that preserves intensity while managing recovery and tissue tolerance.

79.title: The high-performance athlete
79.key_concept: At the elite end the coaching problem inverts. The recreational athlete improves from almost any coherent stimulus; the high-performance athlete has already harvested the easy adaptations, so gains are small, slow and expensive, and the risk of over-reaching outweighs the risk of under-training. Programming becomes an exercise in precision: narrow the number of qualities being developed at once, protect the few sessions that actually drive the result, and treat everything else as maintenance or recovery. Monitoring shifts from motivational to diagnostic — you are looking for early divergence between prescribed and actual output. The elite HYROX profile is a genuine hybrid: the ability to hold near-threshold running for eight repetitions while absorbing eight strength-endurance stations, with roxzone efficiency and station pacing worth minutes. Because the margins are small, the coach's leverage moves toward the non-training variables — sleep, travel, nutrition timing, race-day logistics, and the psychological load of expectation.
key_facts: Diminishing returns: the trained athlete needs a larger, better-targeted stimulus for a smaller adaptation, and the window between productive overload and non-functional overreaching narrows.
Develop one or at most two qualities per block; at elite level attempting three concurrently reliably produces three mediocre outcomes.
Protect the 'key sessions' — usually two or three per week that actually drive the target adaptation. Everything else exists to allow those to be performed at quality.
Polarised or pyramidal intensity distributions dominate elite endurance practice: a large majority of easy volume supporting a small, genuinely hard fraction.
The interference effect becomes more relevant, not less, as both strength and endurance qualities approach their ceilings. Separate incompatible sessions by time or day where possible.
Monitoring must be objective and longitudinal: session RPE and load, HRV trends, morning readiness, power/pace at fixed HR, and — most usefully — performance at a repeated benchmark session.
Elite HYROX performance is limited less often by raw strength than by compromised running and the ability to hold pace on legs already loaded by the sled and lunges.
Roxzone and transition discipline are worth meaningful time even at the front of the field; at elite level these are rehearsed, not improvised.
Pacing at elite level is a modelled plan, not a feel — target splits per run and per station, with a defined response if a station goes badly.
Marginal gains only pay once the fundamentals are saturated: sleep duration and regularity, fuelling, heat and travel management, and equipment familiarity.
Psychological load rises with expectation; performing under pressure and pre-race routine become trainable, programmed content rather than personality traits.
Injury and illness cost more here because the training density leaves no slack. Availability — the proportion of planned sessions actually completed — is itself a top-tier performance metric.
Long-term progression is measured across seasons, not blocks. A year of 2% improvement is an excellent outcome at this level.
79.training_link: With an athlete already near their ceiling, resist the urge to add. Pick the one quality that will actually change the result — usually compromised running or sled-to-run transition — and build the week so two or three key sessions land fresh, with everything else deliberately easy. Set a repeatable benchmark session and run it every four to six weeks; that number tells you more than any wearable. Watch the gap between prescribed and achieved output, because at this level the first sign of overreaching is an athlete quietly failing to hit paces they hit a fortnight ago. Then spend your remaining attention off the training floor: sleep regularity, fuelling, travel, and rehearsing race-day pressure. That is where the last minutes live.

glossary.def: The principle that as training status rises, a given stimulus produces progressively smaller adaptation, requiring greater precision and larger relative effort for less gain.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Accumulated fatigue that produces a performance decrement requiring weeks rather than days to resolve, without the supercompensation that follows functional overreaching.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: A session that directly drives the block's target adaptation. Its quality is protected by scheduling everything else around it.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: An intensity distribution concentrating most volume below the first threshold and a small fraction above the second, with comparatively little time in between.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: The proportion of planned training an athlete actually completes. At elite level it correlates with outcome as strongly as any physiological marker.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A standardised, repeated session used as a longitudinal performance probe, giving a directly comparable data point across a training year.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

79.exam_focus: Explain why programming for a highly trained athlete prioritises precision, session protection and monitoring over added volume, and identify early markers of non-functional overreaching.

80.title: The adapted athlete
80.key_concept: Adapted coaching starts from function, not diagnosis. Two athletes with the same label can have entirely different capacities, so the assessment question is what this athlete can do, what they can do with modification, and what genuinely must be substituted. HYROX supports adaptive participation, and the coaching craft lies in preserving the training intent of each station while changing the movement, load or implement: the sled's intent is heavy horizontal strength-endurance, the wall ball's is repeated squat-to-overhead local muscular endurance, and either intent can survive a substituted movement. Alongside the physical modification sit population-specific medical considerations that a coach must know about and screen for — autonomic dysreflexia and thermoregulatory impairment in spinal cord injury, skin and pressure management, seating and wheelchair configuration, and the higher shoulder-injury burden of wheelchair athletes. The most common coaching failure is not unsafe programming but low expectation: adapted athletes are routinely under-loaded relative to their real capacity.
key_facts: Classify by function, not diagnosis. Assess available range, strength, balance, endurance, thermoregulatory capacity and fatigue pattern in front of you.
Preserve training intent when substituting: match the energy system, the muscular demand and the duration, and accept that the movement itself may change entirely.

Station intents to preserve — SkiErg/Row: upper-body and trunk aerobic-strength endurance; Sleds: heavy horizontal push/pull strength-endurance; Burpee broad jump: whole-body cyclical power with a floor transition; Farmers carry: grip and trunk stiffness under load; Sandbag lunges: unilateral leg endurance; Wall balls: repeated squat-to-overhead local muscular endurance.

Spinal cord injury above roughly T6 carries autonomic dysreflexia risk — a dangerous hypertensive response to a noxious stimulus below the lesion. Know the signs (pounding headache, flushing, sweating above the lesion, bradycardia) and the immediate response: stop, sit upright, find and remove the trigger, seek medical help.
Thermoregulation is impaired below the level of a spinal cord lesion (reduced sweating and vasomotor control). Plan active cooling, shorter heat exposure and more frequent fluid access.
Wheelchair athletes carry a high shoulder-injury burden from propulsion plus overhead training. Balance pushing volume with posterior chain, scapular and external-rotation work.
Skin integrity and pressure management matter: check contact points, transfer technique and equipment fit, because a pressure injury costs far more training time than any session gains.
Boosting — deliberately inducing autonomic dysreflexia for performance — is prohibited and dangerous. Coaches should know it exists and never facilitate it.
Visual impairment coaching relies on verbal and tactile cueing, consistent spatial set-up, and guide protocols; keep equipment layout unchanged between sessions.
For limb difference and prosthetic users, socket tolerance and residual-limb skin load often cap volume before cardiovascular fitness does. Progress running volume conservatively.
Neurological conditions affecting tone, coordination or fatigue (for example cerebral palsy, MS) need session timing built around the athlete's fatigue pattern, not a fixed weekly template.
Communicate directly with the athlete, not a companion, and use the language the athlete uses about themselves.
Work inside the multidisciplinary team — physiotherapist, clinician, prosthetist, equipment specialist — and refer early. Scope of practice tightens, it does not loosen, with medical complexity.
80.training_link: Start with a movement audit rather than a diagnosis: what can this athlete load, through what range, for how long, and what makes them fatigue. Then rebuild each station around its intent — if a standing lunge is not available, you still need unilateral or single-side leg endurance; if a wall ball is not available, you still need repeated squat-to-overhead local muscular endurance under a clock. Screen for the population-specific risks before you write anything: autonomic dysreflexia and cooling for higher spinal cord injuries, shoulder load and skin checks for wheelchair users, socket tolerance for prosthetic users. Keep the training environment physically consistent so an athlete with visual impairment can move confidently. And check your expectations — the most common mistake is prescribing too little, not too much.

glossary.def: Grouping athletes by what they can physically do rather than by medical diagnosis, so that programming and competition reflect actual capacity.
