glossary.def: The physiological and muscular purpose of an exercise, as distinct from its specific movement. Preserving intent lets a coach substitute a movement without losing the adaptation.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A potentially dangerous hypertensive response to a noxious stimulus below a spinal cord lesion, typically at T6 or above. A medical emergency requiring immediate trigger removal and upright positioning.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Deliberately provoking autonomic dysreflexia to raise blood pressure and performance. Prohibited in competition and hazardous to health.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: The load and duration a prosthetic user's residual limb and socket interface can absorb before skin or tissue breakdown. Frequently the true volume limiter.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Replacing a prescribed exercise with an alternative that matches its energy system, muscular demand and duration while fitting the athlete's available function.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

80.exam_focus: Given an adapted athlete's functional profile, substitute HYROX stations while preserving training intent, and identify the population-specific medical risks that must be screened and referred.

81.title: The doubles athlete
81.key_concept: Doubles is a genuinely different event, not a halved single race. Both partners run every metre together, but station work is shared — so the total running volume is unchanged while station volume per athlete roughly halves, and the intensity at which stations are performed rises sharply because each athlete works in bursts with recovery. That changes the physiological profile: doubles rewards repeated high-intensity efforts and fast recovery between them more than steady strength-endurance, and it rewards pace-matching in the runs. The coaching problem becomes pairing and strategy as much as conditioning. Partners must be matched closely enough on running pace that neither is racing at the wrong intensity for the full 8 km, while their station strengths ideally complement each other so the work split can be asymmetric where it pays. Communication, changeover mechanics and a pre-agreed contingency plan for when one partner degrades are the difference between a good pair and two good individuals racing badly together.
key_facts: In doubles both athletes complete all 8 km of running together; only the station work is divided. Running volume per athlete is unchanged from the individual race.
Because station work is shared, each athlete performs roughly half the station volume — but at a higher intensity, with partial recovery between bursts.
The physiological emphasis shifts toward repeated high-intensity work capacity and recovery between efforts, rather than sustained strength-endurance at a moderate intensity.

Running pace compatibility is the single biggest pairing criterion: the pair runs at the slower partner's sustainable pace, and a mismatched faster partner spends the race under-working while the slower one runs over threshold.
Complementary station strengths allow an asymmetric split — give a partner more of the station they are strong at rather than defaulting to 50/50 everywhere.
Changeover cost is real. Every swap has a transition cost, so fewer, larger blocks are usually faster than many small alternations, unless fatigue forces the split.
Agree the split per station in advance, including the fallback if someone is struggling. Improvising splits mid-race under hypoxic stress produces poor decisions.
Wall balls at the end are where pairs most often unravel — plan the break pattern and the swap trigger (a rep count, not a feeling) before the race.
Sled push and pull are usually where a strength mismatch pays most: assign the stronger partner a larger share, since sled time is highly sensitive to absolute strength.
Train together at least some of the time. Changeover mechanics, communication under load and shared pacing are skills, and they degrade under fatigue like any other.
Communication should be pre-agreed and minimal — short, unambiguous calls, because complex verbal exchange at race intensity fails.
Doubles pacing errors usually come from the early runs: the pair feels fresh because station work was shared and goes out too hard, then pays over the back half.
The psychological dimension cuts both ways — accountability to a partner raises effort, but guilt at holding a partner back can push an athlete past sustainable intensity. Manage it explicitly.
81.training_link: Pair on running pace first and station strengths second — if their sustainable 1 km pace differs by much, no amount of clever station splitting will fix the race. Once paired, write the split station by station before race week, giving the stronger partner more of the sled and pre-agreeing the wall-ball break pattern with a rep-count swap trigger rather than 'when I'm cooked'. Train the changeovers, because the transition is a skill and a sloppy swap costs seconds every station. Programme for the actual demand: shorter, harder station intervals with incomplete recovery, run at a shared pace, rather than the long grinding station sets a solo athlete needs. And rehearse the contingency — what happens when one of them blows up — so the answer exists before they need it.

glossary.def: The pre-agreed division of station repetitions or distance between doubles partners, ideally asymmetric to exploit complementary strengths.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="28" cy="20" r="8" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="52" cy="20" r="8" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M36 20h8" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The transition when doubles partners swap on a station. Each swap carries a time cost, so the number of swaps is itself a strategic variable.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: How closely two partners' sustainable running paces match. The pair necessarily runs at the slower athlete's sustainable pace, making this the primary pairing criterion.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="28" cy="20" r="8" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="52" cy="20" r="8" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M36 20h8" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: An objective, pre-agreed cue — usually a rep count or distance — that dictates when partners change over, replacing in-race judgement under fatigue.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: The ability to produce and repeat near-maximal efforts with partial recovery between them. The dominant station quality in doubles racing.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Allocating a larger share of a station to the partner better suited to it, rather than dividing every station equally.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

81.exam_focus: Explain how the doubles format changes the physiological demand relative to the individual race, and justify a pairing decision plus a station-by-station work split with defined swap triggers.

82.title: Self-determination theory & the performance environment
82.key_concept: Self-determination theory is the most useful motivational framework a coach can hold, because it explains not just how much motivation an athlete has but what kind. It proposes three basic psychological needs — autonomy (a sense of volition and ownership), competence (a sense of effectiveness and progress) and relatedness (a sense of genuine connection). Environments that satisfy those needs shift athletes along a continuum from external regulation, where behaviour is driven by reward, punishment or obligation, toward identified and intrinsic regulation, where behaviour is driven by personal value and enjoyment. That shift matters practically: intrinsically motivated athletes show better persistence, higher training quality, greater resilience after setbacks and lower dropout. The corollary is that performance and well-being are not in tension. A need-supportive environment produces both; a controlling environment can buy short-term compliance while eroding the very motivation that sustains a long HYROX build. The coach's leverage sits in small, repeatable behaviours — offering meaningful choice, giving competence-affirming feedback and showing unconditional regard.
key_facts: SDT's three basic psychological needs: autonomy (volition and ownership), competence (effectiveness and visible progress), relatedness (genuine connection and belonging).
Motivation sits on a continuum, not a switch: amotivation → external regulation → introjected → identified → integrated → intrinsic. Coaching moves athletes along it.
External regulation (racing to avoid a coach's disapproval) is fragile and collapses under adversity. Identified and intrinsic regulation persist.
Introjected regulation — training driven by guilt, shame or ego protection — often looks like great commitment and is a common precursor to burnout.

Need-supportive coaching behaviours: offer meaningful choices, explain the rationale for sessions, acknowledge the athlete's perspective and feelings, and give informational rather than controlling feedback.
Need-thwarting behaviours: controlling language ('you must', 'you have to'), conditional regard, guilt induction, and public comparison between athletes.
Autonomy support does not mean athlete-led. The coach still owns method and safety; the athlete owns the 'why' and gets genuine input into the 'how'.
Competence is built by visible, attributable progress — hence benchmark sessions, split comparisons and process goals rather than only outcome goals.
Relatedness is a performance variable in HYROX, where much training is solitary. Group sessions, training partners and community are legitimate programming decisions.
Performance and well-being are complementary, not a trade-off. Environments that sacrifice well-being for short-term output tend to lose both over a season.
A motivational climate can be mastery-oriented (defined by improvement and effort) or ego-oriented (defined by beating others). Mastery climates predict better persistence and lower anxiety.

Practical diagnostic: ask why an athlete trains. Answers about identity, enjoyment and personal standards signal internal regulation; answers about obligation and other people's expectations signal fragility.
Autonomy is cheap to give: a choice between two acceptable sessions, or over session order, restores ownership without compromising the plan.
82.training_link: Notice how you phrase a session. 'You have to hit these splits' and 'here's why these splits matter, and you can run them Tuesday or Wednesday' produce the same training and different athletes. Give real choices where the plan allows — which of two conditioning options, what order the week runs in — and always explain the rationale, because understanding is what converts compliance into ownership. Feed competence with visible progress: keep a benchmark session, show them their splits improving, and praise the process they controlled rather than the outcome they partly didn't. Build in relatedness deliberately, since HYROX training is lonely; a weekly group session is a motivational intervention, not just a workout. And listen for the athlete who trains out of guilt — that one looks like your most committed athlete right up until they burn out.

glossary.def: A motivational framework holding that satisfying the needs for autonomy, competence and relatedness moves behaviour from externally controlled toward intrinsically motivated.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="26" cy="14" r="6" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="40" cy="28" r="6" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="54" cy="14" r="6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M31 18l6 6M49 18l-6 6M32 14h16" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The sense of acting with volition and ownership over one's behaviour. Supported by meaningful choice and rationale, not by removing coach expertise.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: The sense of being effective and making visible progress. Built by attributable improvement, process goals and honest informational feedback.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The sense of genuine connection and belonging within a training environment. A legitimate performance variable in an individual sport.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="26" cy="14" r="6" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="40" cy="28" r="6" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="54" cy="14" r="6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M31 18l6 6M49 18l-6 6M32 14h16" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Behaviour driven by internal pressure such as guilt, shame or ego protection. Superficially resembles high commitment but predicts burnout.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: A motivational environment defining success as personal improvement and effort rather than beating others. Associated with greater persistence and lower anxiety.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

82.exam_focus: Identify which basic psychological need an environment is thwarting from a coaching scenario, and prescribe specific need-supportive behaviours to shift an athlete's regulation.

83.title: Coaching neurodivergent athletes
83.key_concept: Neurodivergence describes natural variation in how brains process information, attention, sensory input and social interaction — including ADHD, autism, dyslexia, dyspraxia and Tourette's. The coaching frame is accommodation and environment design, not deficit correction. Many of the traits involved cut both ways in sport: hyperfocus can produce extraordinary training consistency and also make it hard to stop when stopping is correct; sensory sensitivity can make a loud, crowded, echoing HYROX venue genuinely overwhelming; a strong preference for routine can be a performance asset and a source of distress when a session changes without warning. Practically, the coach's job is to reduce unnecessary cognitive and sensory load — clear unambiguous instructions, predictable structure, advance notice of change, written as well as verbal information — and to ask the athlete directly what helps rather than inferring it. A coach is not diagnosing, and should never attempt to; the skills are inclusive communication, environmental adjustment and knowing when to refer.
key_facts: Neurodivergence covers natural neurological variation — ADHD, autism, dyslexia, dyspraxia, Tourette's among others — not illness or deficit.
Coaches do not diagnose. The role is to accommodate presentation, adjust the environment and refer to appropriate professionals when needed.
Ask the athlete what helps. Self-reported accommodations are far more accurate than assumptions based on a label.
Reduce ambiguity: give instructions that are literal, specific and sequenced. 'Three rounds, 10 wall balls, 200 m run, rest 90 seconds' beats 'just go a few rounds and see how you feel'.
Provide information in more than one channel — written or demonstrated as well as spoken — because processing preferences differ.
Give advance notice of changes to session, venue or timing. Unannounced change is a disproportionate stressor where routine is a coping structure.

Sensory load is a real performance variable: noise, echo, crowding, lighting and heat at a HYROX venue can be overwhelming. Plan arrival timing, warm-up location, and consider ear defenders or noise-cancelling headphones.
Executive function differences affect planning, sequencing, time management and task initiation — not effort or motivation. Structure and external scaffolding help; nagging does not.
Hyperfocus is an asset and a risk: it can drive exceptional consistency and can also override fatigue signals and drive overtraining. Build explicit stop rules.
Break long or complex sessions into discrete, clearly bounded chunks with defined start and end points.
Masking — suppressing natural responses to appear neurotypical — is exhausting and can hide distress. An athlete coping visibly well may still be depleting.
Use the language the athlete uses about themselves, and never disclose their neurodivergence to others without explicit permission.
Inclusive design mostly helps everyone: clearer instructions, predictable structure and lower sensory chaos improve the environment for the whole group.
83.training_link: Start by asking, not guessing: what makes sessions easier, what makes them harder, and how do you like information given. Then write your sessions differently — literal, numbered, unambiguous, with the rest periods and stop points specified rather than left to feel. Send the session in advance and flag any change as early as you can, because a last-minute switch of venue costs some athletes far more than it costs you. For race day, plan the sensory side as deliberately as the pacing: when to arrive, where to warm up away from the noise, whether ear defenders help. And if you have an athlete whose hyperfocus means they never miss a session and never back off, give them an explicit stop rule — they will follow a written rule far more reliably than a vague instruction to listen to their body.

glossary.def: Natural variation in neurological processing of attention, sensory input, information and social interaction. A difference to accommodate, not a deficit to correct.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="26" cy="14" r="6" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="40" cy="28" r="6" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="54" cy="14" r="6" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M31 18l6 6M49 18l-6 6M32 14h16" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Cognitive processes governing planning, sequencing, task initiation, working memory and time management. Differences here affect organisation, not effort or motivation.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: The cumulative demand of noise, light, crowding, heat and touch in an environment. A genuine performance variable at loud, crowded race venues.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 20 Q16 6 24 20 T40 20 T56 20 T72 20" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Consciously suppressing natural responses to appear neurotypical. Highly effortful and capable of concealing significant distress.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: Sustained, intense absorption in a task. An asset for training consistency and a risk factor for overriding fatigue signals.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: A deliberate adjustment to environment, communication or structure that removes an unnecessary barrier without lowering the performance standard.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

83.exam_focus: Given a neurodivergent athlete's presentation, prescribe communication and environmental accommodations, and state the boundary between coaching accommodation and clinical diagnosis.

84.title: The winner's mindset & core performance principles
84.key_concept: A 'winner's mindset' is not a personality type an athlete either has or lacks — it is a set of trainable habits of attention, interpretation and response. The core performance principles that recur across elite sport psychology are: control the controllables and disengage from everything else; focus on process over outcome, because process is what the athlete can actually execute; interpret arousal as readiness rather than threat; hold a growth orientation in which setbacks are information rather than verdicts; and respond to failure with a short, structured reset rather than rumination. Confidence in this model is an output, not an input — it is built by accumulated evidence of competence (successfully completed hard sessions, benchmark improvements, rehearsed race scenarios), which is why it is more reliably grown in training than summoned on race day. Self-talk is the mechanism that connects these principles to behaviour: what an athlete says to themselves at kilometre six determines whether they hold pace or negotiate.
key_facts: Mental skills are trainable and follow the same rules as physical ones — deliberate practice, progressive exposure, repetition. They are not fixed traits.
Control the controllables: effort, attention, technique, pacing decisions, routine and response are controllable; competitors, conditions, sled friction and results are not.
Process focus over outcome focus. Outcome goals motivate direction; process goals govern execution and are what the athlete can act on mid-race.
Challenge vs threat appraisal: the same physiological arousal is performance-enhancing when read as 'I am ready' and performance-degrading when read as 'I am in danger'.
Confidence is an output of evidence. Build it from completed hard sessions, benchmark improvements and rehearsed scenarios rather than from affirmation alone.
Growth orientation treats a bad race as data about what to train next, not a verdict on ability. The behavioural test is what the athlete does in the following week.
Self-talk can be instructional ('drive the arms', 'shorten the stride') or motivational ('hold this', 'you've done this'). Instructional self-talk generally suits technical and pacing tasks better.
Reframing is a skill: replacing 'my legs are gone' with 'this is what kilometre six is supposed to feel like' changes the behavioural response, not just the mood.
A structured reset — a physical cue, a breath, a single instructional word — beats unstructured rumination after a mistake or a bad station.
Attentional focus should be external and task-relevant under load (the pace, the rhythm, the next marker) rather than internal and self-evaluative.
Resilience in practice is the speed of return to task after a setback, not the absence of a reaction to it.
Pre-performance routines make behaviour automatic under pressure, protecting execution when working memory is degraded by stress.
Mental skills must be practised in training under fatigue. Skills rehearsed only when fresh and calm do not survive race conditions.
84.training_link: Treat mental skills as sessions, not speeches. Pick one cue per block — say, an instructional self-talk phrase for the back half of every run — and make the athlete use it in training until it is automatic, because a phrase invented on race morning does nothing. Build confidence out of evidence: log the hard sessions they completed and show them the benchmark trend, so belief has something underneath it. Teach the reset explicitly — one breath, one word, eyes up, back to pace — and drill it after deliberately imperfect stations so the recovery is rehearsed. And when they describe a bad race, listen for whether they are treating it as data or as a verdict; redirecting that interpretation is one of the higher-leverage conversations you will have all season.

glossary.def: The elements of performance an athlete can directly influence — effort, attention, technique, pacing, routine and response. Attention spent elsewhere is wasted.

glossary.def: A goal specifying execution the athlete controls, such as holding a target cadence, rather than an outcome such as a finish position.

glossary.def: The interpretation of physiological arousal as either readiness for a demand or danger. The same arousal produces opposite performance effects depending on the reading.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Task-focused internal cueing directing technique or pacing. Generally more effective than purely motivational self-talk for technical and pacing tasks.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Deliberately reinterpreting a sensation or event to change the behavioural response, such as reading leg discomfort as an expected race marker rather than failure.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M28 12a12 12 0 1 0 12 12" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M24 8l6 4-6 4" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A consistent sequence of actions before a performance that automates behaviour and protects execution when stress degrades working memory.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

84.exam_focus: Distinguish process from outcome focus and challenge from threat appraisal, and design a mental-skills intervention that is rehearsed under fatigue rather than introduced on race day.

85.title: The brain under pressure & calming the threat system
85.key_concept: Under pressure the brain does three things that matter to a coach: it appraises the situation for threat, it narrows and reallocates attention, and it degrades the executive control needed for complex decisions. When the threat system dominates, sympathetic arousal rises, breathing becomes shallow and fast, attention narrows onto the source of threat rather than the task, and working memory — the resource an athlete needs to hold a pacing plan — shrinks. That produces the familiar failures: going out too hard, forgetting the plan, fixating on a competitor, and over-gripping technique. The intervention set is therefore twofold. Down-regulate the physiology, principally through breathing that lengthens the exhale and engages the diaphragm, which raises parasympathetic activity and signals safety. Then redirect attention to the right thing at the right time with a simple, pre-rehearsed cue. Because these tools depend on being automatic, they have to be trained in advance — sport psychology is not an emergency umbrella deployed the night before a race.
key_facts: Three key brain functions under pressure: threat appraisal, attentional allocation, and executive control (planning, decision-making, working memory).
Acute stress narrows attention. Useful when the relevant cue is narrow, harmful when the athlete needs to monitor pace, competitors and their own state.
Working memory degrades under stress, which is why complex race plans fail and pre-rehearsed routines survive.
Diaphragmatic breathing — belly rising rather than chest and shoulders — is the mechanical basis of down-regulation.
Extending the exhale relative to the inhale increases parasympathetic activity and lowers arousal. A longer, slower out-breath is the single most reliable acute tool.
Box breathing (in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4) gives a structured, countable protocol that also occupies attention, which is part of why it works.
A brief body scan aiming to soften tension by only 5-10% is more achievable under arousal than instructions to 'relax', which often backfire.
Down-regulation is a trained skill and a legitimate part of the training week: teach the system to come down as deliberately as you teach it to go hard.
Cue words and physical anchors (a touch of the wrist, eyes to a fixed point) redirect attention faster than reasoning does at high arousal.
Attentional focus should be external and task-relevant under pressure; internal self-monitoring of already-automated technique degrades it.
Not all arousal is bad — the aim is the athlete's optimal zone, not minimum activation. Some athletes need up-regulation before a race, not calming.
Reappraisal ('this racing heart means I'm ready') is more effective than suppression ('calm down'), which tends to increase arousal.
These tools must be practised in training, ideally under fatigue and mild pressure, or they will not be accessible on race day.
85.training_link: Teach the breathing before they need it. Put two or three minutes of box breathing — in four, hold four, out four, hold four — at the end of hard sessions, so down-regulating becomes something the athlete's system has practised rather than a party trick attempted in the corral. Make the exhale longer than the inhale and get the belly moving, not the shoulders; that is the part that actually shifts the nervous system. Give each athlete one cue word and one physical anchor for the race, and rehearse them at the moment they will be needed — entering the roxzone, starting the run after the sled. Then aim for their zone, not for calm: some athletes need bringing down before the start, and some need bringing up, and confusing the two costs races.

glossary.def: The stress-response network that appraises a situation as dangerous and drives sympathetic arousal, attentional narrowing and defensive behaviour.

glossary.def: Breathing that expands the belly rather than lifting the chest and shoulders, enabling parasympathetic activation and effective down-regulation.

glossary.def: A structured protocol of equal-count inhale, hold, exhale and hold — commonly four counts each — that lowers arousal and occupies attention.

glossary.def: The constriction of attentional field under high arousal, which can usefully sharpen focus or harmfully exclude task-relevant information.

glossary.def: The limited store holding information in mind during a task. It degrades under stress, causing complex race plans to fail where rehearsed routines hold.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: Reinterpreting arousal as readiness rather than danger. More effective than attempting to suppress the arousal, which typically amplifies it.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M28 12a12 12 0 1 0 12 12" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M24 8l6 4-6 4" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

85.exam_focus: Explain the three brain functions affected by pressure and prescribe a specific down-regulation and attentional-cue protocol, justifying why it must be rehearsed in training.

86.title: Simulating pressure in training
86.key_concept: Mental skills transfer to competition only if they are practised under conditions resembling competition, which means pressure has to be deliberately manufactured in training. Pressure training adds a stressor — consequence, evaluation, audience, uncertainty, fatigue or time constraint — to a technically familiar task, so the athlete rehearses executing under the arousal they will actually face. The dose matters: too little and nothing transfers, too much and the athlete simply fails and learns that pressure means failure. The aim is a level at which execution is genuinely threatened but still achievable, progressed over a block. For HYROX this means full or partial race simulations with real timing and splits, deliberately imperfect scenarios (starting a run after a botched sled, forcing a wall-ball break at the worst moment), and consequence-loaded sessions. The debrief is the part most coaches skip and the part that carries the learning: a structured downshift back to baseline followed by a reflective review of what the athlete noticed, did and would change.
key_facts: Pressure training = a familiar task plus a deliberately added stressor, so mental skills are rehearsed under competition-like arousal.
Stressor categories: consequence (a forfeit or reward), evaluation (being watched, filmed or scored), audience, uncertainty (undisclosed session details), fatigue, and time constraint.
Dose it. Pressure high enough to threaten execution but low enough that success is achievable — then progress it across the block.
Excessive pressure teaches the wrong lesson: repeated failure under pressure conditions the association between arousal and collapse.
Simulate specifics, not just intensity: replicate race timing, start protocol, station order, transitions, kit and even nutrition where possible.
Rehearse adversity deliberately — a bad sled, a dropped wall-ball set, a competitor surging past — so the recovery response is trained, not improvised.
Partial simulations (a three-station block at race pace) can be run more frequently than full simulations, which carry a real recovery cost.
Full race simulations are training sessions with a taper and recovery cost attached. Schedule them like key sessions, not as extras.
Uncertainty is a potent and cheap stressor: withholding the session details until the warm-up removes the athlete's ability to pre-pace.
Always debrief. Without structured reflection the athlete gets the stress exposure but not the learning.
Debrief structure: down-regulate first (breathing, body scan), then review what they noticed, what they did, what worked, and one change for next time.
Deliberate down-shifting after a pressure session is training in itself — teaching the system to return to baseline is as coachable as driving it up.
Record the outcome and the athlete's subjective experience, so pressure exposure can be progressed systematically rather than by instinct.
86.training_link: Stop running your race simulations clean. Once the athlete can execute the session when everything goes right, start breaking it on purpose — make them start the run after a deliberately awful sled, force a wall-ball break at rep eight, put a camera on them, or tell them the session only at the warm-up. Keep the pressure at a level where they can still just about hold the plan, and turn it up across the block. Then protect the debrief: two or three minutes of box breathing and a body scan to bring the system down, and only then ask what they noticed, what they did about it, and what they would change. That conversation is where the session turns into a skill — without it you have just made them tired and stressed.

glossary.def: Deliberately adding a stressor to a familiar task so that technical and mental skills are rehearsed under competition-like arousal.

glossary.def: A session replicating competition structure, timing and conditions closely enough to rehearse pacing, transitions and decision-making under fatigue.

glossary.def: Deliberately introducing a setback mid-session so the athlete practises the recovery response rather than improvising it on race day.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M28 12a12 12 0 1 0 12 12" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M24 8l6 4-6 4" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The deliberate post-session return to baseline arousal through slow breathing and body scanning — a trainable recovery skill in its own right.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: A guided post-session review — what was noticed, what was done, what worked, what changes — that converts stress exposure into learning.

86.exam_focus: Design a progressive pressure-training intervention for a named HYROX weakness, specifying the stressor, the dose rationale and the debrief structure.

87.title: Routines, journaling & reflective practice
87.key_concept: Routines and journaling are the two habits that make everything else in mental performance durable. A routine is a fixed sequence of actions that automates behaviour when working memory is compromised — pre-race, pre-station, and post-error. Its value is not superstition but load reduction: the athlete does not have to decide anything, so attention stays on the task. Good routines are short, portable, controllable and rehearsed; anything dependent on a specific location, object or condition becomes a liability when a race disrupts it. Journaling serves the parallel function for learning. Sport psychology only compounds if the athlete notices patterns across weeks, and memory for subjective states is poor and biased by recent results. A structured log — what was done, how it felt, what was noticed, what to change — turns scattered experiences into a data set the athlete and coach can act on. The recurring reflective prompt is deliberately simple: three things learned, three things already done well, three things to improve.
key_facts: A routine automates behaviour so attention and degraded working memory are not spent on decisions during high arousal.
Three routine types worth building: pre-race (the hours and minutes before the start), pre-station or pre-effort (seconds before a repeatable task), and post-error reset.
Good routines are short, portable, fully controllable and rehearsed. Routines dependent on a specific object, place or condition break when the race disrupts them.
Distinguish routine from superstition: a routine has a functional mechanism (attention, arousal, sequencing); a superstition attributes outcome to an unrelated act and creates anxiety when broken.
A pre-station routine can be as small as a breath, a grip check and a cue word — small enough to survive fatigue.
The post-error reset is the highest-value routine in HYROX, where a bad station otherwise contaminates the following run.
Rehearse routines in training under fatigue. A routine used only on race day is not a routine.
Journaling counters the unreliability of memory for subjective states, which is heavily biased by the most recent session or result.
A useful log captures both objective (session, splits, load) and subjective (RPE, mood, sleep, stress, what was noticed) data — the interaction is where the insight sits.
The three-by-three reflective prompt — three things learned, three already done well, three to improve — is simple enough to sustain and forces balanced reflection rather than pure fault-finding.
Reflection-in-action (adjusting during the session) and reflection-on-action (reviewing afterwards) are complementary; journaling develops the second and gradually improves the first.
Patterns only emerge across weeks: recurring pre-race sleep disruption, a station that always precedes a mood drop, a taper that consistently feels flat.
Coaches should journal too. Reflective practice is a coach-development tool as much as an athlete one, and modelling it raises athlete adherence.
87.training_link: Give every athlete three routines and make them rehearse all three in training: what they do in the last twenty minutes before a start, what they do in the five seconds before a station, and what they do immediately after something goes wrong. Keep them short and portable — a breath, a cue word, eyes up — because anything elaborate will break on race day. Then get them writing. A few lines after each session covering what they did, how it felt, and what they noticed, plus the three-by-three review at the end of each week: three things learned, three things already going well, three to improve. Read it. The patterns you spot across a month — the station that always precedes a bad run, the week they always feel flat — are things neither of you will remember accurately without the log.

glossary.def: A fixed, rehearsed sequence of actions before a performance that automates behaviour and preserves attention when arousal degrades working memory.

glossary.def: Structured review after the event, converting experience into transferable learning. The habit journaling is designed to build.

87.exam_focus: Distinguish a functional routine from a superstition, specify the three routine types an athlete needs, and justify journaling as the mechanism that makes mental-skills training compound.

88.title: Unlock your hip — extension, not more stride
88.page_refs: Running Biomechanics and Technique for HYROX Performance
88.key_concept: Most athletes trying to run faster reach further forward with the lead leg. The productive change is the opposite: create more range behind the body through hip extension. Propulsion in running comes from the stance leg pushing back and down against the ground behind the centre of mass, so the usable stride is the part behind you, not the part in front. Restricted hip extension — very common in athletes who sit for a living, and worse again in a HYROX athlete whose sled and lunge work loads the hip flexors heavily — forces compensations: the pelvis tips anteriorly, the lumbar spine extends to fake the range, stride opens at the front instead of the back, and the glutes under-contribute while the hamstrings and lower back take the load. Unlocking the hip is therefore a combination of restoring extension range, then teaching the athlete to use it under load. This matters disproportionately in HYROX because every run happens on hip flexors already shortened and fatigued by the preceding station.
key_facts: Propulsion comes from force applied behind the centre of mass during late stance. The functional stride is what happens behind you.
Limited hip extension pushes athletes to lengthen stride at the front instead — the mechanism that produces overstriding and braking.
Common compensation chain: restricted hip extension → anterior pelvic tilt → lumbar extension → apparent range with no propulsive benefit and added spinal load.
Reduced glute contribution shifts propulsive demand onto hamstrings and calf, raising strain risk in both.
The hip flexors (iliopsoas, rectus femoris, TFL) shorten with prolonged sitting and with the exact HYROX stations that dominate a race — sled push, sled pull and sandbag lunges.
In HYROX this is a compounding problem: each run starts on hip flexors more fatigued and more shortened than the last, so extension range degrades across the race.
Assess with a Thomas test or a half-kneeling extension check; watch for the athlete substituting lumbar extension for hip extension.
Restoring range alone rarely changes running. Range must be followed by loaded, patterned work so the nervous system uses the new range.
Useful loading: hip thrusts, split squats and Bulgarians through full range, single-leg RDLs, and A-march variations with a deliberate late-stance push.
Cue the push, not the reach: 'drive the ground back behind you' produces extension; 'lengthen your stride' produces overstride.
Trunk position matters — a slight forward lean from the ankles preserves the extension window; sitting back into the hips closes it.
Improved hip extension typically shows up as a longer stride at the same cadence rather than as a change in cadence itself.
Expect the biggest visible gains in the back half of a race, where the fatigued athlete's extension range collapses first.
88.training_link: If your athlete's runs fall apart in the second half of a HYROX race, check hip extension before you touch their cadence. Test it half-kneeling and watch whether the range comes from the hip or from their lower back arching — the second one is a fake. Then treat it as a strength problem as much as a mobility one: open the range, but immediately load it with split squats and hip thrusts through full range so they actually use it. Cue the push behind them rather than the reach in front, because 'longer stride' reliably produces the overstride you're trying to remove. And schedule it knowing the sled and the lunges are actively working against you — the mobility work matters most in the weeks with the heaviest station volume.

glossary.def: Movement of the thigh rearward relative to the pelvis. The range behind the body that generates propulsion in late stance.

glossary.def: Forward rotation of the pelvis, often compensating for restricted hip extension and creating apparent range through the lumbar spine instead.

glossary.def: The final phase of ground contact, where the hip extends and force is applied behind the centre of mass. The propulsive portion of the gait cycle.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="8" y1="32" x2="72" y2="32" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.4"/><circle cx="40" cy="14" r="4" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M40 18l-12 14M40 18l12 14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M28 32h-6" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The primary hip flexor group. Shortens with prolonged sitting and with sled and lunge work, restricting the extension available for propulsion.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: A clinical assessment of hip flexor length and available hip extension, performed supine with the opposite knee held to the chest.

glossary.def: A substitute movement produced elsewhere when the intended joint lacks range — here, lumbar extension standing in for hip extension.

88.exam_focus: Explain why propulsion depends on range behind the body, identify the compensation chain caused by restricted hip extension, and justify pairing mobility with loaded patterning.

89.title: Reducing braking forces & the overstride
89.page_refs: Running Biomechanics and Technique for HYROX Performance
89.key_concept: Every foot contact produces a horizontal braking impulse before it produces propulsion. The larger the braking component, the more energy the athlete spends re-accelerating, and the higher the impact loading travelling up the leg. Braking scales with how far in front of the centre of mass the foot lands, so the overstride is the primary target: a foot planted well ahead of the body with an extended knee acts as a strut, decelerating the athlete and transmitting a sharp impact peak. Importantly, the fix is rarely a direct instruction about foot placement, which tends to make athletes reach and then pull. The reliable levers are increasing cadence slightly, encouraging a small forward lean from the ankles, and improving hip extension so the athlete gets range behind rather than in front. In HYROX this is doubly important: braking forces are what a fatigued athlete absorbs on eight separate runs, and compromised running after the sled is exactly when overstriding creeps in.
key_facts: Every contact has a braking phase followed by a propulsive phase; net progress depends on minimising the braking cost, not eliminating it.
Braking impulse rises with the horizontal distance between the foot at contact and the centre of mass — the definition of overstriding.
An overstride typically pairs a far-forward foot with a relatively extended knee, creating a strut that decelerates and transmits a high impact peak.
Impact peak and loading rate are associated with tibial stress injuries; braking force is a mechanical driver of injury as well as an energy cost.
Raising cadence by roughly 5-10% is the most reliable single intervention: it shortens stride, moves foot contact closer to the centre of mass and lowers braking without conscious foot placement.
A small whole-body forward lean initiated from the ankles (not by bending at the waist) shifts the centre of mass forward relative to the foot.
Do not cue foot placement directly. 'Land under yourself' commonly produces reaching followed by a backward pull — the exact fault it aims to fix.
Improved hip extension reduces overstride indirectly by giving the athlete somewhere else to find stride length.
Braking cost increases on downhills and when decelerating into turns — relevant to indoor HYROX courses with repeated direction changes.
Fatigue increases overstride: as hip extension and leg stiffness decline across a race, contact drifts forward. Late-race technique work matters more than fresh-state work.
Compromised running after the sled is a high-risk window — the athlete transitions from a pushing pattern to a running pattern with degraded proprioception.
Measure rather than eyeball where possible: cadence from a watch, and slow-motion video from the side to see foot position relative to the hip at contact.
Small changes only. A large deliberate cadence or footstrike change alters tissue loading distribution and can create a new injury while solving an old one.
89.training_link: Take the cadence reading from their watch before you change anything, then nudge it up by about 5% and let the stride shorten itself — that single change fixes most of the overstride without the athlete ever thinking about their feet. Resist telling them to land under their body; say it and they'll reach out and drag the foot back, which is worse than what they started with. Film them from the side at the end of a hard session rather than fresh, because the overstride you care about is the one that appears at kilometre six on legs cooked by the sled. Add a small lean from the ankles, keep the change small, and give the tissue a few weeks to adapt before layering on more.

glossary.def: The rearward horizontal force applied during early stance that decelerates the runner. Its size scales with how far ahead of the centre of mass the foot lands.

glossary.def: A small whole-body inclination initiated at the ankles rather than the waist, shifting the centre of mass forward relative to the contact point.

89.exam_focus: Explain the mechanical link between overstride, braking impulse and injury risk, and select an intervention that reduces braking without cueing foot placement directly.

90.title: Foot separation & the swing leg
90.page_refs: Running Biomechanics and Technique for HYROX Performance
90.key_concept: Foot separation describes how far apart the feet are at a given moment in the gait cycle — most usefully, the gap between the trailing and leading foot at the point of touchdown. It is a practical, visible proxy for whether an athlete is running with the elastic, bouncing pattern of a runner or the low, shuffling pattern of a jogger. Large separation at touchdown with the trailing leg still extended behind indicates good hip extension, real flight time and elastic recycling of the swing leg. Small separation — feet close together, low heel recovery, minimal flight — indicates the athlete is stepping rather than springing, generating little vertical impulse and relying on hip flexion to pull the leg through. Coaching separation is useful precisely because it is observable on video without a lab, and because it responds to the same interventions as overstride: hip extension range, leg stiffness, and cueing heel recovery under the hip rather than reaching in front.
key_facts: Foot separation = the distance between the feet at a defined instant, most usefully at touchdown of the leading foot.
Wide separation at touchdown with an extended trailing hip indicates real flight time and effective use of the range behind the body.
Narrow separation with low heel recovery is a jogging pattern — minimal flight, low vertical impulse, and swing driven by hip flexion rather than elastic recoil.
Separation is largely an output of hip extension and leg stiffness, not something to be manufactured directly by reaching further forward.
Heel recovery height under the hip rises naturally with speed and with elastic quality; forcing a high heel at slow speeds just adds cost.
Separation reduces as fatigue accumulates, so it is a sensitive visual marker of running degradation across a HYROX race.
It is easy to measure: a side-on video at 120-240 fps and a single freeze at touchdown is enough for consistent comparison over a block.
Compare the athlete against themselves over time rather than against an elite reference — absolute values vary with limb length and speed.
Training levers that increase separation: hip extension range, plyometric and stiffness work, strides and hill sprints, and running at genuinely higher speeds.
Cue swing-leg recovery under the hip ('heel to the back pocket') rather than knee drive in front, which encourages reaching.
Separation and cadence interact: at a fixed speed, a very high cadence reduces separation. Judge them together, not in isolation.
In compromised running after a station, separation collapses first — making it a good target for late-session technique drills.
Do not chase separation as an end in itself. It is a diagnostic window onto extension and elasticity, and improves when those improve.
90.training_link: Film your athlete from the side, freeze at the moment the front foot lands, and look at where the back foot is. If the trailing leg is still extended well behind with the heel recovering up under the hip, they are running. If the feet are close together and the back heel is skimming the floor, they are jogging fast — and no amount of arm-drive cueing will change that. Treat it as a hip extension and stiffness problem: strides, short hill sprints and plyometrics, plus the extension work, rather than a cue about picking their knees up. Re-film at the end of a hard session, because separation collapsing at kilometre six is the thing that actually costs them time. Track them against their own footage over a block, not against an elite runner's.

91.title: Jogging vs running — two different patterns
91.page_refs: Running Biomechanics and Technique for HYROX Performance
91.key_concept: Jogging and running are not the same movement performed at different speeds — they are mechanically distinct patterns. Running is a bouncing gait: the leg behaves as a spring, storing elastic energy in tendon during stance and returning it, with meaningful vertical oscillation, real flight time and propulsion generated behind the body. Jogging is closer to a compliant shuffle: low flight time, small vertical displacement, the swing leg pulled through by hip flexion, and the foot often landing ahead of the centre of mass with a heel-first strut. The practical problem for HYROX athletes is that almost all their running volume is slow, so they groove the jogging pattern, and then on race day at threshold pace they attempt to run fast with a movement pattern that has no spring in it. That is why easy volume alone does not produce a faster runner and why strides, hill sprints and genuinely fast running belong in the week even for an endurance-dominant event.
key_facts: Running is a spring-mass gait with elastic energy storage and return in tendon; jogging is a low-amplitude compliant pattern with minimal elastic contribution.
Key mechanical differences: flight time, vertical oscillation, leg stiffness, heel recovery height, foot separation, and whether propulsion comes from behind the body.
Vertical movement is not waste. Some upward impulse is mechanically necessary — attempting to eliminate it is like throwing a discus flat along the ground.
The optimum is an angle, not a direction: too little vertical impulse and there is no flight, too much and energy is wasted lifting the body.
Jogging recruits hip flexion to pull the swing leg through, while running recycles it largely by elastic recoil, which is cheaper at speed.
An athlete who only ever runs slowly grooves the jogging pattern and cannot access the running pattern on demand at race intensity.
This matters in HYROX because race pace sits well above most athletes' habitual easy pace, so the pattern they have practised is not the pattern the race requires.
Strides (short, controlled, fast efforts with full recovery) are the cheapest way to keep the running pattern available without meaningful fatigue cost.
Hill sprints build the same pattern while limiting impact and enforcing hip extension and forward lean naturally.
Plyometrics and heavy strength work develop the tendon stiffness that makes the elastic pattern possible in the first place.
The distinction is diagnostic, not moral — easy jogging volume is still valuable aerobic training. The error is assuming it develops running mechanics.
Watch for the pattern under fatigue: the transition from running to jogging mechanics across a race is a large hidden time loss.
Compromised running after a station is where athletes most often drop into the jogging pattern and fail to climb back out.
91.training_link: If your athlete's easy pace and race pace mechanics look like two different people, that's the problem. Almost all their volume is slow, so they've grooved a shuffle — and race day asks for a spring they haven't practised. Put strides at the end of two easy runs a week: six by twenty seconds, controlled and fast, full recovery, no fatigue cost worth worrying about. Add short hill sprints, which enforce the lean and the extension for free. Back it with plyometrics and real strength work so the tendons can actually behave like springs. Then check what happens after the sled — that's where they'll fall into the jogging pattern, and the athlete who can climb back out of it is the one who holds their splits.

92.title: The problem with some running drills
92.page_refs: Running Biomechanics and Technique for HYROX Performance
92.key_concept: Standard running drills are often taught with an explanation that installs a false model. The classic demonstration — a coach standing still, lifting a foot in front and drawing it backwards to land 'under the body' — teaches that the foot should move rearward relative to the ground. It should not. In real running the body travels forward while the foot descends more or less vertically; the foot ends up under the body because the body has moved to meet it, not because the athlete pulled it back. Athletes who internalise the pulling model reach forward and then claw, which is precisely the overstride the drill was meant to prevent, and they lose the vertical impulse running requires. The same problem afflicts the 'feet move in a circle' cue: taken literally it implies the athlete should complete the front half of the circle by reaching. The cue can be rescued by shifting the imagined wheel rearward so the circle sits behind and beneath the athlete rather than in front. The general lesson is that a drill is only as good as the model it installs.
key_facts: The static demonstration of 'foot forward, pull it back under you' is mechanically wrong: it teaches rearward foot motion relative to the ground.
In running the foot descends roughly vertically while the body translates forward. The foot arrives under the body because the body moved, not because it was pulled back.
Athletes taught the pulling model tend to reach and then claw at the ground, producing overstride and losing the vertical component of propulsion.
Running requires upward as well as forward impulse. The discus analogy: thrown flat it travels a short distance, thrown too steeply likewise — the optimum is an intermediate angle.
Minimising vertical movement deliberately is the equivalent of throwing the discus horizontally: it removes the flight the gait depends on.
B-skip taught with the same forward-throw-and-pull explanation reinforces the identical fault.
The 'foot moves in a circle' cue is only half true: from touchdown through toe-off to recovery is roughly half a circle, so instructing a full circle invites a forward reach to complete it.
The cue can be salvaged by moving the imagined wheel rearward — centred behind and beneath the athlete rather than directly under the centre of mass.
Encouraging heel recovery and knee lift is legitimate; the fault lies in the accompanying explanation, not in the drill itself.
A drill's value lies in the model it installs. Evaluate the explanation as carefully as the movement.
Feel and mechanics diverge: it can feel like a circular foot path even though it is not, and coaching to the feel is acceptable if the resulting mechanics are correct.
Prefer cues describing intent and outcome ('push the ground back behind you', 'run tall') over cues describing joint paths.
Test the cue, not the theory: film the athlete before and after and check whether contact position and separation actually improved.
Drills are a supplement to running fast, not a replacement for it.
92.training_link: Watch your own demonstration before you watch your athletes. If you stand still and draw your foot backwards to show where it should land, you have just taught them to claw at the ground — and the reaching overstride you spend the rest of the session correcting is one you installed. Explain it the honest way: the foot comes down, the body goes forward, and that's why it ends up underneath. Keep the drills, fix the sentence that goes with them. If you like the wheel cue, move the wheel back so the circle sits behind and under them rather than out in front. Then check it worked — film a few strides before and after, look at contact position and foot separation, and keep the cue only if the footage changed.

93.title: The causes of running injuries
93.page_refs: Running Biomechanics and Technique for HYROX Performance
93.key_concept: Running injuries are overwhelmingly load-management failures rather than technique failures. The dominant mechanism is cumulative: tissue is loaded faster than it can adapt, and the injury appears at whichever structure has the lowest reserve. That makes training load history — how much, how fast it changed, and what the tissue was previously accustomed to — the strongest modifiable factor, ahead of footstrike pattern, pronation or any single kinematic variable, none of which predict injury reliably at the individual level. Biomechanics still matters, but as a modifier of where load concentrates rather than as a simple cause: high loading rates and braking forces bias toward bone stress injury, low cadence and overstride increase per-step tissue demand, and reduced hip extension and glute contribution shift load onto hamstrings and calf. Layered on top are the non-mechanical contributors — energy availability, sleep, previous injury and rapid changes in surface, footwear or terrain. HYROX adds its own signature: eight runs performed on legs pre-fatigued by heavy pushing, pulling and lunging.
key_facts: Most running injuries are cumulative overload — load applied faster than tissue adaptation — not acute trauma or a single technique fault.
Training load history is the strongest modifiable risk factor: total volume, rate of change, and what the tissue was previously accustomed to.
Previous injury is the single most consistent predictor of future injury; take the history seriously and address the deficits it left behind.
Footstrike pattern does not reliably predict injury. Changing it shifts load between structures — forefoot loads the calf and Achilles more, rearfoot loads the knee more — rather than removing it.
Pronation has been poorly supported as an injury predictor and is a weak basis for prescribing footwear.
High loading rate and large braking impulse bias toward bone stress injuries, particularly tibial.
Low cadence with overstride raises per-step loading; a modest cadence increase reduces load at the knee, though it may increase demand elsewhere.
Reduced hip extension and glute contribution shift propulsive demand to hamstrings and calf, raising strain risk in both.
Rapid changes in surface, gradient, footwear (including a sudden shift to a different stack height or drop) or session type are common precipitants.
Energy availability, sleep and stress modulate tissue adaptation capacity — a mechanically identical load is riskier in an under-fuelled athlete.
Bone stress injuries in an athlete with menstrual disturbance or restrictive eating warrant medical referral, not a technique session.
The HYROX-specific pattern: runs performed on legs already loaded by sled push, sled pull and sandbag lunges, so the running tissue load arrives on a pre-fatigued system.
Progress load gradually and monitor niggles honestly — an irritable tendon that is managed early costs days, and one that is ignored costs a block.
Technique work is a legitimate adjunct where a specific mechanical fault concentrates load, but it does not substitute for sane load progression.
93.training_link: When an athlete turns up with shin pain, look at their last six weeks before you look at their footstrike. Nine times out of ten you'll find a jump in volume, a new surface, a shoe change or a block where the sled work quietly doubled — and that's your answer. Ask about previous injuries too, because the old one is the best predictor of the next. Only then consider mechanics, and use them to explain where the load concentrated rather than as the villain: overstride and low cadence load the shin, poor hip extension loads the calf and hamstring. Check fuelling and sleep, because the same session is more dangerous in an under-fuelled athlete. And remember the HYROX wrinkle — their runs land on legs already beaten up by the sled and the lunges, so your running load isn't the only running load.

glossary.def: Injury arising from repeated loading exceeding tissue adaptation capacity over time, rather than from a single traumatic event.
