glossary.def: The load a structure can tolerate and adapt to, determined by training history, recovery, and energy availability. Injury occurs when demand exceeds it.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: How quickly ground reaction force rises after contact. Elevated rates are associated with bone stress injury, particularly at the tibia.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: Which part of the foot contacts first. It redistributes load between calf/Achilles and knee rather than predicting injury on its own.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><line x1="8" y1="32" x2="72" y2="32" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.4"/><circle cx="40" cy="14" r="4" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M40 18l-12 14M40 18l12 14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M28 32h-6" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The rate at which training demand increases over time. The most controllable determinant of overuse injury risk.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: A low-grade recurring symptom below the threshold of injury. Managed early it costs days; ignored it commonly costs a training block.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

93.exam_focus: Rank the causes of a running injury presentation, explain why load history outranks footstrike and pronation, and state when a presentation requires referral rather than technique work.

94.title: Working with athletes on nutrition — scope & referral
94.key_concept: Nutrition is the area where coaches most often drift outside their scope of practice, usually with good intentions. The workable boundary is this: a coach can provide general, evidence-based nutrition guidance oriented to performance — fuelling around sessions, hydration, practical race-day strategy, general food-quality advice — while individualised medical nutrition therapy, prescriptive meal plans for clinical conditions, eating-disorder management and supplement prescription for medical purposes belong to a registered dietitian or physician. Knowing the line matters legally and clinically, but the deeper coaching skill is behavioural: most athletes already know roughly what to do and fail on implementation. So the effective work is small, specific, negotiated changes anchored to sessions rather than comprehensive dietary overhauls, and it depends on trust, non-judgemental language and cultural and practical realism about what the athlete actually eats. Red flags — restriction, secrecy, rigid rules, weight preoccupation, unexplained fatigue or menstrual disturbance — trigger referral rather than adjustment.
key_facts: In scope for a coach: general performance-oriented nutrition guidance, fuelling around training, hydration, practical race-day strategy, food-quality basics.
Out of scope: individualised medical nutrition therapy, clinical meal prescription, eating-disorder treatment, and prescribing supplements for medical purposes.
Build a referral network before you need one — dietitian, physician, and a clinician experienced in disordered eating.
Assess before advising: a simple food and training log across a normal week beats a questionnaire and reveals timing problems most athletes can't self-report.
The common failure is implementation, not knowledge. Prioritise one or two specific, negotiated changes over a comprehensive overhaul.
Anchor changes to sessions ('carbohydrate in the two hours before the key session') because they are concrete and easy to evaluate.
Practical constraints — budget, cooking skill, shift work, family, culture, religious observance, travel — determine adherence more than optimality does.
Use non-judgemental, non-moralising language. 'Good' and 'bad' foods framing predicts guilt and secrecy rather than change.
Avoid routine body-composition measurement without a clear purpose and a plan for the result; it is a common trigger for restriction.
Red flags for referral: restriction, food secrecy, rigid rules, weight preoccupation, unexplained fatigue, menstrual disturbance, recurrent bone injury, GI symptoms.
Document your advice and your referrals. It protects the athlete and it protects you.
Athletes get most of their nutrition information from social media. Part of the job is respectfully correcting misinformation without shaming them for holding it.
Evaluate the change you made before adding another. An unmeasured intervention is a guess.
94.training_link: Ask for a week's food and training log before you say anything about nutrition — you'll usually find the problem is timing, not content, and that's a much easier fix. Then change one thing. Pick something concrete and tied to a session, like getting carbohydrate in before the key run, and check in two weeks later whether it actually happened. Work with their real life rather than an ideal one: shift patterns, budget and what their family eats will decide adherence far more than the optimal macro split. Keep the language neutral — no good foods and bad foods — and skip the body-composition checks unless you have a specific reason and a plan. And know your exit: restriction, secrecy, missing periods or repeated bone injuries mean you refer, not adjust.

glossary.def: The boundary of services a coach is qualified and permitted to deliver. Nutrition guidance sits inside it; clinical nutrition therapy does not.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Individualised, clinically directed dietary treatment of a diagnosed condition. Requires a registered dietitian or physician.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 6l16 6v10c0 8-7 12-16 14-9-2-16-6-16-14V12z" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M34 20l5 5 8-9" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A concurrent record of intake and sessions across a normal week — the most useful low-cost assessment tool available to a coach.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Tying a dietary change to an existing concrete event, such as a specific session, so it is easy to remember and easy to evaluate.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A sign warranting referral rather than coaching adjustment — restriction, secrecy, rigid rules, weight preoccupation, menstrual disturbance, recurrent bone injury.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: The dietitian, physician and clinical specialists a coach has identified in advance, so referral is immediate rather than improvised.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

94.exam_focus: State what nutrition guidance is inside and outside a coach's scope, identify red flags requiring referral, and design a single anchored behavioural change rather than a dietary overhaul.

95.title: Training the gut
95.key_concept: Gastrointestinal distress is one of the most common reasons endurance athletes underperform, and it is substantially trainable. The gut adapts to what it is regularly asked to do: repeated exposure to carbohydrate during exercise upregulates intestinal transporters, increases gastric emptying rate and improves tolerance, so an athlete who never practises fuelling cannot suddenly absorb race-day carbohydrate. The mechanism sits alongside the exercise-induced splanchnic blood flow reduction — blood is diverted to working muscle and skin, reducing gut perfusion and impairing absorption, an effect worsened by high intensity, heat and dehydration. Practically, gut training means progressively increasing carbohydrate intake during sessions over weeks, rehearsing the exact race-day products, and using multiple transportable carbohydrates (glucose plus fructose) to exceed the roughly 60 g/h ceiling imposed by a single transporter pathway. HYROX adds a specific complication: bouncing, bracing, wall balls and lunges mechanically agitate the gut in a way steady running does not.
key_facts: The gut is adaptable: regular carbohydrate exposure during exercise upregulates intestinal transporters, speeds gastric emptying and improves tolerance.
Glucose absorption via SGLT1 saturates at roughly 60 g/h; adding fructose, absorbed via GLUT5, allows total intakes around 90 g/h or higher in well-trained guts.
Typical multiple-transportable-carbohydrate ratios are around 2:1 glucose:fructose, with some newer products using 1:0.8.
Splanchnic hypoperfusion — reduced gut blood flow as blood is diverted to muscle and skin — impairs absorption and is worsened by high intensity, heat and dehydration.
Dehydration markedly worsens GI symptoms; fluid strategy and fuelling strategy cannot be planned separately.
Train the gut progressively across weeks, raising intake per hour in steps rather than jumping to race targets.
Rehearse with the exact race-day products, concentrations and timing. Novel products on race day are a common and avoidable failure.
High-fibre, high-fat and high-protein intakes close to competition slow gastric emptying and raise symptom risk; lower-residue choices in the final 24 hours help symptom-prone athletes.
Symptoms split into upper (nausea, reflux, fullness) and lower (cramping, urgency, diarrhoea), with somewhat different drivers and fixes.

HYROX-specific mechanical agitation — jumping, bracing under the sandbag, repeated squat-to-overhead — provokes symptoms that steady-state running does not, so rehearse fuelling in station work, not just on runs.
Very high carbohydrate concentrations and hypertonic drinks slow gastric emptying; dilute appropriately.
Some athletes are genuinely low absorbers and will not reach 90 g/h. Individualise to the tested tolerance rather than a published target.
Persistent or severe symptoms, blood in stool, or symptoms outside exercise warrant medical referral rather than further gut training.
95.training_link: If your athlete's stomach is the reason their race falls apart, treat it as a trainable system and put it in the plan. Start below their current tolerance and add carbohydrate per hour in steps over six to eight weeks, using the exact gel or drink they'll race with — not a similar one. Use a glucose-fructose product if you're going past about 60 g an hour, since that's where the single transporter tops out. Practise it during station work as well as running, because bracing under a sandbag and throwing wall balls upsets a full stomach in a way a steady jog never will. Get the hydration right at the same time, since dehydration makes everything worse. And if symptoms are severe, persistent or happening outside training, that's a referral.

glossary.def: Progressive, repeated exposure to carbohydrate and fluid during exercise, upregulating absorption capacity and improving tolerance over weeks.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M20 30c0-10 8-10 8-18M28 12c8 0 8 8 0 8M28 20c10 0 10 10 0 10M28 30h20" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>

glossary.def: Combining glucose and fructose to use separate intestinal transporters, allowing oxidation rates above the ~60 g/h single-pathway ceiling.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: The intestinal transporters for glucose and fructose respectively. Their separate saturation points are why mixed-carbohydrate products work.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Reduced blood flow to the gut during exercise as blood is redirected to muscle and skin, impairing absorption and driving GI symptoms.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: The rate at which stomach contents pass to the small intestine. Slowed by high intensity, dehydration, and hypertonic or fat- and fibre-rich intake.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Reduced-fibre eating in the final 24 hours before competition, used to lower gut contents and symptom risk in susceptible athletes.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

95.exam_focus: Explain the transporter basis of the ~60 g/h ceiling and how mixed carbohydrates raise it, and design a progressive gut-training protocol rehearsing race products under HYROX-specific mechanical load.

96.title: Post-competition recovery nutrition
96.key_concept: After a HYROX race the athlete has depleted glycogen, sustained muscle damage from eccentric loading (lunges, wall balls, sled deceleration), lost fluid and electrolytes, and taken an immune and inflammatory hit. Recovery nutrition addresses each, and how aggressively it must be pursued depends almost entirely on when they next need to perform. With a week or more before the next hard session, normal good eating across the following days will restore everything and the classic thirty-minute window is largely irrelevant. With another race or a hard session within roughly 24 hours — a doubles athlete racing again, or a training weekend — timing genuinely matters and rapid refuelling becomes worthwhile. The practical priorities are carbohydrate for glycogen resynthesis, protein for muscle protein synthesis and repair, fluid plus sodium to restore plasma volume, and a return to normal eating patterns quickly. Alcohol and severe energy restriction after competition are the two most common self-inflicted delays to recovery.
key_facts: Four recovery targets after a race: glycogen resynthesis, muscle repair, rehydration with electrolytes, and restoration of immune and overall energy status.
The urgency of nutrient timing scales with the interval to the next performance. Long recovery windows make the 'anabolic window' largely irrelevant.
For rapid refuelling (next hard effort within ~24 h) aim for roughly 1.0-1.2 g/kg/h of carbohydrate for the first several hours.
With ≥24 h recovery, total daily carbohydrate intake matters far more than the timing of the first feed.
Post-exercise protein around 0.3-0.4 g/kg per serving supports muscle protein synthesis; total daily protein intake remains the dominant variable.
Rehydration requires replacing roughly 125-150% of the fluid deficit, because some intake is lost as urine — and it must include sodium to retain the fluid.
Plain water without sodium after a large sweat loss can promote diuresis and delay rehydration.
Eccentric-heavy stations (sandbag lunges, wall balls, sled deceleration) drive delayed-onset muscle soreness and a longer repair timeline than the metabolic cost alone suggests.
Alcohol impairs glycogen resynthesis, muscle protein synthesis and rehydration, and worsens sleep quality — the single most common post-race recovery error.
Appetite is often suppressed after hard racing; liquid carbohydrate and protein are more practical than solid food in the first hour.
Post-race energy restriction (common when athletes 'earn' a rest week by eating less) impairs repair and immune recovery precisely when demand is highest.
Return to normal eating patterns as quickly as possible — the following days matter more than the following hour in most cases.
Anti-inflammatory supplementation immediately post-training may blunt some adaptive signalling; after a target race, where adaptation is not the goal, this concern is much less relevant.
96.training_link: Ask one question before you plan any of this: when do they need to perform again. If the next race is months away, tell them to drink, get some salt and food in, skip the alcohol and eat normally for a few days — nothing more sophisticated is required, and the thirty-minute window myth just adds stress. If they're racing again tomorrow or doing a hard session, then timing genuinely matters: carbohydrate at roughly 1.0-1.2 g/kg/h for the first few hours, protein with it, and fluid at about 1.5 times what they lost, with sodium in it or it just runs straight through. Expect them not to feel hungry, so lead with liquids. And warn them about the two classic own goals — a big night out, and 'earning' the rest week by under-eating.

glossary.def: Replenishment of muscle and liver glycogen after exercise. Rate-limited early on, making carbohydrate timing relevant only when recovery time is short.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The need to consume roughly 125-150% of fluid lost, since a portion is excreted as urine, with sodium included to retain the remainder.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M20 30c0-10 8-10 8-18M28 12c8 0 8 8 0 8M28 20c10 0 10 10 0 10M28 30h20" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/></svg>

glossary.def: The repair and remodelling process stimulated by protein intake after exercise; total daily intake dominates over precise timing.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 32 C24 30 34 14 44 14 S62 22 72 10" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="44" cy="14" r="2.5" fill="#5ec8ff"/></svg>

glossary.def: Force production while a muscle lengthens — prominent in lunges, wall balls and sled deceleration. Drives muscle damage and delayed-onset soreness.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: The proposed short post-exercise period of heightened nutrient sensitivity. Real but far less consequential than once claimed when recovery time is long.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Urinary fluid loss triggered by drinking large volumes of low-sodium fluid, which delays full rehydration after heavy sweat loss.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

96.exam_focus: Prescribe post-race nutrition scaled to the interval before the next performance, and justify why sodium and the 125-150% rehydration factor matter after heavy sweat loss.

97.title: Vegetarian & vegan athletes
97.key_concept: A well-planned plant-based diet can support HYROX performance at any level, and the coach's role is to make the planning explicit rather than to argue about the choice. The genuine risks are specific and manageable: protein quantity and quality, iron, vitamin B12, omega-3, calcium, vitamin D, zinc and iodine. Plant proteins are generally lower in leucine and less digestible, so plant-based athletes need somewhat higher total protein intake and more attention to distributing it across the day and pairing complementary sources. Iron is the most performance-relevant risk, because non-haem iron from plants is far less bioavailable than haem iron, and endurance training raises requirements — a combination that makes deficiency common and endurance-limiting well before anaemia appears. Vitamin B12 is the one genuinely non-negotiable supplement for vegans, since reliable food sources are fortified products only. Energy density is a quieter problem: high-fibre, high-volume diets can make it hard to eat enough, which slides into low energy availability.
key_facts: A well-planned plant-based diet can meet the demands of endurance and strength training; problems come from poor planning, not from plant sources per se.
Plant proteins are typically lower in leucine and less digestible, so plant-based athletes generally need a higher total protein intake than omnivores.
Distribute protein across the day and combine complementary sources (legumes with grains) to cover the full amino acid profile.
Vitamin B12 is not reliably available from unfortified plant foods. Vegan athletes require supplementation or fortified foods — this is non-negotiable.
Non-haem iron from plants is far less bioavailable than haem iron from animal foods; requirements are effectively higher for plant-based athletes.
Vitamin C consumed with iron-rich plant foods enhances non-haem absorption; tea, coffee and calcium taken with the meal inhibit it.
Iron deficiency impairs endurance well before frank anaemia appears — screen symptomatic athletes rather than waiting for haemoglobin to fall.
Omega-3: plant ALA converts poorly to EPA and DHA; an algae-derived supplement is the practical route for vegans.
Calcium and vitamin D matter for bone health, particularly alongside the bone-stress risks of running volume. Fortified plant milks and supplementation cover most cases.
Zinc and iodine are frequently under-consumed on plant-based diets; iodine is a particular gap where iodised salt is not used.
Creatine and beta-alanine stores tend to be lower in vegetarians, so supplementation may produce a larger relative benefit than in omnivores.
High fibre and low energy density can make it difficult to consume adequate energy — a route into low energy availability that looks like discipline.
Refer to a dietitian for a new or struggling plant-based athlete rather than improvising a plan; blood screening for iron, B12 and vitamin D is a reasonable early step.
97.training_link: Don't debate the diet — plan it. Push total protein a bit higher than you would for an omnivore and spread it across the day, pairing legumes with grains rather than relying on one source. Check B12 is covered by a supplement or fortified foods, because there's no reliable food route for a vegan and the deficiency is slow and silent. Treat iron as the performance issue it is: get it screened if they're tired, pair iron-rich meals with vitamin C, and keep the coffee away from those meals. Add algae-based omega-3, and check calcium and vitamin D given the running volume. Then watch total energy — high-fibre eating fills people up, and an athlete quietly under-eating on a virtuous-looking diet is heading for low energy availability. When in doubt, refer.

glossary.def: Plant-derived iron with substantially lower bioavailability than haem iron from animal foods. Absorption improves with vitamin C and is inhibited by tea, coffee and calcium.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: The amount of leucine needed to maximally stimulate muscle protein synthesis. Lower leucine content in plant proteins means larger servings are required.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Combining plant sources with differing limiting amino acids, such as legumes with grains, to provide a complete profile across the day.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: A nutrient absent from unfortified plant foods and essential for neurological and haematological function. Supplementation is mandatory for vegans.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 6l16 6v10c0 8-7 12-16 14-9-2-16-6-16-14V12z" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M34 20l5 5 8-9" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: The inefficient metabolic conversion of plant-derived omega-3 into the long-chain forms, making algae-based supplementation the practical option.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Energy per unit volume of food. Low density plus high fibre can cap intake and drive inadvertent low energy availability.

98.title: HYROX for longevity & health
98.page_refs: Sports Medicine: Optimizing Health, Recovery & Performance
98.key_concept: Most HYROX participants are not chasing a podium; they are using the format as a structure for lifelong fitness. That makes the health case worth understanding, because it changes how a coach programmes for the majority of their clients. HYROX training happens to combine the two strongest predictors of all-cause mortality risk reduction — cardiorespiratory fitness and muscular strength — in a single format, alongside functional capacity work (carrying, lunging, pushing, pulling) that maps directly onto the physical tasks that determine independence in later life. Cardiorespiratory fitness in particular shows a strong graded inverse relationship with mortality, with the largest absolute gains at the low-fitness end, meaning the deconditioned beginner has more to gain than the athlete chasing a five-minute PB. Set against that are the real risks: overuse injury from rapid load progression, the RED-S and overtraining risks of chasing performance, and event-day cardiac risk in older participants with undetected disease. The coach's job is to keep the health return while managing those risks.
key_facts: Cardiorespiratory fitness and muscular strength are each independently associated with reduced all-cause mortality; HYROX training develops both.
The fitness-mortality relationship is graded and steepest at the low-fitness end — the deconditioned beginner gains most from the first improvements.
Resistance training independently associates with reduced all-cause mortality and is essential for preserving muscle mass and bone density with age.
HYROX movements map onto real functional capacity: carrying load, lunging, pushing, pulling and repeated sit-to-stand are the tasks that determine later-life independence.
Weight-bearing and resistance loading maintain bone mineral density, relevant to osteoporosis and fracture risk in ageing populations.
The community and event structure supports adherence, which is the variable that actually determines long-term health outcomes.
Metabolic health benefits — insulin sensitivity, blood pressure, lipid profile, visceral fat — follow from the combined aerobic and resistance stimulus.
Risks scale with how the training is done: rapid load progression drives overuse injury, and performance chasing can drive RED-S and overtraining.
Event-day cardiac events, while rare, cluster in older participants with undetected cardiovascular disease during unaccustomed maximal effort.
Pre-participation screening matters for older or previously inactive athletes: a health history questionnaire and medical clearance where risk factors or symptoms exist.
Exertional symptoms — chest pain, unusual breathlessness, syncope or near-syncope during exertion — require medical assessment before further training, always.
For the health-focused participant, consistency and injury avoidance outrank intensity. A block completed beats a block attempted.
Frame goals accordingly: for most clients the meaningful outcome is training for another twenty years, not a personal best this season.
98.training_link: Most of the people who walk into your gym want to be fit at seventy, not fast in November — programme for that. The good news is the format already does the heavy lifting: it builds aerobic fitness and strength together, which is about as good as exercise prescription gets for long-term health, and the carrying, lunging and pushing translate directly to staying independent later. So protect consistency above all else. Progress load slowly enough that they never lose a month to a niggle, because the block they complete is worth more than the block they attempt. Screen the older or previously sedentary ones properly before you load them up, and treat chest pain, unusual breathlessness or dizziness on exertion as a hard stop and a referral — never something to train through.

99.title: Functional neuroscience & injury prevention
99.page_refs: Sports Medicine: Optimizing Health, Recovery & Performance
99.key_concept: Injury prevention has traditionally been framed around tissue: make the muscle stronger, the tendon stiffer, the joint more stable. The functional-neuroscience lens adds the control layer — injuries frequently occur not because tissue lacked capacity but because the nervous system did not organise the movement well enough under the conditions of the moment. That control depends on sensory input (proprioception from muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs and joint receptors, plus vestibular and visual input), on the speed and quality of central processing, and on the motor output that results. Fatigue, distraction, pain and previous injury all degrade this loop, which is why injuries cluster late in sessions, under cognitive load and in athletes with injury history. Practically this means prevention work should include reactive and unanticipated elements, dual-task and fatigued conditions, and progressive exposure rather than only clean, pre-planned, fresh-state strength work. It also explains why an athlete can pass a movement screen and still get hurt on the eighth run.
key_facts: Injury risk depends on both tissue capacity and neuromuscular control — the ability to organise movement appropriately in the moment.
Proprioception draws on muscle spindles (length and velocity), Golgi tendon organs (tension) and joint receptors, integrated with vestibular and visual input.
Feedforward control anticipates load and pre-activates muscle before contact; feedback control corrects after the fact and is too slow for high-speed events.
Previous injury degrades proprioceptive acuity and alters motor patterns, which partly explains why it is the strongest predictor of future injury.
Fatigue degrades the whole loop: slower reaction, reduced proprioceptive accuracy, altered recruitment. Injuries therefore cluster late in sessions and late in races.
Cognitive load and distraction reduce available attentional resources for movement control, raising risk in unpredictable environments.
Pain alters motor control independently of tissue damage, producing protective patterns that can persist after the tissue has healed.
Clean, pre-planned, fresh-state screening can miss athletes who fail under fatigue or unanticipated conditions — a common false negative.
Effective prevention programmes combine strength, plyometric, balance and agility work; multi-component programmes consistently outperform single-mode approaches.
Include reactive and unanticipated elements — reacting to a call or a visual cue rather than executing a known sequence.
Train under fatigue deliberately, so control is rehearsed in the state where injuries actually happen.
In HYROX, the compromised-running transition after a station is the highest-risk control moment: proprioception is degraded and the movement pattern changes abruptly.
Progressive exposure to the demand, rather than avoidance of it, is what builds durable control — tissue and nervous system both adapt to what they meet regularly.
99.training_link: Stop testing your athletes only when they're fresh and the movement is pre-planned — that's not when they get hurt. Put some of the prevention work at the end of hard sessions, and add reactive elements: change of direction on a call, a landing they didn't know was coming, a dual-task element. Pay particular attention to the moment they come off a station into a run, because that transition is where proprioception is worst and the pattern changes fastest — practise it deliberately rather than letting race day be the first rehearsal. Take injury history seriously as a control problem, not just a tissue one; an old ankle sprain leaves a proprioceptive deficit that outlasts the healing. And build multi-component work — strength, plyos, balance, agility — because the combination beats any single ingredient.

glossary.def: The sense of body position and movement, drawn from muscle spindles, Golgi tendon organs and joint receptors, and integrated with vestibular and visual input.

100.title: Training & competing while sick
100.page_refs: Sports Medicine: Optimizing Health, Recovery & Performance
100.key_concept: Athletes get ill, and the recurring question is whether to train, modify or stop. The most widely used practical heuristic is the neck check: symptoms above the neck alone — mild sore throat, nasal congestion, sneezing without fever — generally permit light-to-moderate training with a symptom review, while symptoms below the neck, or any systemic sign, mean stop. The systemic red flags are fever, muscle aches, unusual fatigue, productive cough, chest tightness, breathlessness, vomiting or diarrhoea. Fever specifically is an absolute contraindication to training: it raises resting metabolic and cardiovascular demand, impairs thermoregulation, and — critically — training with a systemic viral illness carries a risk of myocarditis, which is a rare but potentially fatal cause of exercise-related sudden cardiac death. Return should be graded rather than immediate, typically requiring a symptom-free and fever-free period before resuming, then a progressive rebuild. Heavy training loads and competition transiently increase infection susceptibility, so prevention through hygiene, sleep, adequate energy and load management is a legitimate performance intervention.
key_facts: The neck check: symptoms confined above the neck (mild sore throat, nasal congestion, sneezing, no fever) generally permit reduced training with review.
Symptoms below the neck — productive cough, chest tightness, breathlessness, GI symptoms — mean do not train.
Any systemic symptom (fever, myalgia, unusual fatigue, swollen glands) means stop, regardless of where the local symptoms sit.
Fever is an absolute contraindication to training. It raises cardiovascular and metabolic demand and impairs thermoregulation.
Training with a systemic viral illness carries a risk of myocarditis — rare, but a recognised cause of exercise-related sudden cardiac death in athletes.
When training is permitted, reduce intensity and volume first and reassess daily rather than pushing through to a planned session.
Return to training should be graded: a fever-free and symptom-free period first, then progressive rebuild over several days, with a longer runway after systemic illness.
As a rough guide, allow at least as many easy days returning as days missed after a systemic illness, and longer if fever was present.
Watch for post-illness fatigue and unexpectedly high heart rate at easy paces — a sign the athlete has returned too fast.
Heavy training and competition transiently increase upper respiratory infection susceptibility, particularly around long-haul travel and major events.
Prevention is programmable: sleep, adequate energy availability, hand hygiene, avoiding sharing bottles and towels, and managing load spikes.
Vitamin D sufficiency and adequate energy availability support immune function; megadose supplementation is not a substitute for either.
Medication caution: some over-the-counter cold remedies contain substances restricted in sport, so check status before an athlete competes.
Never let an athlete race with fever or systemic illness, whatever the entry fee or the training block behind it.
100.training_link: Teach your athletes the neck check so they can make the call without texting you at 6am: stuffy nose and a scratchy throat with no fever, train easy and reassess tomorrow. Anything below the neck, or a fever, aches or unusual fatigue, and they stop — no negotiation, because training through a systemic viral illness carries a small but real myocarditis risk and that's not a gamble worth a session. Bring them back gradually rather than straight into the key session, and give at least as many easy days as they missed if it was systemic. Watch their heart rate at easy pace on the way back; if it's high for the effort, they've come back too soon. And if a target race lands on a fever, they don't race.

glossary.def: A practical heuristic permitting reduced training for symptoms above the neck without fever, and prohibiting it for symptoms below the neck or any systemic sign.

101.title: Anti-doping & WADA essentials
101.page_refs: Sports Medicine: Optimizing Health, Recovery & Performance
101.key_concept: Anti-doping rests on a principle that surprises many athletes: strict liability. An athlete is responsible for any prohibited substance found in their sample regardless of intent, negligence or how it got there — which means 'my supplement was contaminated' is an explanation, not a defence. The World Anti-Doping Agency publishes a Prohibited List updated at least annually, organised into substances prohibited at all times, substances prohibited in competition only (including stimulants, cannabinoids and glucocorticoids by certain routes), and substances prohibited in particular sports. Beyond the presence of a substance, there are further anti-doping rule violations that catch out the unwary: whereabouts failures, tampering, refusing a test, trafficking, complicity, and — directly relevant to coaches — administration and association with sanctioned personnel. A Therapeutic Use Exemption allows a legitimately needed medication under defined criteria. For a coach, the practical duties are to check every medication and supplement, to advise batch-tested products where supplements are used at all, and never to supply anything.
key_facts: Strict liability: the athlete is responsible for what is in their body, regardless of intent or how it got there.
The WADA Prohibited List is updated at least annually. Check it each year rather than assuming last season's knowledge holds.
List structure: substances and methods prohibited at all times, those prohibited in competition only, and those prohibited in particular sports.
Prohibited methods matter too — manipulation of blood and blood components, chemical and physical manipulation, and gene doping.

Anti-doping rule violations extend well beyond a positive test: use or attempted use, refusing or evading a test, whereabouts failures, tampering, possession, trafficking, administration, complicity, and prohibited association.
Coaches can personally commit violations through administration, complicity or association with sanctioned support personnel.

A Therapeutic Use Exemption permits a prohibited substance where there is a clear medical need, no reasonable permitted alternative, no additional performance benefit beyond a return to normal health, and the need is not the result of prior non-therapeutic use.
Apply for a TUE in advance where required; retroactive applications are limited to defined circumstances such as emergency treatment.
Supplements are the most common route to inadvertent violations, through contamination and undeclared ingredients rather than deliberate cheating.
Where supplements are used, choose third-party batch-tested products (for example Informed Sport or similar schemes) — this reduces but does not eliminate risk.
Coaches should never supply supplements or medication to an athlete. Advise, document and refer to a physician or pharmacist for checking.
Check every medication before use, including over-the-counter cold and allergy remedies, some of which contain in-competition prohibited stimulants.
Education is part of the coaching role: athletes who understand strict liability behave differently from those who assume good intent protects them.
101.training_link: Have the conversation before there's a problem, not after. Explain strict liability plainly — whatever ends up in their sample is their responsibility, and 'I didn't know' has never worked for anyone. Make it a rule that every medication and supplement gets checked against the current Prohibited List before it's taken, including the cold and flu tablets from the pharmacy, which are a classic way to fail an in-competition test. If they insist on supplements, steer them to third-party batch-tested products and be honest that it reduces rather than removes the risk. Never hand them anything yourself — advise, document, and send them to a pharmacist or physician. And if they have a genuine medical need for something on the list, get the TUE sorted in advance rather than hoping.

glossary.def: The principle that an athlete is responsible for any prohibited substance in their sample regardless of intent or negligence.

glossary.def: Any of the defined breaches — including use, refusal, whereabouts failures, tampering, trafficking, administration, complicity and prohibited association — not merely a positive test.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

102.title: Analysing a station — the three expert lenses
102.key_concept: Module 7.4 examines each of the eight stations three times over, through a biomechanist's eyes, a physiotherapist's and a strength coach's. The value is that the three lenses disagree productively. The biomechanist asks how force is produced and where it leaks, and reasons in terms of sequencing, force vectors, moment arms and spinal position. The physiotherapist asks what is restricting the athlete, and typically finds the limiter upstream of the complaint — a tight hip or thorax capping performance at a station that looks like a strength problem. The strength coach asks which physical qualities underpin the station and what exercises build them. An athlete who is slow on the sled might be weak (S&C), might be leaking force through a collapsed trunk (biomechanics), or might be unable to transfer force from the floor because their hips are restricted (physiotherapy). Diagnosing which of the three is limiting the athlete in front of you is the actual coaching skill; applying the wrong lens produces training that is technically sound and useless. Somatotype runs through all three: compact, mesomorphic athletes and tall, ectomorphic athletes need genuinely different strategies at the same station.
key_facts: The module analyses all eight stations through three lenses: biomechanics (how force is produced and lost), physiotherapy (what restriction limits the athlete), strength & conditioning (which qualities and exercises build capacity).
The same poor station time can have three different causes — insufficient strength, faulty sequencing, or a mobility restriction upstream. Diagnose before you prescribe.
Recurring biomechanical themes: proximal-to-distal sequencing, trunk stiffness, force-vector alignment, moment-arm management, and neutral spinal position under load.
Force leakage is the unifying biomechanical concept — energy generated proximally that fails to reach the implement because a segment in the chain yields.
Recurring physiotherapy theme: hip and thoracic restriction limit output at nearly every station, often presenting as a strength or cardiovascular problem rather than a mobility one.
Restriction of the thorax limits rib-cage expansion and therefore breathing, which is why a mobility problem can present as a cardiovascular ceiling.
Recurring S&C theme: build maximal strength for the heavy stations, strength-endurance for the repeated ones, and elastic/power qualities where a stretch-shortening cycle is involved.

Somatotype changes the optimal strategy: shorter mesomorphs have compact levers, a lower centre of mass and strong proximal power; taller ectomorphs gain range and stroke length but face larger moment arms on the spine and shoulders.
Mesomorph general priority: rhythm and consistency rather than chasing maximal range per repetition.
Ectomorph general priority: trunk stiffness and sequencing, so long levers become an asset rather than a mechanical liability.
Fatigue is the fourth lens implicitly present throughout — every station's technical model degrades late in the race, and the coaching target is the fatigued pattern.

The physiotherapy lens in this module also advances nutritional and supplement claims (glutamine as a lactate buffer, essential fatty acids to raise oxygen uptake, iron for female athletes). Treat the mobility reasoning as clinically mainstream and the supplement claims as weakly evidenced — iron status is the one with genuine support, and only where deficiency is confirmed by testing.
Practical diagnostic order: rule out restriction first (it is quickest to change), then check sequencing on video, then treat it as a strength deficit.
102.training_link: When an athlete is slow at a station, resist prescribing strength work by reflex. Run the three lenses in order. First check restriction, because it is the cheapest to fix and often the real cause — get them into the position the station demands and see whether they can actually achieve it. Then film them and look for sequencing: arms breaking early, a trunk that folds, a hip that lags. Only when both come back clean should you conclude they need to be stronger. Then factor their build honestly: a compact athlete and a tall one are not doing the same task on the sled, and coaching them to the same technical model will hold one of them back. And do all of this on a fatigued athlete, because the pattern that costs them time is the one that appears at station six, not the one they show you fresh.

glossary.def: Energy generated by the large proximal muscles that fails to reach the implement because a segment in the kinetic chain yields under load.

102.exam_focus: Given a station deficit, work through the biomechanical, physiotherapy and S&C lenses to identify the true limiter, and adapt the technical model to the athlete's somatotype.

103.title: SkiErg — sequencing, force transfer & the shoulder
103.key_concept: The SkiErg is the race's most coordinated expression of full-body force production, and it comes first, when the athlete is still relatively fresh but heart rate is climbing. That makes it a pacing trap: there is a real opportunity to establish rhythm without spiking heart rate, and a real temptation to spend too much too early. Mechanically the station rewards proximal-to-distal sequencing — the pull is initiated by the lats, trunk flexors and hip hinge, with the arms finishing rather than starting the stroke. Athletes who break at the elbows early hand the work to biceps and triceps, small muscles that fatigue fast, and efficiency collapses. Two further principles matter: the athlete should begin tall and elongated so the lats and trunk flexors work through their strongest mid-range, and the upward return should be used to preload the posterior chain rather than as rest, storing elastic energy for the next stroke. The physiotherapy lens is unusually productive here, because shoulder-girdle and thoracic restriction couple tightly and limit output — opening both often produces immediate gains at this station.
key_facts: Race position: station one, athlete relatively fresh, heart rate rising. The goal is establishing rhythm without spiking heart rate, not maximum output.
Sequence the pull proximal to distal: lats, trunk flexors and hip hinge initiate; the arms finish the stroke. Early elbow break shifts work to biceps and triceps and drops efficiency sharply.
Hinge at the hips rather than squatting each stroke — the hinge is what recruits the posterior chain and lats effectively.
Start tall and elongated. Optimal length-tension means the lats and trunk flexors generate peak force from a lengthened start through a strong mid-range.
Use cyclical elastic recoil: the upward return preloads the posterior chain rather than being passive recovery.
Chase power per stroke rather than a high stroke rate — stroke rate is the faster route to an uncontrolled heart-rate response.
Safety point one: keep neutral cervical alignment. Neck flexion under fatigue disrupts scapular mechanics and loads the upper traps.
Safety point two: keep the hip hinge dominant over lumbar flexion. Rounding the spine to reach further costs power and spinal integrity simultaneously.

Physiotherapy lens: the shoulder girdle and thorax are mechanically coupled, and protracted, tight shoulders are extremely common. Restoring shoulder and thoracic mobility can improve SkiErg output quickly.
Even modest latissimus tightness measurably reduces SkiErg performance, so mobility here is a performance intervention rather than a warm-up formality.
S&C qualities: anterior-chain endurance (lats, abdominals, hip flexors), trunk stiffness for force transfer, and power endurance.

Key exercises: neutral-grip chin-ups (replicating the SkiErg line of pull), dumbbell pullovers for the lats, medicine-ball slams for the velocity side of power, and Pallof presses, ab rollouts or long planks for trunk stiffness.
A high damper setting is a useful specific tool for developing power endurance on the machine itself.

Somatotype: compact mesomorphs produce high force per stroke and should prioritise rhythm and consistency; tall ectomorphs gain stroke length but must control larger moment arms on spine and shoulders through stiffness and sequencing.
103.training_link: Watch where the stroke starts. If the elbows break before the hips and lats have done anything, your athlete is skiing with their arms and will be cooked by station three — cue them to start tall, hinge, and let the hands arrive last. Coach power per stroke rather than a fast stroke rate, because rate is how they arrive at the sled with their heart rate already gone. Before you add strength work, check their shoulders and thoracic spine: protracted, tight shoulders are near-universal in desk-bound athletes and opening them up often buys more here than a month of pulling. Then build the specific qualities — neutral-grip chin-ups and dumbbell pullovers for the line of pull, Pallof presses for the trunk, medicine-ball slams for velocity — and use a high damper setting for power endurance.

glossary.def: Initiating the SkiErg stroke with lats, trunk and hip hinge and finishing with the arms. Reversing it hands the work to small, rapidly fatiguing muscles.

103.exam_focus: Identify a sequencing fault on the SkiErg from a description, explain why early elbow break costs efficiency, and prescribe the mobility and strength work that addresses each lens.

104.title: Sled push — horizontal vector & triple extension
104.page_refs: Performance Enhancement and Injury — Sled Push
104.key_concept: The sled push is the purest horizontal force production in the race, and its defining requirement is vector alignment: torso angle, shin angle and push direction unified into a single forward line. Any deviation bleeds force into the floor or into the athlete's own spine instead of the sled. The second principle is triple extension sequencing — hips, knees and ankles extending in coordinated order to produce continuous drive; when one joint lags, and it is usually the hips, the athlete stalls. The third is specific to friction: because the sled's resistance is frictional rather than gravitational, resistance is highest at rest, so any pause is expensive. Continuous force output beats a powerful but intermittent one, which is the mechanical justification for the familiar advice never to stop the sled. Safety rests on neutral lumbar alignment — flexion under this load raises shear on the spine and simultaneously prevents the hips from contributing — and a stable shoulder girdle with the scapulae protracted but not collapsed. The physiotherapy lens locates the most common hidden limiter in the hips: dysfunction there destabilises the lower back and prevents force transferring from the floor into the sled, often without producing any pain at all.
key_facts: Defining principle: horizontal force-vector alignment. Torso angle, shin angle and push direction must form one unified forward vector to minimise energy leakage.
Triple extension sequencing of hips, knees and ankles generates continuous drive; a lagging hip is the usual culprit when an athlete stalls under load.
The sled's resistance is frictional, not gravitational, so static friction makes restarting far harder than continuing. Any pause is disproportionately expensive.
Maintain neutral lumbar alignment. Lumbar flexion under load raises spinal shear and simultaneously reduces the hips' ability to contribute power.
Keep the shoulder girdle stable with scapulae protracted but not collapsed — this stabilises the kinetic chain and protects the anterior shoulder.
Physiotherapy lens: hip dysfunction destabilises the lumbar spine and blocks force transfer from floor to sled. Many athletes lose substantial performance here with no back pain at all.
The thoracolumbar fascia and quadratus lumborum are implicated in that lower-back instability, with the primary restriction usually sitting at the hips.
Reported ankle issues at this station — including Achilles complaints — are attributed to tightness in calf and anterior ankle structures, the same restrictions that affect running.
S&C qualities: maximal lower-body strength, horizontal power production, and bracing under load.
Bilateral maximal strength via front squats, back squats and barbell or trap-bar deadlifts, where a stable position permits maximal recruitment.
Heavy unilateral work — dumbbell or barbell Bulgarian split squats — targets the glutes and hamstrings driving hip extension.
Train the movement itself: heavy horizontal sled work is non-negotiable, because the goal is moving a sled horizontally and forcefully.
Core bracing is essential — treat the legs as an extension of the sled, so a weak trunk becomes the point where force is lost.

Somatotype: compact mesomorphs adopt a low torso angle without losing stability and must avoid over-shortening their steps; tall ectomorphs benefit from a slightly higher torso angle and should prioritise rhythm and stiffness over maximal drive per step.
104.training_link: Get behind your athlete and look for one line from the ankle through the hip to the hands — if the hips are riding high or the back is rounding, force is going into the floor rather than the sled. Cue continuous movement above all else, because friction means a stopped sled costs far more than a slow one, and athletes who rest mid-lane pay for it twice. Before adding load, check their hips: restriction there quietly caps this station and usually presents as weakness rather than tightness, often with no back pain to give it away. Then train it heavy and specific — front squats and trap-bar deadlifts for maximal strength, Bulgarians for the hip extensors, and actual heavy sled work, because nothing else transfers as directly. Keep the trunk braced; a soft core is where the leg drive disappears.

glossary.def: Unifying torso angle, shin angle and push direction into a single forward line, so generated force reaches the sled rather than the floor or the spine.

104.exam_focus: Explain why frictional resistance makes stopping costly, identify the vector and sequencing faults that stall a sled push, and justify hip assessment before prescribing strength work.

105.title: Sled pull — force redirection, traction & grip
105.page_refs: Performance Enhancement and Injury — Sled Pull
105.key_concept: The sled pull inverts the push. Rather than applying force directly into the implement, the athlete must anchor their own body and redirect force through a rope, which makes ground reaction force management the defining problem: the feet must generate backward traction while the upper body pulls horizontally. The efficient pattern initiates with the lats and trunk rather than the arms, keeping the load on large proximal musculature, and treats the arms as an extension of the rope in exactly the way a deadlift treats them as an extension of the barbell. Breaking early at the elbows both fatigues the athlete and degrades force transfer. Counterbalance positioning is the third principle — leaning back shifts the centre of mass behind the base of support, increasing traction and reducing slippage — but the lean must come without spinal flexion, since a rounded spine under tension raises shear and reduces pulling efficiency. Grip is frequently the true limiter, and the physiotherapy lens attributes much of that to inhibition from a tight shoulder girdle rather than to forearm weakness, which changes the intervention entirely.
key_facts: Defining principle: force redirection. The athlete anchors their body and redirects force through the rope rather than applying it directly to the sled.
Ground reaction force management is central — the feet create backward traction while the upper body generates horizontal pull.
Initiate with the lats and trunk, not the arms, so large proximal muscles carry the majority of the load.
Treat the arms as an extension of the rope, exactly as a deadlift treats them as an extension of the bar. Early elbow break adds fatigue and reduces force transfer.
Counterbalance positioning: leaning back moves the centre of mass behind the base of support, increasing traction and reducing foot slippage.
Avoid spinal flexion when leaning back — a rounded spine under tension increases shear force and reduces pulling efficiency.
Keep elbows tracking close to the body to protect shoulder integrity and reduce strain on the biceps tendon.
Physiotherapy lens: grip failure is frequently caused by inhibition from a tight shoulder girdle rather than by forearm weakness. Mobilising the shoulder girdle can restore grip quickly.
Lower-back complaints and heavy lactate accumulation in the legs at this station are attributed largely to hip restriction reducing blood flow and limiting clearance.
S&C qualities: posterior chain strength above all — glutes, hamstrings and lower back — developed through deadlift variations, squats and barbell hip thrusts.
Grip strength deserves specific work where it is the weakest link, since the whole station is capped by it.
Vastus medialis works hard during the backward stepping pattern; sled drags and quarter squats target it directly.
Body mass is a genuine advantage here: heavier, more muscular athletes gain traction and leverage, while lighter runners typically need dedicated strength work to compete at this station.

Somatotype: compact mesomorphs lean back aggressively without losing balance but must maximise rope length per pull; tall ectomorphs take longer rope segments but face greater spinal torque and must prioritise trunk stiffness and controlled footwork.
105.training_link: If your athlete's grip goes before their legs do, don't jump straight to farmer's holds — check their shoulder girdle first, because tightness there inhibits grip and mobilising it often restores more than forearm work will. Coach the arms as rope, not as pullers: long arms, elbows close, initiation from the lats and trunk, exactly like a deadlift set-up. Get them leaning back for traction but watch that the lean comes from the hips rather than a rounding spine. Build the posterior chain hard — deadlift variations, hip thrusts — and add sled drags and quarter squats for the vastus medialis that takes the backward stepping. And be realistic with your lighter runners: they are at a genuine mass disadvantage here, so this is a station where they need dedicated strength work rather than more conditioning.

glossary.def: Anchoring the body and channelling force through a rope rather than applying it directly to the implement — the mechanical signature of the sled pull.

glossary.def: Glutes, hamstrings and lower back — the muscle groups producing the hip extension that moves the sled.
