105.exam_focus: Contrast the mechanics of sled pull and sled push, explain grip failure as shoulder-girdle inhibition, and justify why body mass advantages differ between athlete types at this station.

106.title: Burpee broad jump — elastic power & landing control
106.page_refs: Performance Enhancement and Injury — Burpee Broad Jump
106.key_concept: The burpee broad jump combines a cyclical ground-to-standing transition with explosive horizontal jumping, and it is the station where elastic quality separates athletes most clearly. The ones who excel are not those who muscle each jump but those who load, store and release force efficiently, repetition after repetition. Each landing preloads the tendons of both the lower and upper body, and athletes with good elastic qualities convert that stored energy into longer, easier jumps while reducing muscular effort. Four mechanical principles govern it: energy recycling through elastic recoil rather than resetting each phase; hip-dominant propulsion, since horizontal displacement comes from the hips rather than the knees; landing force attenuation through coordinated hip, knee and ankle flexion; and centre-of-mass control, keeping momentum forward without wasteful vertical oscillation. The jump-length decision is a real trade-off — longer jumps demand more explosive power, drive heart rate higher, and impose greater eccentric landing loads, so an athlete choosing them must have trained the eccentric strength to absorb them.
key_facts: The station rewards elastic power — the ability to store and release force rapidly via the stretch-shortening cycle — rather than raw strength applied to each jump.
Each burpee landing preloads tendons in both lower and upper body, letting tendon do part of the work and reducing muscular effort.
Principle one, energy recycling: transition from burpee to jump using elastic recoil rather than resetting each phase.
Principle two, hip-dominant propulsion: horizontal displacement is driven from the hips, not the knees.
Principle three, landing force attenuation: absorb through coordinated hip, knee and ankle flexion. Poor landings lengthen ground contact and raise injury risk.
Principle four, centre-of-mass control: maintain forward momentum without excessive vertical oscillation, which wastes energy.
Safety: keep neutral wrist alignment during the burpee to limit compressive load on the carpal joints.
Safety: control spinal flexion descending to the floor. Collapsing into the burpee increases lumbar strain and breaks movement rhythm.
Longer jumps cover ground in fewer reps but demand more explosive power, produce a higher heart-rate spike, and impose greater eccentric landing load.
If the athlete opts for longer jumps, train eccentric strength — heavy controlled squat repetitions are the primary tool.
Elastic qualities are trainable through plyometrics: bounding, hopping and reactive drills for the lower body, plus reactive press-up variations off the deck for the upper body.
Physiotherapy lens: lower-back and shoulder pain at this station is attributed to thoracic and shoulder-girdle tightness plus tight hip flexors, causing lumbar compensation or instability.
The same restrictions are held to limit cardiovascular output at this station, so mobility work can raise a ceiling that looks like a conditioning ceiling.

Somatotype: compact mesomorphs produce powerful efficient jumps with little energy loss and must manage jump frequency; tall ectomorphs cover more distance per rep but face higher landing forces and need superior control descending into the burpee.
106.training_link: Watch whether your athlete bounces or resets. The ones who pause at the bottom, stand up, then jump are doing three separate movements and will fade badly — you want one continuous elastic action where the landing loads the next jump. Train that with actual plyometrics: bounding, hops, reactive drills, and reactive press-ups off the floor for the upper body, since the arms are storing energy too. Then have an honest conversation about jump length. Longer jumps mean fewer reps but a bigger heart-rate spike and much more eccentric load to absorb, so if they choose that route, build the eccentric strength first with heavy controlled squats. And check hip flexors and thoracic mobility — the athlete collapsing into each burpee with a sore lower back is usually tight rather than weak.

glossary.def: The ability to store energy in muscle and tendon during rapid loading and release it explosively via the stretch-shortening cycle.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 20h8l4-8 6 16 6-16 6 16 4-8h22" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A rapid eccentric-to-concentric sequence in which pre-stretch stores elastic energy that augments the following contraction.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 20h8l4-8 6 16 6-16 6 16 4-8h22" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Carrying momentum from one phase into the next rather than resetting, conserving substantial energy across repeated repetitions.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Absorbing landing forces through coordinated hip, knee and ankle flexion, reducing ground contact time and injury risk.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: Force production while a muscle lengthens — the quality required to absorb the landing of longer broad jumps without breaking down.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Up-and-down movement of the centre of mass. Excess in a horizontal jump wastes energy that should be directed forward.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 30h44M48 25l8 5-8 5" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M12 30L44 12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M12 30a18 18 0 0 1 9-15" fill="none" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.3"/></svg>

106.exam_focus: Explain the role of the stretch-shortening cycle at this station, evaluate the trade-off between long and short broad jumps, and prescribe plyometric and eccentric work accordingly.

107.title: Rowing — kinetic sequence, knee tracking & rhythm
107.key_concept: Rowing is sequenced power transfer: legs to hips to trunk to arms, in a smooth uninterrupted chain that lets the large proximal groups initiate acceleration while the distal segments refine and extend the stroke. Roughly 60% of the stroke's effort comes from the legs. Disrupting the order — most commonly by flexing the arms early — shortens the stroke, drops peak force and raises metabolic cost, because small muscles take on work meant for large ones. Stroke length is the second anchor: maximise reach at the catch without sacrificing trunk stiffness, since lumbar flexion both reduces force transmission through the posterior chain and increases spinal shear. Rhythm is the third: a consistent drive-to-recovery ratio stabilises power output, and athletes who rush the recovery raise heart rate and oxygen demand without gaining boat speed. The station's characteristic late-race fault is knee valgus during the drive, which signals glute medius under-activation or quad dominance — and in HYROX, arriving fatigued, even athletes with strong glutes will show it.
key_facts: Kinetic sequence: legs → hips → trunk → arms, smooth and uninterrupted. The legs contribute roughly 60% of stroke effort.
Early arm flexion breaks the sequence — the stroke shortens, peak force drops and metabolic cost rises as small muscles do large-muscle work.
Maximise reach at the catch without losing trunk stiffness. Excessive lumbar flexion reduces posterior-chain force transmission and increases spinal shear.
Overreaching with the shoulders destabilises the thoracic spine and delays force application.
Rhythm: a consistent drive-to-recovery ratio stabilises power. Rushing the recovery raises heart rate and oxygen demand without increasing speed.
Avoid exaggerated layback at the finish — it increases posterior shear. Keep rib cage stacked over pelvis throughout.
Knee valgus (knees caving in) during the drive indicates glute medius under-activation or quad dominance; the body collapses inward seeking stability.
In HYROX the row arrives late, so fatigue alone will produce knee valgus even in athletes with strong glutes. Cue knees tracking outward over the toes.
Glute medius remedial work: lateral band walks, clamshells and monster walks; plus hip thrusts, glute bridges and single-leg RDLs for robust glutes.
Lower-body strength and power: back squats and front squats for leg drive and upright posture, deadlifts for hip-hinge power, leg press where back squatting is contraindicated.
There is substantial crossover from sled push training, which reinforces leg drive without the technical complexity of the barbell lifts.

Posterior chain: hip thrusts, Nordic hamstring curls and back extensions transfer force through the pull. Power: power or hang cleans, kettlebell swings and box jumps for explosive triple extension off the catch.
Core requirement is anti-flexion and anti-rotation, so planks, dead bugs, Pallof presses and hanging leg raises beat classic sit-ups for this station.

Physiotherapy lens: hip restriction limits force and can tighten the rib cage, restricting expansion and capping cardiovascular output — with athletes compensating by breathing through tight neck flexors. Opening the chest and hips is presented as a fast route to more oxygen and better rowing performance.

Somatotype: compact mesomorphs generate high peak power per stroke but must avoid over-compact strokes that sacrifice mechanical advantage; tall ectomorphs gain natural stroke length but must keep the trunk rigid to avoid collapse at the catch.
107.training_link: Look at the knees on the last twenty strokes, not the first ten. Caving knees late in the piece tell you the glute medius is losing the argument with fatigue, and the fix is band walks, clamshells and monster walks alongside the bigger hip thrust and single-leg RDL work — plus a simple cue to drive the knees out. Fix the sequence too: legs first, long arms, and nothing bending at the elbow until the hips have finished, because arms-early is how athletes turn a leg exercise into an arm exercise. Coach a steady drive-to-recovery ratio rather than a frantic one, since rushing the slide buys heart rate and no speed. And if their chest and hips are locked up, mobilise before you condition — a tight rib cage caps breathing, and that shows up as a cardio problem on the rower.

glossary.def: The ordered transfer of force legs → hips → trunk → arms. Disrupting it shortens the stroke and raises metabolic cost.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="18" cy="20" r="5" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="34" cy="20" r="5" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="50" cy="20" r="5" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="66" cy="20" r="5" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M23 20h6M39 20h6M55 20h6" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.4"/></svg>

glossary.def: The front position where the stroke begins. Reach should be maximised without sacrificing trunk stiffness or spinal position.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M12 30h44M48 25l8 5-8 5" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M12 30L44 12" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M12 30a18 18 0 0 1 9-15" fill="none" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.3"/></svg>

glossary.def: The timing relationship between the working drive and the recovery slide. Consistency stabilises power; rushing recovery raises oxygen cost without gaining speed.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Inward collapse of the knees during the drive, indicating glute medius under-activation, quad dominance, or simply accumulated fatigue.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

glossary.def: The smaller lateral gluteal muscle responsible for keeping the knees tracking outward. The usual culprit when knees cave late in a race.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="28" cy="12" r="4" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M28 16v10M22 20h12M28 26l-5 10M28 26l5 10" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M52 8v26" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M48 12h8M48 30h8" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.4"/></svg>

glossary.def: Trunk training that resists flexion and rotation — planks, dead bugs, Pallof presses — rather than producing it, as sit-ups do.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

107.exam_focus: Explain the rowing kinetic sequence and the cost of early arm break, diagnose late-race knee valgus, and prescribe glute medius and anti-flexion core work.

108.title: Farmers carry — anti-lateral flexion & grip
108.page_refs: Performance Enhancement and Injury — Farmers Carry
108.key_concept: The farmers carry is a moving demonstration of anti-lateral flexion stability. The load constantly tries to pull the athlete off centre, and the obliques, quadratus lumborum and deep spinal stabilisers work isometrically to hold a stacked rib-cage-over-pelvis relationship. Any deviation costs energy and disrupts gait. Gait mechanics are the second principle, and the counter-intuitive finding is that the ideal pattern is not a walk but a compressed, stabilised march — short controlled steps that reduce oscillation of the centre of mass and minimise medial-lateral sway, since long strides amplify ground reaction variability and raise ankle instability risk. Postural control is equally important: scapular depression stops the shoulders being dragged into elevation and overloading the upper traps, while a neutral spine with slight thoracic extension lets the diaphragm and pelvic floor coordinate for bracing. Grip is the obvious limiter, but the physiotherapy lens locates much of it upstream — in a tight shoulder girdle and, specifically and unusually, in the opponens muscle of the thumb, which is often too tight to contract fully.
key_facts: Defining principle: anti-lateral flexion stability. Obliques, quadratus lumborum and deep spinal stabilisers work isometrically to resist side-to-side deviation.
Maintain a stacked rib-cage-to-pelvis relationship. Any deviation increases energy expenditure and disrupts gait mechanics.
Optimal gait is a compressed, stabilised march rather than a normal walking pattern — short, controlled steps.
Short steps reduce centre-of-mass oscillation and medial-lateral sway; long strides amplify ground reaction variability and raise ankle instability risk.
Maintain scapular depression so the load does not drag the shoulders into elevation and overload the upper trapezius.
A neutral spine with slight thoracic extension allows the diaphragm and pelvic floor to coordinate effectively for bracing.
Avoid excessive trunk lean, which increases spinal loading, and keep a stable head position to preserve vestibular alignment.
Ideally postural control should fail before grip does — if grip goes first, the station is grip-capped rather than trunk-capped.
Physiotherapy lens on lower-back instability: dysfunction or tightness of quadratus lumborum, psoas and often gluteus maximus prevents the lower back stabilising during the carry.
Physiotherapy lens on grip: tightness around the shoulder girdle and latissimus/brachialis region inhibits grip, so grip failure is frequently an upstream problem.

A specific and unusual claim from the module: the opponens pollicis of the thumb is often too tight to contract fully, and deep self-massage of the thenar eminence can noticeably improve grip. Cheap to test on an individual; treat the magnitude claim with healthy scepticism.
Practical self-treatment suggested: massage the thumb musculature, the forearms, and the teres minor region around the shoulder.
Grip strength deserves dedicated training where it is the weakest link, since the whole station is capped by it.

Somatotype: compact mesomorphs excel through a lower centre of mass and strong trunk musculature, absorbing force with less sway; tall ectomorphs face longer moment arms at the spine and usually benefit from a slightly slower cadence to control oscillation.
108.training_link: Watch what fails first. If the trunk is still stacked and the hands are giving out, this is a grip-capped station and you should train grip directly — but check the shoulder girdle and thumb before you assume it's forearm weakness, because tightness upstream inhibits grip and mobilising it is free. The thumb massage trick is odd but costs nothing to test on an individual athlete; judge it by whether their carry actually improves. Then fix the gait: most athletes try to walk normally and sway all over the lane, when what you want is a short, compressed march with the ribs stacked over the pelvis and the shoulders pulled down away from the ears. And if their lower back is wobbling, look at the hips and quadratus lumborum rather than adding more carries.

glossary.def: Isometric resistance to sideways trunk bending under an offset load — the core demand of a loaded carry.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 6v28" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M16 14h48" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="10" y="16" width="12" height="8" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.6"/><rect x="58" y="16" width="12" height="8" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: A deep lateral trunk muscle spanning the lower ribs to the pelvis, central to resisting lateral flexion and implicated in carry-related back instability.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="28" cy="12" r="4" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M28 16v10M22 20h12M28 26l-5 10M28 26l5 10" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M52 8v26" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M48 12h8M48 30h8" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.4"/></svg>

glossary.def: Positioning the rib cage directly over the pelvis so bracing is efficient and force is not lost to trunk deviation.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="14" y="10" width="52" height="22" rx="3" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M40 10v22" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M20 21h14M46 21h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: The short-step, low-oscillation gait pattern that suits a loaded carry better than a normal walking stride.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Actively holding the shoulder blades down against a load that pulls them upward, protecting the upper trapezius and shoulder integrity.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="28" cy="12" r="4" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M28 16v10M22 20h12M28 26l-5 10M28 26l5 10" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M52 8v26" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M48 12h8M48 30h8" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.4"/></svg>

glossary.def: Reduced grip output caused by restriction upstream — shoulder girdle, lat and thumb musculature — rather than by forearm weakness.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 12 C26 13 44 22 72 33" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="34" x2="72" y2="34" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1"/></svg>

108.exam_focus: Explain anti-lateral flexion demand and why a compressed march beats a walking stride, and distinguish a grip-capped from a trunk-capped farmers carry.

109.title: Sandbag lunges — overhead position & bilateral drive
109.page_refs: Performance Enhancement and Injury — Sandbag Lunges
109.key_concept: Station seven, with the end in sight and the wall balls still to come — which is exactly why the most consequential coaching point here is not the lunge itself but how much the athlete has left afterwards. It begins with a sandbag clean: grip the outside handles, the inner-outside or the closest inside handles, drive the bag to a front rack, then get it overhead onto the shoulders, where it stays for the whole 100 m. The lunge pattern has two dominant faults. The first is walking a tightrope — placing the feet in line as though on a beam — when they should stay in parallel lines at roughly squat width. The second, and more expensive, is standing up out of each lunge using only the front leg. Driving up with both feet and pushing off the back leg distributes body weight plus bag weight across two legs instead of loading one quadriceps repeatedly. Athletes who overload the front leg feel it on the final run and arrive at the wall balls with nothing, turning a manageable finish into a grim one.
key_facts: Race position: station seven of eight, with a final run and 100 wall balls still to come. Preserving the legs matters more than the split at this station.
The station opens with a sandbag clean — grip the outside, inner-outside or closest inside handles, drive to a front rack, then position overhead onto the shoulders.
Once overhead the bag stays there for the full 100 m, so the athlete must find a position they can genuinely hold, staying tight to the shoulders and keeping hold of the grip.
Fault one — the tightrope walk. Feet should stay in parallel lines at roughly squat width, moving forward on those lines, not placed one in front of the other.
Fault two, and the costly one — standing up out of the lunge with the front leg only. Keep the back leg engaged.
Correct pattern: step, drive up with both feet, then push off the back leg to finish the extension. Weight distribution should be equal across both feet on the way up.
Loading the front leg and knee repeatedly taxes one quadriceps far more than necessary, and the cost is paid on the final run and at the wall balls.
Reach full extension every repetition — that is the movement standard, whichever stepping style is used.
Pacing option when breathing is the limiter: bring the feet together at the top of each rep and take a beat before the next one.
Speed option when going for time: a step-through, or a tap-to-step-through, is typically the fastest pattern.
The overhead position couples shoulder and thoracic mobility to the station — an athlete who cannot hold the bag overhead comfortably will compensate through the lumbar spine.
Unilateral leg endurance is the underlying quality; the lunge is where a runner's lack of single-leg strength endurance becomes visible.
This station and the wall balls together determine the finish, so treat them as a coupled pair in both pacing and training.
Practise the clean and the overhead transition specifically — fumbling the set-up wastes time and energy before the lunging even starts.
109.training_link: Coach the exit from the lunge, not the entry. Most athletes step nicely and then haul themselves up on the front leg alone, and that single habit is what empties their legs before the last run — cue them to drive with both feet and push off the back leg to finish. Get their feet out of a line: parallel tracks at squat width, not a tightrope. Practise the clean and the overhead set-up separately, because fumbling that at station seven costs time and energy they don't have. Then decide the pattern in advance based on what limits them — feet together and a beat between reps if they're gasping, step-through if they're chasing time. And train it as a pair with the wall balls, because how they lunge decides what they've got left for the finish.

glossary.def: Lifting the bag from the floor to a front rack and then overhead onto the shoulders, using outside, inner-outside or closest inside handles.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="24" cy="20" r="9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M40 20h22M54 13l8 7-8 7" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/></svg>

glossary.def: Keeping the feet on two tracks at roughly squat width rather than placing them in a single line, preserving lateral stability under load.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M40 6v28" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><path d="M16 14h48" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="10" y="16" width="12" height="8" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.6"/><rect x="58" y="16" width="12" height="8" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: Standing out of each lunge using both legs and finishing with a push off the rear foot, rather than loading the front leg alone.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: A continuous lunge pattern moving directly from one repetition into the next, typically the fastest option when time rather than breathing is the limiter.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="18" cy="20" r="5" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="34" cy="20" r="5" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="50" cy="20" r="5" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.8"/><circle cx="66" cy="20" r="5" fill="none" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M23 20h6M39 20h6M55 20h6" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.4"/></svg>

glossary.def: Holding the bag on the shoulders overhead for the full distance. Requires shoulder and thoracic mobility, or the athlete compensates through the lumbar spine.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><circle cx="28" cy="12" r="4" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M28 16v10M22 20h12M28 26l-5 10M28 26l5 10" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M52 8v26" stroke="#ffb86b" stroke-width="1.8"/><path d="M48 12h8M48 30h8" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1.4"/></svg>

glossary.def: Fatigue resistance of a single leg under load — the quality the sandbag lunge exposes and the one runners most often lack.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

109.exam_focus: Identify the two dominant sandbag-lunge faults, explain why front-leg-only extension costs the final run and wall balls, and select a stepping pattern based on the athlete's limiter.

110.title: Wall balls — triple extension & posture under fatigue
110.page_refs: Performance Enhancement and Injury — Wall Balls
110.key_concept: Wall balls are a triple threat — a squat, a vertical power throw and a postural endurance test — combined into the final station, performed on completely spent legs. Mechanically it runs on triple extension of hips, knees and ankles, followed by proximal-to-distal transfer through the torso, shoulders and arms, so that the ball's trajectory is driven by leg power rather than upper-body fatigue. The arms guide the ball rather than muscling it; over-relying on the shoulders produces rapid fatigue and inconsistent trajectory. Efficient athletes use elastic recoil, storing energy in the musculotendinous structures during the descent and releasing it into the upward drive. The characteristic failure is postural, not muscular: under fatigue the upper back rounds, the elbows drop forward, and the athlete's ability to drive the ball up and receive it again collapses. That makes upper-back strength endurance and trunk rigidity the decisive trainable qualities across 100 repetitions, alongside squat endurance and shoulder endurance.
key_facts: Wall balls combine a squat, a vertical ballistic throw and a postural endurance test in one station — and it is the last one, on pre-fatigued legs.
Triple extension of hips, knees and ankles drives the throw, followed by proximal-to-distal transfer through torso, shoulders and arms.
When sequencing is efficient the ball's trajectory comes from leg power, not from the upper body.
The arms guide the ball rather than muscling it. Over-reliance on the shoulders causes rapid fatigue and inconsistent trajectory.
Descend to regulation depth while maintaining trunk stiffness and neutral lumbar alignment; lumbar flexion at the bottom compromises force transfer and loads the spine.
Use elastic recoil — store energy in the musculotendinous structures on the descent and release it into the upward drive.
Keep rib-to-pelvis alignment during the throw; over-arching increases lumbar shear. Avoid the catch pulling the athlete into thoracic flexion.
The signature fatigue failure is postural: upper back rounds, elbows drop forward, and both the drive and the catch degrade.

Upper-back strength endurance is therefore decisive — weak mid and lower traps, rhomboids or spinal erectors mean posture collapses. Train with scapular depressions, prone Y-raises and cable face pulls.
Squat endurance builds the strength reserve: barbell front squats, plus goblet squats with dumbbell or kettlebell to reinforce mechanics in both lower and upper body.
Core bracing maintains the rigid trunk that prevents forward trunk flexion — front planks with a reach and loaded front carries are the recommended tools.
Shoulder endurance via barbell or dumbbell push press, working heavier loads in a movement plane that closely replicates the wall-ball pattern.
Physiotherapy lens: shoulder-girdle mobility is presented as the single fastest route to improved wall-ball performance, with thoracic and hip mobility close behind.

Somatotype: compact mesomorphs cycle reps quickly on strong hip drive but must avoid inefficient high arcs; tall ectomorphs benefit from reduced effective throw height and longer reach but must control long levers through the squat to keep timing consistent.
110.training_link: The thing that ends wall balls is posture, not legs. Watch for the upper back rounding and the elbows dropping — once that happens the drive and the catch both fall apart, and no amount of grit fixes it mid-set. So train the upper back specifically: scapular depressions, prone Y-raises, face pulls, plus front planks with a reach for the rigid trunk. Build squat endurance with front squats and goblets, and shoulder endurance with push press, which sits in nearly the same plane as the throw. Cue the legs to launch the ball and the arms only to guide it — athletes who press with the shoulders are finished by rep forty. And check shoulder mobility first, because on this station it is the cheapest and fastest gain available.

glossary.def: Coordinated extension of hips, knees and ankles that generates the upward drive projecting the ball.

glossary.def: Energy stored in musculotendinous structures during the squat descent and released into the upward drive, reducing muscular cost per repetition.

glossary.def: The characteristic fatigue failure — upper back rounding and elbows dropping forward — that degrades both the drive and the catch.

glossary.def: Fatigue resistance of mid and lower traps, rhomboids and spinal erectors, the muscles that hold posture across 100 repetitions.

glossary.def: An overhead press initiated with a leg drive, training shoulder endurance in a plane closely replicating the wall-ball throw.

110.exam_focus: Explain why wall-ball failure is postural rather than muscular, identify the muscle groups whose endurance prevents it, and prescribe the squat, upper-back and shoulder work required.

111.title: Off-feet conditioning — the test matrix
111.key_concept: Off-feet conditioning is only useful if you know what it is substituting for, and that requires measuring the athlete on both sides of the comparison. A test matrix is a small, repeatable battery that profiles aerobic capacity across each modality the athlete might use — running, bike, SkiErg, rower — so their off-feet work can be prescribed at an equivalent physiological cost rather than guessed at. The core insight is that fitness is only partly transferable between modalities: an athlete's threshold on the bike may sit at a very different absolute output from their running threshold, and mode-specific economy and local muscular endurance differ substantially. Without a matrix you end up prescribing 60 minutes on the bike as though it equals a 60-minute run, which it usually does not. Running the same tests every 4-8 weeks also turns the matrix into a monitoring tool, showing whether off-feet volume is maintaining the aerobic base or quietly allowing it to erode. Anchor every modality to a common internal-load currency — heart rate, RPE and, where available, lactate — so the numbers can be compared at all.
key_facts: Purpose of a test matrix: profile the athlete in every modality they will train in, so off-feet work can be prescribed at equivalent physiological cost rather than by assumed equivalence.

Transfer between modalities is partial. Central adaptations (cardiac output, plasma volume) transfer well; peripheral and mode-specific adaptations (local muscular endurance, economy, motor pattern) transfer poorly.
Minimum viable matrix: a running threshold or time-trial test, a bike test, a SkiErg test and a rowing test — each with heart rate and RPE recorded.
Anchor to internal load, not external: HR, RPE and where available lactate are what make outputs from different machines comparable.
Record both the output (pace, watts, split, distance) and the internal cost (HR, RPE) so you can express any modality as a percentage of that athlete's own maximum in that modality.
Practical test options: a 5 km or 30-minute run test; a 20-minute or ramp bike test; 1000 m SkiErg; 1000 m or 2000 m row.
Standardise the conditions — same damper setting, same machine where possible, similar time of day, similar prior-day load — or the matrix compares noise.
Re-test every 4-8 weeks. The matrix is a monitoring tool as much as a prescription tool.

The matrix exposes profile asymmetry: a runner with a weak SkiErg or row is common, and it tells you which off-feet modality is a genuine substitute versus which is itself a limiter needing development.
Heart rate at a fixed submaximal output, tracked over time in each modality, is a low-cost durability and fitness marker.
Beware conflating a station test with a conditioning test: a 1000 m row is both a race-station benchmark and an aerobic probe, and the two purposes need different pacing instructions.
Where lactate testing is available it sharpens threshold anchoring considerably, but a well-standardised HR-and-RPE matrix is sufficient for most coaching decisions.
The matrix is not a fitness test for its own sake — its output should be a table you actually consult when writing the week.
111.training_link: Before you start swapping runs for bike sessions, spend a week testing. Get a running threshold number, a bike number, a 1000 m Ski and a 1000 m row, and write down heart rate and RPE alongside every result — those are the only things that let you compare a watt to a pace. What usually falls out is an asymmetry: the runner whose Ski is dreadful, or the strong rower whose bike is untrained. That tells you which modality is a genuine substitute for running volume and which is actually a weakness you should be training on its own terms. Keep the conditions identical each time, re-test every month or two, and actually put the table somewhere you'll look at it when you write the week — an unused matrix is just a hard training session.

glossary.def: A small repeatable battery profiling an athlete across every training modality, so work in one can be prescribed at equivalent physiological cost to another.

glossary.def: The physiological cost of a session — heart rate, RPE, lactate — as opposed to external output such as pace or watts. The common currency across modalities.

glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M8 26 C20 26 22 32 32 32 C46 32 46 12 66 12" fill="none" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="2"/><line x1="8" y1="24" x2="72" y2="24" stroke="#3a4a5e" stroke-width="1" stroke-dasharray="3 2"/></svg>

glossary.def: A marked gap between an athlete's capacity in different modalities, revealing which off-feet options are true substitutes and which are limiters.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Holding test conditions — machine, damper, time of day, prior load — constant so repeated measurements reflect fitness change rather than noise.
glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

111.exam_focus: Design a minimum off-feet test matrix, justify anchoring to internal load, and explain why modality transfer is only partial.

112.title: Off-feet conditioning — the decision tree
112.key_concept: A decision tree turns the question 'should this session be off-feet?' into a repeatable rule rather than a mood. The first branch is always tissue status: if running is contraindicated or provoking symptoms, the session goes off-feet regardless of what the plan said. The second branch is the session's purpose — if the aim is aerobic development or recovery, the modality is largely interchangeable and off-feet is a legitimate choice; if the aim is running-specific economy, compromised-running practice, or bone and tendon loading, then off-feet cannot substitute and the session should be modified rather than swapped. The third branch is cumulative impact load: an athlete already near their tolerated running volume gains aerobic stimulus more cheaply off-feet. The fourth is context — travel, weather, heat, time constraints and equipment access. Used consistently the tree stops two opposite errors: the athlete who bikes away from every niggle and never develops running durability, and the coach who insists on running through symptoms because the plan said run.
key_facts: Branch 1 — tissue status. Pain, an irritable tendon, a bone stress concern or a medical restriction sends the session off-feet immediately, whatever the plan said.
Branch 2 — session purpose. Aerobic development and active recovery transfer well off-feet; running economy, compromised-running practice and bone/tendon loading do not.
If the purpose cannot be met off-feet, modify the running session (shorter, slower, softer surface) rather than substituting a different modality.
Branch 3 — accumulated impact load. An athlete near their tolerated weekly running volume can add aerobic stimulus more cheaply off-feet than by adding mileage.
Branch 4 — context. Travel, extreme heat, air quality, darkness, time available and equipment access are legitimate inputs, not excuses.
Match intensity by internal load using the test matrix, not by duration. Sixty minutes of easy cycling is not sixty minutes of easy running.
Bike is generally the lowest-impact, highest-volume substitute; rowing and SkiErg add upper-body and trunk demand that doubles as race-station practice.
Because bike and row are seated and non-weight-bearing, they do not maintain bone loading, tendon stiffness or running-specific leg stiffness — a real cost of over-substituting.
Two failure modes the tree prevents: the athlete who bikes away from every niggle and never builds running durability, and the coach who runs an athlete through symptoms because the plan said run.
For HYROX specifically, off-feet work is doubly valuable because SkiErg, row and bike are either race stations or close analogues — the substitution can be race-specific rather than merely aerobic.
Set a standing rule for how much of weekly aerobic volume may be off-feet, then vary it deliberately by phase rather than session by session.
In a heavy race block or when returning from injury, the off-feet share rises; in a running-development block it falls.
Document the decision. If you cannot say which branch sent the session off-feet, you made a mood-based call, not a coaching one.
112.training_link: Write the tree down once and then follow it, because the whole value is that it removes the argument. Anything sore or symptomatic goes off-feet immediately — that branch is not negotiable. Then ask what the session was actually for: if it was aerobic volume or recovery, the bike or rower is fine; if it was economy, compromised running, or getting load through bone and tendon, off-feet won't do it, so shrink the run rather than replace it. Match the intensity using your matrix numbers rather than the clock. And set a ceiling on how much of the week can be off-feet — otherwise the athlete drifts into a very fit cyclist who falls apart on the eight runs.

glossary.def: An ordered set of branching rules converting a recurring coaching question into a repeatable decision rather than an ad hoc judgement.

glossary.def: The cumulative weight-bearing stress of running. The variable off-feet conditioning is usually chosen to reduce.

glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><path d="M10 20h20M30 20l14-9M30 20l14 9" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="2"/><circle cx="48" cy="11" r="3" fill="#67e8b0"/><circle cx="48" cy="29" r="3" fill="#ffb86b"/></svg>

glossary.def: Choosing an off-feet modality that is itself a race station — SkiErg or row — so the session serves conditioning and skill simultaneously.

112.exam_focus: Apply the decision tree to a scenario, state which session purposes cannot be met off-feet, and explain the cost of over-substituting non-weight-bearing work.

113.title: The 5 Level System
113.key_concept: The 5 Level System is Module 4's framework for placing an athlete on a competence ladder and coaching them at the rung they are actually on. Its logic is the same one that governs any staged progression: a level is defined by demonstrated capability, not by ambition or training history, and an athlete only advances when the criteria of their current level are met consistently under fatigue — not once, fresh, on a good day. The coaching payoff is that it prevents the most common programming error in HYROX, which is prescribing competitive-level intensity and complexity to an athlete who has not yet secured movement competence or an aerobic base. It also gives the coach a shared language with the athlete for why a session is being held back. Note honestly: the specific level definitions and advancement criteria in the official course are delivered as audio and were not verifiable when these notes were written, so the ladder below is a reconstruction from the module's surrounding material and general staged-development practice — treat the structure as sound and the exact wording as unverified.
key_facts: A level describes demonstrated current capability, not training age, ambition, or what the athlete used to be able to do.
Advancement requires meeting the current level's criteria consistently and under fatigue, not once in a fresh state.
Reconstructed ladder — Level 1: movement competence. Can the athlete perform each pattern safely with no load and no clock?
Level 2: loaded competence. Can they hold that technical standard under race-representative load for the required volume?
Level 3: conditioned competence. Can they hold the standard under fatigue, which is the state the race actually imposes?
Level 4: race execution. Can they pace, transition and self-regulate across a full or near-full race distance?
Level 5: competitive optimisation. Marginal gains, individualised pacing models, peaking — appropriate only once levels 1-4 are secure.
The dominant error the system prevents: prescribing level 4-5 intensity and complexity to a level 1-2 athlete, which produces injury and technical breakdown rather than fitness.
Levels are movement-specific as well as global — an athlete can be level 4 on the row and level 1 on the sandbag lunge, and should be coached accordingly at each station.
Regression is normal and expected after injury, illness or a long lay-off. Re-assess rather than resuming at the previous level.
The system gives coach and athlete shared language for holding a session back, which makes the decision feel principled rather than arbitrary.
Assess at the level the race demands: judge competence under fatigue, because a standard that only holds when fresh will not hold at station six.

Unverified: the official course delivers this section as audio and the precise level names, criteria and thresholds could not be checked against the source. Confirm the exact definitions against the module before quoting them in an assessment.
113.training_link: Be honest about which rung your athlete is actually on, and coach that rung rather than the one they want to be on. The classic failure is a keen beginner given a competitive athlete's session — heavy sled, high volume, tight clock — when they can't yet hold a lunge pattern under load. Assess each station separately, because almost everyone is several levels apart across the eight, and coach each at its own level. Test competence when they're tired rather than fresh, since fresh competence tells you nothing about station six. And when someone comes back from injury or a long break, re-assess rather than picking up where they left off — regression is normal and pretending otherwise is how people get hurt twice.

glossary.def: Module 4's staged competence framework placing an athlete on a ladder from movement competence through to competitive optimisation, coached at their demonstrated level.

114.title: Safety, efficacy & efficiency
114.page_refs: HYROX Performance Pillars — Safety, Efficacy, Efficiency
114.key_concept: Safety, efficacy and efficiency is Module 4's ordering principle for judging any movement, and the order is not arbitrary — it is a hierarchy. Safety comes first: can the athlete perform this without unacceptable injury risk, now, in their current state? Efficacy comes second: does the movement actually achieve its purpose — for a race station, does it meet the movement standard and count as a rep? Efficiency comes last: is it being done at the lowest energetic cost? The hierarchy matters because coaches routinely invert it, chasing efficiency cues on an athlete who cannot yet hit depth on a wall ball, or who is loading a spine they cannot brace. A rep that is not safe is not coachable; a rep that is safe but does not meet standard is a no-rep and therefore worthless however efficient it looks; only once both hold does economy become the productive thing to work on. The framework also connects back to mobility and flexibility, which serve all three: range protects the athlete in compromised positions, allows them to hit the required standards, and lets them move smoothly.
key_facts: The three criteria in strict order: safety, then efficacy, then efficiency. The order is a hierarchy, not a list.
Safety: can the athlete perform the movement without unacceptable injury risk in their current state, under the load and fatigue prescribed?
Efficacy: does the movement achieve its purpose — for a race station, does it meet the movement standard and count?
Efficiency: is it performed at the lowest energetic cost, so the athlete arrives at the next station with more left?
The common coaching inversion is chasing efficiency cues on an athlete who cannot yet meet the standard, or who is loading a structure they cannot control.
A no-rep is worthless however elegant it is — wall-ball depth and target height, and burpee broad jump stance, are the classic efficacy failures.
Judging standards matters competitively: penalties for staggered stance on the burpee broad jump and no-reps for missed wall-ball depth decide races at the sharp end.
Safety and efficacy both degrade under fatigue, which is why the criteria must be judged late in a session rather than fresh.
Mobility and flexibility serve all three: range protects the athlete in compromised positions, permits the required standards to be hit, and enables smooth movement.
Strength contributes to safety directly — it supports joints, builds tendon and ligament resilience, and preserves form when the athlete is fatigued or compromised.
Coordination sits mostly under efficiency but crosses into efficacy, because a loss of precision at speed produces no-reps and penalties.
Practical use: when a movement looks wrong, diagnose in order — is it unsafe, is it not meeting standard, or is it merely wasteful — and coach the first one that fails.
The framework applies to programming as well as technique: a session can be unsafe, ineffective for its stated purpose, or simply an expensive way to get a cheap adaptation.
114.training_link: When something looks wrong, work down the list in order rather than saying the first thing you notice. Is it dangerous? Fix that and nothing else today. Is it safe but not meeting the standard — not hitting depth, not reaching extension, staggered on the burpee? Then that's the whole session, because a no-rep is worth nothing no matter how pretty it is. Only when both of those hold should you start refining economy. Judge all of it on a tired athlete, since safety and efficacy are exactly what fatigue erodes. And remember mobility buys you all three at once — it protects them in bad positions, it's often what's stopping them hitting depth, and it makes the movement cheaper.

glossary.def: Module 4's ordered hierarchy for judging any movement: is it safe, does it achieve its purpose, and only then is it economical.

glossary.svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 80 40" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><rect x="16" y="8" width="34" height="26" rx="2" fill="none" stroke="#5ec8ff" stroke-width="1.6"/><path d="M22 16h22M22 22h22M22 28h14" stroke="#67e8b0" stroke-width="1.6"/></svg>

glossary.def: A body position adopted under fatigue or load in which control is reduced and injury risk rises. Mobility and strength are the buffers.
